[Theorema 2 ({\Cref{criterion-decomp-log}}) of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(X\) be a smooth \(k\)-variety of dimension \(d\), and let \(D\)
be a simple normal crossings divisor on \(X\).  Then the following
conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The pair \((X,D)\) is log HT-split.
\item There is an isomorphism
\begin{equation}
F_{*}\Omega_{X/k}^{\bullet}(\log D)
\simeq
\bigoplus_{i=0}^{d}
\Omega_{X/k}^i(\log D)[-i]
\end{equation}
in \(\mcalD_{\qcoh}(X)\).
\end{enumerate}
If \(X\) is projective, these equivalent conditions imply logarithmic
Akizuki--Nakano vanishing and the \(E_1\)-degeneration of the
logarithmic Hodge-to-de Rham spectral sequence (\Cref{vanishing}). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: {\Cref{criterion-decomp-log}}

body:
Write f = u + iv with real u, v. If f is complex-differentiable at z = x + iy then the partial derivatives satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x there, and f'(z) = u_x + i v_x. Conversely, if u, v have continuous first partials satisfying the Cauchy-Riemann equations on an open set, then f is holomorphic there. Consequently u and v are harmonic (Laplace equation), and are harmonic conjugates.
f = u + iv on an open set; sufficiency needs continuous partials

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The chi law of parameter $n\in\mathbb N$, appearing as
$$\chi_n=law\left(\sqrt{f_1^2+\ldots+f_n^2}\right)$$
with $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ being independent, each following $g_1$, has density given by
$$\chi_n=\frac{x^{n-1}e^{-x^2/2}}{2^{n/2-1}\Gamma(n/2)}\,dx$$
and its moments are given by the following formula, valid for any $k\in\mathbb N$,
$$M_k=2^{k/2}\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{n+k}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)}$$
with $\Gamma$ being as usual the gamma function.

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2606.17381, 'Large deviation principle for friendship-biases\\ in Galton--Watson trees'] {\bf [Properties of the rate function]}

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\rm (a)}] On $\cD$, $(x,s) \mapsto J(x,s)$ is marginally convex and achieves its unique zero at $(x^*,s^*)$ given by
\[
(x^*,s^*) = \big(\|G(\nu^*)\|_1,G(\nu^*)/\|G(\nu^*)\|_1\big)
\] 
with $\nu^* = (\zeta^{\otimes 2})^{\otimes 3}$, which equals
\[
x^* = \frac{1}{1-p}, \qquad s^* = \big((1-p)-(1-p)^4,\, p^3 + (1-p)^4,\, p-p^3\big).          
\]
\item[{\rm (b)}] 
For every $(x,s) \in \mathrm{int}(\cD)$, the infimum defining $J(x,s)$ is achieved and equals
\[
J(x,s) = -\lambda(x,s) - x \sum_{\chi \in S} s^\chi \lambda^\chi (x,s), 
\]
where $\lambda(x,s)$ and $\lambda^\chi(x,s)$, $\chi \in S$, are Lagrangian multipliers that uniquely solve four equations involving rational functions whose coefficients depend on $(x,s)$ and $p$ (see Section \ref{sec:ProofLDP2}).
\item[{\rm (c)}]
On $\mathrm{int}(\cD)$, $(x,s) \mapsto J(x,s)$ is analytic and marginally strictly convex.
\item[{\rm(d)}] 
$\mathrm{int}(\cD) = \big\{(x,s)\in(0,\infty)\times\mathcal S_2\colon\, 1 < x < \infty,\,s^- < 1/x < s^-+s^0 < 1 < 3s^-+s^0\big\}$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 4 of arXiv:2606.17381

[Definition 30 of arXiv:2608.30570, '2608.30570'] If a smooth curve $\sigma_i: [t_i^-, t_i^+]\to \mathcal{A}_k$ satisfies
 \begin{align*}
 \frac{d f\circ\sigma_i}{dt}(t)<0, \forall t\in (t_i^{-} ,t_i^+),
 \end{align*}
 we call $\sigma_i$ a {\bf negative gradient curve of $f$} in $\mathcal{A}_k$.

 If $\{\sigma_i\}_{i=1}^{l}$ are finite many  negative gradient curves of $f$ in $\mathcal{A}_k$ such that for each $1\le i<l$,  there exists a curve
 $\eta_i:[\tau_i^{-},\tau_i^+]\to \mathcal{A}_k$ satisfying
 \begin{align}
f(\eta_i(\tau))&\ge f(\sigma_{i}(t_i^+)), \forall \tau\in [\tau_i^-,\tau_i^+],\\
 \eta_i(\tau_i^-)=\sigma_i(t_i^+) \text{ for } 1\le i\le l, \quad &\text{ and } \quad \eta_i(\tau_i^+)=\sigma_{i+1}(t_{i+1}^-), \text{ for } 1\le i<l.
 \end{align}
 then we call $\sigma=\cup_{i=1}^l (\sigma_i\cup \eta_i)$ a {\bf pseudo negative gradient curve of $f$} in $\mathcal{A}_k$.    Note that we can choose new parametrization of the curves such that $t_{i+1}^{-}=\tau_{i}^+$ and $t_i^+=\tau_i^-$ such that $\sigma$ is a continuous curve defined on an interval. In the following, we always assume this.

 We say that a pseudo negative gradient curve $\sigma=\cup_{i=1}^{l} \sigma_i\cup \eta_i$ {\bf joins $x$ and $y$} if $\sigma_1(t_1^-)=x$ and $\eta_l(\tau_l^+)=y$.

Moreover, we introduce the notation $c(\sigma)=\cup_{i=1}^l\{\sigma_i(t_i^-),\sigma_i(t_i^+)\}$ and call it the {\bf joint points} of $\sigma$.
title: Definition 30 of arXiv:2608.30570

[Prop GTASEP of arXiv:2510.23430, 'On the Martin boundary for discrete TASEP'] Let $\lambda,\mu$ be partitions such that $l(\mu)\leq t$, and $n\in\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}$. Then
$$
\mathbb P(Y(t+n)=\lambda+\delta\mid Y(t)=\mu+\delta)=p^{|\lambda|-|\mu|}(1-p)^nG^{(0,-p)}_{\lambda/\mu}(1^n).
$$
In particular, $\mathbb P(Y(n)=\lambda+\delta)=p^{|\lambda|}(1-p)^nG^{(0,-p)}_{\lambda}(1^n)$.

	\[
	\dcx\circ h \sqleq h\circ \dc.
	\]

	The category of conic frames and morphisms is denoted~$\dcFrm$.

[Lemma omega-fewer-quantifiers of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $X\in\cat{$\bm G$-$\textbf{\textup{L}}$-Sp}$ be levelwise closed, i.e. for all inner product spaces $V\in \textbf{\textup{O}}$, $X(V)$ is a closed orthogonal $G$-space. Then $X$ is a $G$-global $\Omega$-spectrum if and only if $\tilde\sigma({\mathcal{U}}_H)^\varphi\colon X(V)({\mathcal{U}}_H)^\varphi\to(\Omega^WX(V\oplus W)(\mathcal U_H))^\varphi$ is a weak homotopy equivalence for every homomorphism of compact Lie groups $\varphi\colon H\to G$, some (hence any) complete $H$-universe ${\mathcal{U}}_H$, and all $H$-representations $V,W$.
    \begin{proof}
        The assumptions guarantee that both $X(V)$ and $\Omega^WX(V\oplus W)$ are closed orthogonal $(G\times K)$-spaces for all $K$-representations $V,W$. Thus, Lemma~(lemma:we-between-closed of the paper) shows that $X$ is a $G$-global $\Omega$-spectrum if and only if \[\tilde\sigma({\mathcal{U}}_H)\colon X(V)({\mathcal{U}}_H)\to\Omega^WX(V\oplus W)({\mathcal{U}}_H)\]
        is a $\mathcal G_{H,K\times G}$-equivariant weak equivalence for all compact Lie groups $H,K$ and all $K$-representations $V,W$. As ${\mathcal{U}}_H$ is also a complete universe for every closed subgroup of $H$ (Remark~(rk:universe-subgroup of the paper)), this is equivalent via replacing $H$ by its subgroups to $\tilde\sigma({\mathcal{U}}_H)$ inducing a weak homotopy equivalence on $(\psi,\varphi)$-fixed points for all compact Lie groups $H$ and $K$, $K$-representations $V$ and $W$, and homomorphisms $\psi\colon H\to K$ and $\varphi\colon H\to G$. Restricting $V$ and $W$ to $H$-representations along $\psi$, this simplifies to the condition from the statement of the lemma, finishing the proof.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma omega-fewer-quantifiers of arXiv:2608.28504

[Proposition prop:eigenvec of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] Define the $\chi^2$-based retention proxy
\[
  \tilde r(x)
  :=\frac{\chi^2(P(x,\cdot)\|\pi)}{\log(1/\pi(x))}
  =\frac{\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2\,\phi_i(x)^2}{\log(1/\pi(x))}.
\]
Then $r(x)\le\tilde r(x)$ pointwise, $\bar r_\pi\le\mathbb{E}_\pi[\tilde r]$,
and $M\le\max_x\tilde r(x)$.

[Definition 13 of arXiv:2608.29157, 'Dilator-based analysis of $\KP$'] A \emph{$\rmbeta$-language} is a many-sorted first-order language $\calL$ with a distinguished type $\ord$ together with a distinguished binary predicate $\le_\ord$, and the only terms in $\calL$ of type $\ord$ are variables. In particular, we do not allow constant symbols of type $\ord$ or function symbols of value $\ord$. A \emph{$\rmbeta$-theory} is a theory in some $\rmbeta$-language.
    
    A structure $M$ in a $\rmbeta$-language $\calL$ is a \emph{pre-$\rmbeta$-model} if the \emph{ordinal part} $(\ord^M,\le_\ord^M)$ of $M$ is a linear order. If the ordinal part of $M$ is a well-order, we call $M$ a \emph{$\rmbeta$-model}.
    We also define the following semantic implication notions: For a $\rmbeta$-language $\calL$ and a $\rmbeta$-theory $T$ in $\calL$, and a formula $\phi$ in $\calL$,
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $T\vDash_{\pre\rmbeta} \phi$ if every pre-$\rmbeta$-model of $T$ satisfies the universal closure of $\phi$. We call $\phi$ is \emph{pre-$\rmbeta$-valid in $T$}.
        \item $T\vDash_{\rmbeta} \phi$ if every $\rmbeta$-model of $T$ satisfies the universal closure of $\phi$. We call $\phi$ is \emph{$\rmbeta$-valid in $T$}.
    \end{enumerate}
    We omit $T$ in the previous notations when $T=\varnothing$.

[Lemma lemma tauBM of arXiv:2412.08932, 'Gaussian heat kernel asymptotics for conditioned random walks'] For any $x \geqslant 0$, $n\geqslant 1$ and $0 \leqslant a < b \leqslant \infty$, it holds  
\begin{align*}
\bb P \left( x +  \sigma B_{n} \in \left[a, b\right],  \tau_{x}^{\sigma B}>n \right) 
=  \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{ n} } \int_{a}^{b}  \psi \left( \frac{x}{\sigma \sqrt{n}},\frac{y}{\sigma \sqrt{n}} \right) dy. 
\end{align*}
In particular, by taking $a = 0$ and $b = \infty$, for any $x \geqslant 0$ and $n\geqslant 1$, 
\begin{align*}
\bb P \left( \tau_{x}^{\sigma B} > n \right) 
= 2 \Phi \left( \frac{x}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \right)-1 
= \frac{2}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi n} } \int_{0}^x  e^{ - \frac{s^{2}}{2 \sigma^2 n} } ds.   
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lemma tauBM of arXiv:2412.08932

A real $n \times n$ matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ is nonnegative ($A \ge 0$) if all entries are $\ge 0$, and positive ($A > 0$) if all entries are $> 0$. Associate to $A \ge 0$ the directed graph $G(A)$ on vertices $1, \dots, n$ with an edge $i \to j$ iff $a_{ij} > 0$; then $(A^m)_{ij} > 0$ iff there is a walk of length $m$ from $i$ to $j$. $A$ is irreducible if $G(A)$ is strongly connected (every vertex reaches every other), equivalently if there is no permutation matrix $P$ with $P A P^{\mathsf T} = \begin{pmatrix} B & C \\ 0 & D\end{pmatrix}$ with $B, D$ square nonempty blocks, equivalently (for $n \ge 2$) if $(I + A)^{n-1} > 0$; a $1 \times 1$ matrix is irreducible by convention (some authors exclude the zero $1\times1$ matrix). The period (index of imprimitivity) $h$ of an irreducible $A$ is the greatest common divisor of the lengths of all closed walks in $G(A)$; it does not depend on the vertex, and $h = 1$ iff $A$ is aperiodic. $A$ is primitive if $A \ge 0$ and $A^m > 0$ for some $m \ge 1$; for nonnegative matrices, primitive $\iff$ irreducible and aperiodic, and then $A^m > 0$ for all $m \ge (n-1)^2 + 1$ (Wielandt's bound). Every positive matrix is primitive. Warnings: irreducible does not imply primitive (the cyclic permutation matrix of an $n$-cycle is irreducible with period $n$); a matrix with a positive diagonal entry that is irreducible is automatically primitive; irreducibility is a property of the zero pattern only, not of the magnitudes; a matrix with some negative entries is outside this theory entirely.
A is a square real matrix with nonnegative entries
title: Nonnegative, irreducible, primitive matrices; period

[Lemma 129 (Differential operator pointwise comparison estimates; \cite{abbrescia2022emergence}*{Lemma 14.6}) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] Let $\varphi$ be a scalar function on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$. 
	Then the following pointwise estimates hold:
	\begin{subequations}
		\begin{align}
			|\angrmD \varphi|_{\gtorus}^2 
			& = \left\lbrace
			1 + \mathcal{O}_{\mydiam}(\mathring{\upalpha}^{1/2}) 
			\right\rbrace
			\sum_{A = 2}^3 |\Yvf{A} \varphi|^2, 
			 
			\\
			\left|\angD^2 \varphi\right|_{\gtorus}^2 
			& \leq 
			\left\{1 + C_{\mydiam} \mathring{\upalpha}^{1/2}\right\} 
			\sum_{A = 2}^3 |\angrmD \Yvf{A} \varphi|_{\gtorus}^2 
			+ 
			C \auxbootsmall |\angrmD \varphi|_{\gtorus}^2,  \\
			|\angLap \varphi|^2

			\sum_{A = 2}^3 |\angrmD \Yvf{A} \varphi|_{\gtorus}^2 
			+ 
			C \auxbootsmall |\angrmD \varphi|_{\gtorus}^2. 
			 
		\end{align}
	\end{subequations} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Theorem (campaign status: proved): No boundary-preserving admissible sign basis repairs the NAE-star absorption failure. Whatever the basis takes as its single private member (q, or one Y_j, up to sign), two of the three forms - call them Y_i, Y_k - remain, and for EVERY signed selector choice their residuals are linearly independent. Their span therefore has dimension at least 2 while its private projection has dimension at most 1, so the span contains a nonzero pure-boundary vector. With R_< = 0, connector absorption is impossible. Notes: Proof of the independence: the residual Y_i -/+ g retains at least one of the two boundary coordinates x_i, z_i private to that row; a residual from Y_k meets at most one of x_i, z_i, since a basis selector has at most one such boundary coordinate and the sole nonboundary basis form is supported on the j-th pair; if the two were proportional, the first would have to cancel one of its own pair coordinates by selecting it and would then have no support on x_k, z_k, while the second necessarily retains one - contradiction. Quantifier is over ALL boundary-preserving admissible sign bases AND all signed selector choices. R_< = 0 is essential: the leak is fatal only when ancestors have paid nothing.

[Definition 1 (Channel and index convention) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Set
\begin{equation}
  \mathfrak C:=\{\W,\K\},
  \qquad \W^\perp:=\K,
  \qquad \K^\perp:=\W.
\end{equation}
The letters $a,b,c$ are reserved for elements of $\mathfrak C$; the symbols
$\W$ and $\K$ are the two values of a channel index.  Repeated channel
indices are not summed unless a summation sign is displayed, and
$\delta_{ab}$ denotes the Kronecker symbol on $\mathfrak C$.

The four index triples used below are
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \mathfrak L_{\mathrm{diag}}
 &:=\{(\W;\K,\K),(\K;\W,\W)\},\\
 \mathfrak L_{\mathrm{off}}
 &:=\{(\W;\W,\K),(\K;\K,\W)\},\\
 \mathfrak L
 &:=\mathfrak L_{\mathrm{diag}}\,\dot\cup\,
    \mathfrak L_{\mathrm{off}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For a label $(a;b,c)\in\mathfrak L$, the first entry $a$ is the Duhamel
channel, $b$ is the color of the stochastic factor in the inner
low--high paraproduct, and $c$ is the color of the stochastic factor in the
outer resonant product.  Thus $b=c$ on $\mathfrak L_{\mathrm{diag}}$, whereas
$b\ne c$ on $\mathfrak L_{\mathrm{off}}$.

The variables $q,\ell,r,n$ denote spatial frequencies and
$N,Q,R,L,M$ denote dyadic scales.  Within the abstract Gaussian operator argument, $\mu,\nu$ index orthonormal coordinates and
$\varkappa\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ indexes the four flattenings.
title: Channel and index convention

[Lemma of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_l \in \mathbb{R}$, and $l$ is fixed. Then the Harish-Chandra integral satisfies, for every fixed $r \in \mathbb{N}$,
  \[ \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \log \text{} H \text{} C (x_1, \ldots, x_r,
     0^{N - r} ; N \theta_1, \ldots, N \theta_l, 0^{N - l}) = \sum_{i = 1}^r
     \sum_{j = 1}^l \log (1 - \theta_j x_i)^{- 1}, \]
  where the above convergence is uniform in a neighborhood of $0^r$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2608.26974, 'Why not to use the Gaussian kernel'] Consider a stationary strictly positive-definite kernel $k(x, y) = \Phi(x - y)$ for a continuous and integrable $\Phi \colon \R^d \to \R$.
  Suppose that there are $C \geq 0$ and $a > 0$ such that $(\mathcal{F}\Phi)(\omega) \leq C \exp(-a \lVert \omega \rVert_2)$ for all $\omega \in \R^d$.
  Let $\sigma \geq 0$.
  If $X_n = \{x_1, \ldots, x_n \}$ for a sequence $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^\infty \subset \R^d$ of pairwise distinct points whose closure has non-empty interior, then
  \begin{equation*}
     \sup_{x \in K} \V_\sigma(x \mid \mathcal{D}_n) \to 0 \quad \text{ as } \quad n \to \infty \quad \text{ for any compact } \quad K \subset \R^d.
  \end{equation*}
title: Theorem 9 of arXiv:2608.26974

[Corollary cor:product-compact-box of arXiv:2606.21006, 'Law of the Iterated Logarithm for Weighted Sums of Functionals of Long-Memory Gaussian Seq'] For \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in\mathbb R^m\), define
\[
\Psi_n(x):=\prod_{j=1}^m \psi_n(x_j),
\qquad
\Psi(x):=c_f^{m/2}\prod_{j=1}^m |x_j|^{(\alpha-1)/2}.
\]
Let
\(
D_R:=[-R,R]^m,
\quad
K_{\varepsilon,R}:=\{x\in D_R:\min_{1\le j\le m}|x_j|\ge\varepsilon\}.
\)
Then for every \(R>0\), every \(\varepsilon\in(0,R)\), and every \(\eta\in(0,\alpha)\),

\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)]
\(
\sup_{x\in K_{\varepsilon,R}}
|\Psi_n(x)-\Psi(x)|
\longrightarrow0;
\)

\item[(b)] for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\(
|\Psi_n(x)|^2
\le
C_{R,\eta}\prod_{j=1}^m |x_j|^{\alpha-1-\eta},
\qquad
x\in D_R;
\)

\item[(c)]
\(
\|\Psi_n-\Psi\|_{L^2(D_R)}
\longrightarrow0.
\)
\end{itemize}

[Proposition prop: rad_blow of arXiv:2412.07690, 'A law of large numbers concerning the distribution of critical points of random Fourier se'] Fix a box $B\subset \mathscr{V}$ and $r<\dist(B,\mathscr{V})$.  Denote by $S=S(r,B)$ the compact set set
\[
S=\big\{\, v\in \mathscr{V};\;\;\dist(v,B)\leq r\,\,\big\}.
\]
Suppose that $F\,\big\vert_B$ is $C^2$,  $2$-ample and $J_1$-ample, i.e., for any ${\boldsymbol{v}}\in B$ the Gaussian vector $\big(\, F(v),F'(v)\,\big)$   is nondegenerate.  Define 
\[
w_F:B^2_*\to {\mathbb R}, \,\, w_F({\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{y}})=|{\boldsymbol{x}}-{\boldsymbol{y}}|^{m-2}\rho_F^{(2)}({\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{y}}).
\]
There exists a constant $C(m, \vol[B], r)>0$,  that depends only on $m$, $\vol[B]$  and $r$ such that
\begin{equation}
\sup_{{\boldsymbol{p}}\in B^2_*}|{w}_F({\boldsymbol{p}})\,\big\vert \leq  C(m,\vol[B], r)\Vert \EuScript{K}_F\Vert^{3m-1/2}_{C^6(S\times S)}.
\end{equation}
In particular $\var\big[\, Z_B\,\big]<\infty$.

body:
[Definition 11 (Octahedron recurrence) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{def:oct}
We use the max-plus form of the octahedron recurrence, in the sense of
\cite{KTW,Speyer,NarSheffTao}.  One starts with real values assigned to a
stepped surface in the parity sublattice of \(\mathbb Z^3\).  A local move
replaces one face of an elementary octahedron by the opposite face.  If the
six vertices of this octahedron are
\[
(i,j,k\pm 1),\qquad (i\pm 1,j,k),\qquad (i,j\pm 1,k),
\]
and all values except \(F(i,j,k+1)\) are already known, then the missing value
is defined by
\[
F(i,j,k+1)
=
\max\{F(i+1,j,k)+F(i-1,j,k),\,
F(i,j+1,k)+F(i,j-1,k)\}
-F(i,j,k-1).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
F(i,j,k+1)+F(i,j,k-1)
=
\max\{F(i+1,j,k)+F(i-1,j,k),\,
F(i,j+1,k)+F(i,j-1,k)\}.
\]
Iterating these local moves transports the data from one stepped surface to
another.  In the hive setting this transport is the
Knutson--Tao--Woodward/Speyer piecewise-linear, volume-preserving bijection
between the two hive decompositions corresponding to associativity
\cite{KTW,Speyer,NarSheffTao}; we denote it by \(\oct\).

For the applications below, Proposition~\ref{gt-rem}(iv) first lets us regard
Gelfand--Tsetlin patterns as hives with one large-gap side.  With this
identification, \(\oct\) sends a pair of Gelfand--Tsetlin patterns, equivalently
a double hive, to an augmented hive, or to a pair of hives glued along their
common boundary.  Throughout the paper \(h_n\) denotes the hive component of
this image when the input is the deformed GUE double hive.
title: Octahedron recurrence

[Definition 6 of arXiv:2608.30551, 'Critical Discrete Hardy Inequalities in $L^p$'] Let $\Omega\subseteq X$. A \emph{Hardy weight} for
$\mathcal{E}_p^{X,k}$ on $\Omega$ is a nonnegative function
$w:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ such that
$$
\mathcal{E}_p^{X,k}(u)
\geq
\sum_{x\in\Omega}w(x)|u(x)|^p,
\qquad u\in C_c(\Omega).
$$
A Hardy weight $w$ is called \emph{critical} if every Hardy weight
$\widetilde w$ on $\Omega$ satisfying
$$
\widetilde w(x)\geq w(x),
\qquad x\in\Omega,
$$
coincides with $w$.
title: Definition 6 of arXiv:2608.30551

body:
[Definition 8 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Let $\Sigma \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ and $\Lambda \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval. A {\em $\Sigma$-indexed line ensemble $\mathcal{L}$} is a random variable defined on a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ that takes values in $\left(C (\Sigma \times \Lambda), \mathcal{C}_{\Sigma}\right)$. Intuitively, $\mathcal{L}$ is a collection of random continuous curves (sometimes referred to as {\em lines}), indexed by $\Sigma$, each of which maps $\Lambda$ into $\mathbb{R}$. We will often slightly abuse notation and write $\mathcal{L}: \Sigma \times \Lambda \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, even though it is not $\mathcal{L}$ which is such a function, but $\mathcal{L}(\omega)$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$. For $i \in \Sigma$, we write $\mathcal{L}_i(\omega) = (\mathcal{L}(\omega))(i, \cdot)$ for the curve of index $i$ and note that the latter is a map $\mathcal{L}_i: \Omega \rightarrow C(\Lambda)$, which is $\mathcal{F}/\mathcal{C}$ measurable. 

We say that a line ensemble $\mathcal{L}$ is {\em non-intersecting} if $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely $\mathcal{L}_i(t) > \mathcal{L}_j(t)$ for all $i < j$ and $t \in \Lambda$. We say that a line ensemble $\mathcal{L}$ is {\em ordered} if $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely $\mathcal{L}_i(t) \geq \mathcal{L}_j(t)$ for all $i < j$ and $t \in \Lambda$. If $[a,b] \subseteq \Lambda$, we let $\mathcal{L}_i[a,b]$ denote the restriction of $\mathcal{L}_i$ to $[a,b]$, and note that the latter is a measurable map $\mathcal{L}_i[a,b]: \Omega \rightarrow C([a,b])$. If $\Sigma_1 \subseteq \Sigma$ and $[a,b] \subseteq \Lambda$, we let $\mathcal{L}\vert_{\Sigma_1 \times [a,b]}$ denote the restriction of $\mathcal{L}$ to $\Sigma_1 \times [a,b]$, which is a measurable map $\mathcal{L}\vert_{\Sigma_1 \times [a,b]}: \Omega \rightarrow C(\Sigma_1 \times [a,b])$.
title: Definition 8 of arXiv:2603.24616

body:
[Lemma lem:regularized_solutions of arXiv:2609.01984, 'Instantaneous shrinking of supports for stochastic PDEs\footnote{JY was supported by a KIA'] For each $n\ge1$, equation (equation eq:regularized-measure-equation of the paper) has a unique
nonnegative solution $u_n$. Moreover, for every bounded stopping time
$\tau\le T$, every $p\ge2$, and every $\kappa\in(0,1/2)$,
\[
    u_n\in\mathcal H_p^{1/2-\kappa}(\tau).
\]
In addition, if $(1-2\kappa)p>6$ and
\[
    \frac1p<\mathbb{a}<\mathbb{b}<
    \frac14-\frac{\kappa}{2}-\frac1{2p},
\]
then
\[
    u_n\in
    C^{\mathbb{a} -1/p}
    \bigl([0,\tau];C^{1/2-\kappa-2\mathbb{b}-1/p}(\mathbb{R})\bigr)
    \qquad\text{a.s.}
\]
Furthermore, for every $\rho>0$, there exists $N_n= N(\nu,\kappa,p, \mathbb{a}, \mathbb{b}, \mathbb{c}_1 ,T, n)$ such that 
\begin{equation}

    \mathbb{E}
    \left\|
        u_n\zeta_{\rho/p}
    \right\|_{C^{\mathbb{a} -1/p}
    ([0,\tau];C^{1/2-\kappa-2\mathbb{b} -1/p})}^p
    \le
    N_n+
    N_n\|\mu_0\zeta_{\rho/p}\|_{U_p^{1/2-\kappa}}^p.
\end{equation} Consequently,
\begin{equation}

    \mathbb{E}
    \left[
        \sup_{t\le\tau,\ x\in\mathbb{R}}
        u_n(t,x)^p e^{-\rho|x|}
    \right]
    \le N_n.
\end{equation}

body:
[Proposition prop:balance of arXiv:2509.04155, 'An Approach to Sub-Gaussian Heat Kernel Estimates via Analysis on Metric Spaces'] Let $q > p$ and assume that $\nu$ is a doubling measure on $X$ that satisfies the $(q,p)$-balance condition. Then $\nu$ satisfies the following Sobolev--Poincar\'e inequality for all $t \in [1,q)$. There are constants $C,\sigma \geq 1$ so that for all open balls $x \in X$, $r > 0$ and $f \in \mathcal{F}_p$,
    \[
        \left( \vint_{B(x,r)} \abs{\tilde{f} - f_{B(x,r)}}^t \, d\nu\right)^{\frac{1}{t}} \leq C \left( \frac{\Psi(x,r)}{\mu(B(x,r))}\int_{B(x,\sigma r)} \, d\Gamma_p\Span{f}  \right)^{\frac{1}{p}}.
    \]
title: Proposition prop:balance of arXiv:2509.04155

body:
[Definition def:qualify of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $z\in\mathcal Z_i$ and write $\pi_z(s)=z+\gamma_{s-\tau\beta}$ for the reference path issued
from $z$. Throughout this definition $X_v$ and $\mathcal R_v$ denote the trajectory and the
recovery marks of $v$ in the configuration $\omega$ of (sec:graphical of the paper), before the
substitution of (sec:auxpath of the paper). Only $\pi_z$ and $\mathcal A^{(i,\tau)}_{\to v}$ are auxiliary
objects of the cell. The set $\Upsilon_z$ defined below is thus a functional of $\omega$ and of
the auxiliary objects of $(i,\tau)$ alone, and the two are independent. A particle $v$
\emph{qualifies at $t_j$}, $j\in\mathcal J'$, if
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $|\pi_z(t_j)-X_v(t_j)|\le r/2$;
\item $v$ displaces by at most $r/4$ during $[t_j,t_j+\mathfrak d]$; and
\item $\mathcal A^{(i,\tau)}_{\to v}$ has a mark in $[t_j,t_j+\mathfrak d]$.
\end{enumerate}
It \emph{qualifies freshly at $t_j$} if in addition $|\pi_z(t_k)-X_v(t_k)|>r/2$ for every
$k\in\mathcal J'$ with $k>j$. We let $\Upsilon_z$ be the set of particles which qualify freshly at
some $j\in\mathcal J'$, carry no recovery mark during $[\tau\beta,\tau\beta+T_L]$, and remain in
the reduced super-cube $Q^{*}_-(i)$ throughout $[\tau\beta,\tau\beta+T_L]$.
title: Qualifying proximity to a reference path

body: [Thm 2 (Unique ergodicity) of arXiv:2606.27035, 'R\'emy's diffusion on Brownian trees'] Let $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}^{\, \bullet}$ be any rooted real tree equipped with a mass measure with total mass $1$ and a marked point different from the root. Let $B$ be an independent Brownian motion. Then $\frac{1}{ \sqrt{1+t}} \cdot \Psi(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}^{\, \bullet}, B)_t$ converges in distribution towards $ \boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}_{2\mathbb{e}}^{\, \bullet} = (\mathcal{T}_{2 \mathbb{e}}, X)$ as $t\to\infty$ in the marked Gromov--Hausdorff--Prokhorov topology. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem 27 of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $[S,T]\subseteq\Rsf$ be an interval and let $m,n\in\Nsf$. Let $p\in [1,3)$, let $\omega$ be a control function on the interval $[S,T]$, and let $X$ be an $n$-dimensional branched rough path on the interval $[S,T]$ with regularity $p$ and control $\omega$. Let $f:\Rsf^m\to R_n^2\Rsf^m$ be a compactly supported admissible rough velocity field. Finally, let $Y, \widetilde{Y}: [S,T]\to \Rsf^m$ be two integral curves of $f$ driven by $X$ such that $Y(S)=\widetilde{Y}(S)$. Then there exists $\varepsilon\in (0,\infty)$ such that $Y=\widetilde{Y}$ on $[S,S+\varepsilon]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 27 of arXiv:2609.01190

[Defn def:dl of arXiv:2606.30517, '\textsc{Convergence towards Ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations with a focus on Diestel--'] Given natural numbers $p,q\geq 2$, consider $(T\coloneqq \mathcal{T}^{(p)},\mathbf{o},\omega_0)$ and $(T'\coloneqq \mathcal{T}^{(q)},\mathbf{o}',\omega'_0)$ as above. The \textbf{\textit{Diestel--Leader graph}} of order $(p,q)$, denoted by ${\rm DL}(p,q)$, is the {directed} graph whose vertex set $V$ is
		$$
		V \overset{\rm def}{=} \{ (v,v') \in T\times T' \,:\;  h(v)+h'(v')=0 \}
		$$
		and whose edge set is defined by
		$$
		(v,v') \sim_{\rm DL}(p,q) (w,w') \iff v\sim_{T} w  \quad \text{and} \quad v'\sim_{T'} w' \; .
		$$
		The direction of the edges are defined by adding the condition $h(w)=h(v)-1$ {(i.e., $h'(w')=h'(v')+1$).}

body:
[Corollary 14 (Quadratic exponential direct image) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] Let \(A\in\Sym_d(\R)\) and
\[
 B(t)=I_d-2itA,
 \qquad C(t)=B(t)^{-1}.
\]
Over \(\C[t,\det B(t)^{-1}]\), the relative exponential direct image of
\[
 \exp\!\left(-\frac{q(x)}{2}+itx^{\mathsf T}Ax\right)
\]
has rank one and is concentrated in relative de Rham degree \(d\).  Its
normalised period over the real Gaussian contour is
\[
 \Phi_A(t)=\det(I_d-2itA)^{-1/2},
 \qquad \Phi_A(0)=1,
\]
and satisfies
\[
 \left(
 \partial_t-i\,\operatorname{tr}(AC(t))
 \right)\Phi_A(t)=0.
\]
In particular, the real Gaussian cycle is cyclic in this rank-one direct
image.

Let Omega be a finite set, R a random subset of Omega where elements are chosen independently, and let {S_i}_{i in I} be a family of non-empty subsets of Omega. Let A_i be the event S_i subset R, X = sum_{i in I} 1_{A_i}, mu = E[X], and Delta = sum_{i ~ j} P(A_i \cap A_j) where the sum is over ordered pairs with S_i \cap S_j \neq \emptyset. Then for any 0 <= t <= mu, P(X <= mu - t) <= exp(- t^2 / (2 (mu + Delta))). In particular, P(X = 0) <= exp(- mu + Delta / 2).
A_i are increasing cylinder events based on independent choices

Let $\mu$ be a non-atomic measure on $[0,t]\times[\delta,1]$, finite on bounded sets. Suppose that the simple point process $\mathcal N$ is such that for any set $\Delta$ which is a finite union of rectangles
\[
P(\mathcal N(\Delta) = 0) = \exp\{-\mu(\Delta)\}.
\]
Then $\mathcal N$ is a Poisson process with intensity measure $\mu$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem 1.5 of arXiv:2512.17823, 'van den Berg-Kesten--type correlation inequalities for disjoint polymers in the KPZ univer'] Fix any real numbers $x_{1}<x_{2}$ and $y_{1}\in\mathbb R$. Let $\mathsf{A}\subseteq\mathcal{C}([0,K],\mathbb R)$ for some $K>0$ be an increasing Borel measurable set. Then for any $s<t$, $R>0$, and a.e. $f\in\mathcal{C}([y_{1}-R,y_{1}],\mathbb R)$, $\displaystyle\mathbb P\Bigl(\log\mathcal{K}_{2}((x_{1},x_{2}),s;(y_{1},\bm{\cdot}),t)|_{[y_{1},y_{1}+K]}-\log\mathcal{Z}(x_{1},s;y_{1},t)\in\mathsf{A}\ \Big|\ \log\mathcal{Z}(x_{1},s;\bm{\cdot},t)|_{[y_{1}-R,y_{1}]}=f\Bigr)$ $\displaystyle\leq\mathbb P\Bigl(\log\mathcal{Z}(x_{2},s;\bm{\cdot},t)|_{[y_{1},y_{1}+K]}\in\mathsf{A}\Bigr).$ The same also holds when the conditioning is replaced by $\log\mathcal{Z}(x_{1},s;y_{1},t)|_{[y_{1}-R,y_{1}]}\geq f$. The same also holds under both conditionings when $+K$ and $-R$ are simultaneously replaced by $-K$ and $+R$ in the above.

[Proposition prop:doubly-transient-really-general of arXiv:2604.13968, 'Divisible sandpiles via random walks in random scenery'] Let~$G = (V,E)$ be an infinite, locally finite, connected graph. Assume the simple random walk on $G$ is transient, that $\sum_{v\in V}g(o,v)^2<\infty$ for every $o\in V$,
		and that $G$ admits a uniform local trap condition.
		Let $(\xi(v))_{v\in V}$ be i.i.d.\ and independent of the walk with $\mathbb{E}[\xi]=0$, $\var(\xi)>0$, and $\mathbb{E}[\xi^2]<\infty$. Then~$\sup_{\tau}\mathbb{E}_o[S_\tau\mid\xi]=\infty$ almost surely for every~$o\in V$, where the supremum is over bounded stopping times. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Doubly transient

[Definition Entropy functional of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] The \emph{entropy functional} relative to~$\pi$ is
\[
  \mathrm{Ent}_\pi(f)
  := \sum_{x\in S} f(x)\log f(x)\,\pi(x)
     - \Bigl(\sum_{x\in S} f(x)\pi(x)\Bigr)
       \log\Bigl(\sum_{x\in S} f(x)\pi(x)\Bigr)
\]
for non-negative functions $f\ge 0$ on $S$.
When $\mu$ has density $f=d\mu/d\pi$ with respect to $\pi$, one has
$\mathrm{Ent}_\pi(f) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\pi)$.
title: Entropy functional

 =

      {\sqrt\pi\,(-\log\alpha)^{1/(2H)}}\,t .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

and 
\[
\mathbf{d}_W \left(  \frac{H - \E H} {\sqrt{\Var H}}, N \right) \leq C_K \cdot (M^{\xi}_{5,W})^{2/5} \frac{\nu(W)^{1/2}}{\Var H} + C_W \cdot (M^{\xi}_{5,W})^{3/5} \frac{\nu(W)}{(\Var H)^{3/2}},
\]
where $C_K,C_W$ and $M^\xi_{5,X}$ are as in Theorem~\ref{mainthm1} (resp. as in Corollary~\ref{cor:spaceonly}).

If $\Var H \geq c_0 \nu(W)$ for some positive constant $c_0$ then
there is a $C>0$ depending on $c_0,C_K,C_W,M^\xi_{5,X}$
such that for 
${\bf{d}} \in \{\mathbf{d}_W, \mathbf{d}_K\}$ 
\begin{equation} 
{\bf{d}}\left(  \frac{H - \E H} {\sqrt{\Var H}}, N \right) \leq \frac{ C}{\sqrt {\Var H}}. 
\end{equation}

[Proposition 4 of arXiv:2609.01166, 'Nonparametric inference for density-dependent McKean--Vlasov diffusions'] Assume \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) are i.i.d. from \(\pi_0^M\) and the likelihood ratios satisfy, for all \(\xi\in\cX_m\), 
\(
 \gamma_M \le \pi_0^M/\pi_\xi^M \le \gamma_M^{-1}
\)
with some 
\(\gamma_M\in(0,1)\). If a data-dependent \(\widetilde\Xi_{n,M}\in\cX_m\) satisfies
\begin{equation}
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log\pi_{\widetilde\Xi_{n,M}}^M(Y_i)
 \geq
\sup_{\xi\in\cX_m}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log\pi_\xi^M(Y_i)-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt},M},
\end{equation}
then with probability at least $1-\delta$,
\begin{align}
\KL(\pi_0^M\Vert\pi_{\widetilde\Xi_{n,M}}^M)
 \leq
C_1\inf_{\xi\in\cX_m}\KL(\pi_0^M\Vert\pi_\xi^M)
 &+C_2\frac{B_{\gamma_M}(\mathcal H_m(\ve,M)+\log(2/\delta))}{n} \nonumber\\
 &\quad +C_3\omega_m(\ve,M)+C_4
 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt},M}
\end{align}
with some positive constants \(C_i\), \(i\in\{1,2,3,4\}\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 39 of arXiv:2608.18075, '2608.18075'] Let $u=Kw$ be the velocity corresponding to the vorticity solution, with the
unit viscosity rescaling used above.  There is a number $\eta_0>0$ such that,
for every $T<\infty$, $m<\infty$, $C_0<\infty$, and $2<\zeta<3$, there are
$R<\infty$ and $C<\infty$ for which
\begin{align}
 &\mathbf E_{u_0}\left[
  \exp\left(C_0\int_0^T\|u_t\|_{H^\zeta}\,\dd t\right)
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}(1+\|u_t\|_{H^{b+1}}^2)^m
  \right]                                                      \notag\\
 &\hspace{25mm}\le C(1+\|u_0\|_{H^{b+1}}^2)^R
                 \exp(\eta_0\|u_0\|_{H^1}^2).
 
\end{align}
Equivalently, in the original vorticity variables, for every
$m,r\in[1,\infty)$,
\begin{align}
 \mathbf E_w\left[1+\|w\|_{C([0,T];H^b)}^m\right]^r
 \le C_{T,m,r}(1+\|w\|_{H^b}^2)^R
                    \exp(\eta_0\|w\|_2^2).
 
\end{align}
For $s_*<\gamma<\alpha_{\rm H}/2$ and every $q<\infty$,
\begin{align}
 \mathbf E\left[
  \sup_{0\le t\le1}(1+\|u_{S+t}\|_{C^\gamma})^q
  \;\middle|\;\mathcal F_S\right]
 \le C_q(1+\|u_S\|_{C^\gamma})^{R_q}
 
\end{align}
after every finite stopping time $S$ for which $u_S\in C^\gamma$.
Moreover, for every fixed $t_{\rm v}>0$,
\begin{align}
 \mathbf E\left[
  (1+\|u_{S+t_{\rm v}}\|_{C^\gamma})^q
  \;\middle|\;\mathcal F_S\right]
 \le C_{q,t_{\rm v}}
  (1+\|u_S\|_{H^{b+1}}^2)^{R_{q,t_{\rm v}}}
  e^{\eta_0\|u_S\|_{H^1}^2}.
 
\end{align}
The same estimate holds for the supremum over a compact interval bounded
away from $S$.  The maximal and exponential estimates also hold
conditionally after a finite stopping time, with the state at that time on
the right hand side.

Let $X = Z\Sigma^{1/2}$ be $n \times p$ with $Z$ having i.i.d. entries of mean $0$ and variance $1$, $\Sigma$ positive semidefinite, and let $S = \frac{1}{n}X^T X$. Assume $p/n \to c \in (0, \infty)$ and that the empirical spectral distribution of $\Sigma$ converges weakly to a probability measure $H$ on $[0, \infty)$. Then almost surely the empirical spectral distribution of $S$ converges weakly to a nonrandom probability measure $F = F^{c, H}$, characterised as follows: with $\underline F = (1 - c)\delta_0 + cF$ (the limiting spectral distribution of the $n \times n$ companion $\frac{1}{n}XX^T$) and $\underline m(z) = \int \frac{d\underline F(t)}{t - z} = -\frac{1 - c}{z} + c\,m_F(z)$, for every $z \in \mathbb{C}^+$ the value $\underline m(z)$ is the unique solution in $\mathbb{C}^+$ of $$z = -\frac{1}{\underline m} + c\int \frac{\tau\, dH(\tau)}{1 + \tau\,\underline m}.$$ Equivalently, $m_F$ solves $m_F(z) = \int \frac{dH(\tau)}{\tau\,(1 - c - c z\, m_F(z)) - z}$. For $H = \delta_1$ (identity population covariance) the equation is the quadratic $c z\underline m^2 + (z - 1 + c)\underline m + 1 = 0$ whose solution is the Stieltjes transform of the Marchenko-Pastur law with ratio $c$; the support of $F$ and its density are read off by Stieltjes inversion, and the density is analytic inside the support and behaves like a square root at its edges.

the spectral distribution of Sigma converges weakly to H; p/n -> c in (0, infinity)

Own-work draft, proof (unaudited), T280-w716-C10 v1, kind route-failure, Target 3. For any fixed degree-1 fitting accuracy q1 in (0,1), there is a two-atom aligned exponential initialization on scales 0,h, h<=1/10, whose ordinary all-parameter population mean-field flow fits degree 1 by dimension-independent time. After retaining every actual trained parameter and changing the target to the same-axis degree-1-plus-unit-degree-2 harmonic, full residual energy cannot reach 1/2 in any fixed additional time as d grows. The Gaussian squared projection floor on span{1,exp(hZ)} is at least 79/100. For q1 in (0,1), choose h<=min(1/10,sqrt(q1)/(4L1)); the initial scales are 0,h and a=b=0, with all Euclidean parameters trained. At the first degree-1 risk-q1 crossing, change only the target to Z+p2,d, retaining all parameters. For every fixed additional horizon T2, full residual energy remains >1/2 for all sufficiently large d. The proof uses finite-time scale drift O(1/d) and the Gaussian formula Delta_h^2=2-(h+h^2/sqrt(2))^2/(exp(h^2)-1)>=79/100. This is not an obstruction to hitting a threshold in the degree-2 projection alone. C8/C9 dependencies and this proof remain unaudited; no novelty or full Target 3 resolution is asserted.
Uniform unit sphere and sqrt(d)-scaled known-axis initialization; equal atom masses and initial a=b=0
The first stage uses target Z; the second keeps degree 1 in the target Z+p2,d and retains all parameters
Full residual energy is asserted, not the hitting behavior of one degree projection

[Theorem thm:weight-removal-obstruction of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] For standard Brownian motion in $\mathbb R^3$ started from the origin, there exist a
bounded Borel field $B_{\mathrm{dw}}:Q\to\mathsf{S}^3$, a terminal datum
$\psi\in H^2(\mu_T)$, and a nonzero field $u$ with source $F$ such that
\begin{equation}
 F=B_{\mathrm{dw}}:D_x^2u,
 \qquad
 -(\partial_t+\tfrac12\Delta)u=F\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(Q),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Tr}_T^Xu=\psi(X_T).
 
\end{equation}
The coefficient also satisfies
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{29}{200}I_3
 \preceq\frac12I_3+B_{\mathrm{dw}}(t,x)
 \preceq\frac{39}{50}I_3,
 \qquad (t,x)\in Q.
\end{equation*}
The optimal Hessian Lipschitz constant of the driver
$f(t,x,y,z,H)=B_{\mathrm{dw}}(t,x):H$ is
$L_{\mathrm{dw}}=\sqrt{134}/25<1/2$, and the following assertions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item The same field $u$ is a weighted Sobolev solution for
every Brownian power weight $w(t)=t^\alpha$ with $\alpha>0$.
\item With $\alpha_*:=4\sqrt{67}/25-1\in(0,1)$, the same field is the unique
weighted Sobolev solution for the power weight $w(t)=t^\alpha$ whenever
$\alpha>\alpha_*$.
\item The equation in (equation eq:weight-removal-solution-pair of the paper) has no
unweighted Sobolev solution.
\end{enumerate}
title: Theorem thm:weight-removal-obstruction of arXiv:2608.16119

body:
[Lemma 56 (Scalar Wiener realization of a centered block) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Fix a concrete pulled-back dyadic form $\mathbf H^\sharp$ and assume that its
first flattening $F_1^\sharp$ is Hilbert--Schmidt.  For
$f\in\mathcal C_{0,Q}$ and $g\in\mathcal E_M$, define the scalar coefficient
kernel on the two Gaussian Hilbert spaces by
\[
 \mathfrak k_{f,g}(F,G):=\mathbf H^\sharp(F,G,f,g).
\]
Then $\mathfrak k_{f,g}\in\mathcal G_b\otimes_2\mathcal G_c$ and
\begin{equation}
 \|\mathfrak k_{f,g}\|_{\mathcal G_b\otimes_2\mathcal G_c}
 \le \|F_1^\sharp\|_{\Sch_2}\|f\|_{\mathcal C_{0,Q}}
 \|g\|_{\mathcal E_M}.
\end{equation}
For distinct colors, the scalar pairing of the centered operator with $(f,g)$
is the ordered double Wiener integral of $\mathfrak k_{f,g}$.  For equal
colors, it is the second Wiener integral of the symmetrization of
$\mathfrak k_{f,g}$.  In either case, simultaneous finite-rank Gaussian
compressions converge in $L^2(\Omega)$ to this scalar integral.  If, in
addition, all four flattenings of $\mathbf H^\sharp$ lie in $\Sch_r$ for
some $2\le r<\infty$, this scalar limit agrees with the pairing of the
operator-valued completion in
Theorem~\ref{thm:centered-gaussian-operator}.

At finite spectral cutoff, pairing \eqref{eq:finite-wick-identity} with the
localized deterministic kernel gives this scalar Wiener integral.  The
auxiliary plateaux act as the identity on the ranges of the synthesis maps,
so the coefficient has the multiplier in \eqref{eq:two-leg-multiplier}; for
equal colors, the covariance term is \eqref{eq:same-color-shell-contraction}.
title: Scalar Wiener realization of a centered block

[Definition 4 (ULDP) of arXiv:2608.19753, 'Uniform large deviation principles for the stochastic heat equation over unbounded sets of'] Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a Polish space, completely metrized by a metric $d$. 
Let $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ be a probability space.  Let $ \mathcal{E}_0$ be any set, and let $\{X^\eps_x: \eps>0,x\in \mathcal{E}_0\}$ be a family of $\mathcal{E}$-valued random variables. Let $\{I_x : x \in \mathcal{E}_0\}$ be a collection of lower-semicontinuous maps $I_x : \mathcal{E} \to [0,+\infty]$. 
Let $\mathscr{A}$ be a collection of subsets of $\mathcal{E}_0$.  
Then, the family $\{X^\eps_x: \eps>0,x\in \mathcal{E}_0\}$ is said to satisfy a \emph{Freidlin--Wentzell uniform large deviation principle (ULDP) with respect to the rate functions $I_x$ uniformly over $\mathscr{A}$}, if
\begin{itemize}
\item For any $A \in \mathscr{A}$, $s_0 > 0$, and $\delta > 0$,
\[
\liminf_{\eps \to 0} \inf_{x \in A} \inf_{\varphi \in \Phi_x(s_0)} \big(\eps\log \mathbb{P}(d(X^\eps_x, \varphi) < \delta) + I_x(\varphi)\big) \geq 0.
\]
\item For any $A \in \mathscr{A}$, $s_0 > 0$, and $\delta > 0$,
\[
\limsup_{\eps \to 0} \sup_{x \in A} \sup_{s \in [0,s_0]} \big(\eps \log \mathbb{P}(\mathrm{dist}_d(X^\eps_x, \Phi_x(s)) \geq \delta) + s\big) \leq 0,
\]
\end{itemize}
where $\Phi_x(s) \ceqq \{\varphi \in \mathcal{E} : I_x(\varphi) \leq s\}$.
title: ULDP

[Corollary 4 (Rectangular intermediate singular-value profile) of arXiv:2608.30722, 'Intermediate Singular Values of Random Matrices\\ under Second-Moment and Anti-Concentrati'] Let $B$ be an $N\times n$ random matrix, $N\ge n$, with independent entries
satisfying
\[
  \mathbb{E}B_{ij}=0,\qquad
  \mathbb{E}B_{ij}^2=1,\qquad
  \sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{P}(|B_{ij}-z|<a)\le b
\]
for some fixed $a>0$ and $b\in(0,1)$. For every
$\delta\in(0,1)$, there exist constants $c,C>0$, depending only on
$a,b,\delta$, such that if
\[
  1\le N-n+l\le(1-\delta)N,
\]
then for every $t\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{P}\!\left(
  ce^{-t}\bigl(\sqrt{N+1}-\sqrt{n-l+1}\bigr)
  \le s_{n+1-l}(B)\right. \\
&\hspace{3.5cm}\left.
  \le Ct\bigl(\sqrt{N+1}-\sqrt{n-l+1}\bigr)
\right)  \\
&\hspace{1.5cm}\ge
1
 -\exp\!\left(-c\min\!\left\{t(N-n+l),N\right\}\right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Rectangular intermediate singular-value profile

  graph
  \begin{itemize}
    \item with vertex set
          $V_{x} = \{x\} \cup \bigcup_{d \geq 1} \left\{ x \right\}\times \vertices^{d}$,
          and
    \item such that given
          $\gamma = (x, y_{1}, \ldots, y_{d})\in V_{x}$ and
          $\gamma' = (x, y'_{1}, \ldots, y'_{d'}) \in V_{x}$ with
          $d \leq d'$, we have
          $\left\{ \gamma, \gamma' \right\} \in \Tree_{x}$ if and only
          if $d' = d + 1$, $y_{1}=y'_{1}, \ldots, y_{d} = y'_{d}$, and
          $Z_{xy'_{1}\cdots y'_{d'}} = 1$ (respectively
          $\check{Z}_{xy'_{1}\cdots y'_{d'}} = 1$).
  \end{itemize}

body:
[Lem ordinary-factorial-bispectrum of arXiv:2605.13004, 'Orientation in Poisson Cluster Processes via Imaginary Bispectra'] Assume that the reduced second factorial cumulant measure and the reduced third factorial and complete cumulant measures are finite signed measures, so that the Fourier--Stieltjes transforms below are ordinary bounded functions. Let $B_{\mathrm{comp}}$ denote the Fourier--Stieltjes transform of $\gamma_3^{\mathrm{red}}$, the reduced complete, or ordinary, third cumulant measure, and let $B_{\mathrm{fac}}$ denote the transform of $\kappa_3^{\mathrm{red}}$, the reduced third factorial cumulant measure, under the same Fourier convention. When the latter measure has an $L^1$ density, $B_{\mathrm{fac}}$ is its factorial bispectrum. Then
\begin{equation}
B_{\mathrm{comp}}(\omega_1,\omega_2)
=
B_{\mathrm{fac}}(\omega_1,\omega_2)
+\Gamma(\omega_1)+\Gamma(\omega_2)+\Gamma(\omega_1+\omega_2)-2\lambda.
\end{equation}
In particular, since the second reduced factorial cumulant is symmetric and $\Gamma$ is real-valued,
\[
\mathrm{Im} B_{\mathrm{comp}}=\mathrm{Im} B_{\mathrm{fac}}.
\]
The finite-measure formulation above is the one used below; distributional variants require a separate specification of test-function classes and diagonal embeddings. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Frequency-domain relation between complete and factorial third cumulants

body:
[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2607.29536, 'Multi-hop visibility through the vacant set of Poissonian obstacles'] Let $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ be lines in $\R^d$ intersecting in a single point $z$, and let $\theta\in(0,\frac\pi2]$ be the angle between them. 
Let $u_1$ be a unit vector parallel to $\ell_1$. 
Then for any $\delta>0$,  
\[
B(\ell_1,\delta)\cap B(\ell_2,\delta)\subseteq 
z + \Big\{x\in B(\ell_1,\delta)\,:\,\big|\langle x,u_1\rangle\big|\leq \frac{\delta}{\tan(\theta/2)}\Big\}.
\]
In words, the intersection of $\delta$-neighborhoods of the two lines is contained in the finite cylinder centered at $z$ of radius $\delta$ and length $2\frac{\delta}{\tan(\theta/2)}$ whose axis is aligned with $\ell_1$.

		\Lmc(Y \, | \, Z,\phi(X,Z),\psi(Y,Z)) &= \Lmc(Y \, | \, Z,\psi(Y,Z)).
	\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:unbounded-L1-pointwise-mass of arXiv:2608.11931, '\texorpdfstring{Nonlinear parabolic characterizations of stochastic completeness at infini'] Assume that \(G\) satisfies \hyperref[def:SC-infinity]{\textup{{(SC\textsubscript{$\infty$})}}}{} and
that either $\mu(X)<\infty$ or $\phi$ satisfies \hyperref[eq:LG]{\textup{(LG)}}{}.
Let \(u_0\in\ell^{1,+}(X,\mu)\) and
let \(u\) be a positive pointwise solution on \([0,T]\times X\) such
that
\[
    u\in C\bigl([0,T];\ell^1(X,\mu)\bigr),
    \qquad u(0)=u_0,
\]
and
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{(s,x)\in[\tau,T]\times X}u(s,x)<\infty
    \qquad\text{for every }\tau\in(0,T).
\end{equation}
Then, \(u\) satisfies~\hyperref[eq:nonlinear-generalized-mass]{\textup{(MB)}}{}. In
particular, $\mathsf M_u(t)$ satisfies the
differential form of the generalized mass balance, i.e., $\mathsf M_u \in AC([0,T])$
and $\mathsf M_u'(t)=-\sum_{x\in X}\kappa(x)\phi(u(t,x)).$

Then, with high probability, the following holds: (i) for 1 <= k <= r_+, lambda_{n-k+1}(H(sqrt d)) = (sqrt d - mu_k^+)(sqrt d - d/mu_k^+) + O(sqrt(r_+ d)); (ii) for 1 <= k <= r_-, lambda_{n-k+1}(H(-sqrt d)) = (sqrt d - mu_k^-)(sqrt d - d/mu_k^-) + O(sqrt(r_- d)); (iii) in particular, assume d -> infinity and d >> r: for k in [r_+], lambda_{n-k+1}((1/d) H(sqrt d)) = (1 - 1/sqrt(tau_k^+))(1 - sqrt(tau_k^+)) + o(1), and for k in [r_-], lambda_{n-k+1}((1/d) H(-sqrt d)) = (1 - 1/sqrt(tau_k^-))(1 - sqrt(tau_k^-)) + o(1). Here the regime (7) lets the parameters scale with n so that r, d <~ polylog(n); mu_1^+ >= ... >= mu_{r_+}^+ > sqrt d and mu_1^- <= ... <= mu_{r_-}^- < -sqrt d are the informative eigenvalues of the signal matrix (mu^2 > d), r_0 = r_+ + r_- of them; tau_i = d/mu_i^2 and tau_k^+- = d/(mu_k^+-)^2; H(t) := t^2 - tA + (D - I); lambda_{n-k+1} is the k-th smallest eigenvalue.

[Lemma 8 (Exact specialized MLP) of arXiv:2608.24007, '2608.24007'] On the support of the data distribution,
\[
    F(x)
    =\sum_{c=1}^K\left[
        \phi\bigl(v_c^\top x\bigr)
        -\phi\left(
            \left(v_c-\frac{\mu_c}{R^2}\right)^\top x
        \right)
    \right]
\]
equals $f^\star(x)$ exactly.  Moreover,
\[
    \|F\|_{\mathcal P}
    \leq B_R
    :=K\left(1+\sqrt{1+R^{-2}}\right).
\]
It also admits a parameterization satisfying
$\|\theta\|_{\mathrm F}^2\leq B_R$.

[Lemma cover of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] The mapping composed of first mapping the disk to the ellipse via the Schwarz map
$$ \psi(z)=\sin\Big(\frac{\pi}{2K(r^2)}F(z/r, r^2)\Big),$$
and then following with the Joukowsky map
$$\mathcal{J}(z) = z + \sqrt{z^2-1},$$
gives a branched double cover of the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$ by the annulus $\mathcal{A}_R$ with branch-points at $\pm r$. 
The radius $R$ is given by $\log R = \pi K'(r^2)/4K(r^2)$.
The corresponding covering automorphism is $w \to w^{-1}$.

Further, if $\mathcal{A}_R$ is endowed with the cylindrical metric $g_{\rm cyl}(w) := \vert w\vert^{-2}\, |dw|^2$, then its pull-back behaves around $\pm r$ like $\hat g = \hat \Omega^2 |dz|^2$, with 
$$\hat \Omega^2(\pm r + \varepsilon \omega) =  
\varepsilon^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{c}}(r)+O(\varepsilon^{-1/2}),
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf{c}}(r) = \frac{\pi^2}{8K(r^2)^2 r(1-r^4)},
$$ 
for $|\omega| = 1$, as $\varepsilon \to 0$.

[Lemma 52 (Wick realization after covariance pullback) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $b,c\in\mathfrak C$.  Let $\mathbf W_b,\mathbf W_c$ be the real isonormal processes on the Gaussian Hilbert spaces
of colors $b,c$.  Let $S_1:\mathfrak H_b\to\mathcal A$ and
$S_2:\mathfrak H_c\to\mathcal C_1$ be bounded, and let $\mathbf H$ be a
finite-rank four-linear form.  Put
\[
 \mathbf H^\sharp(f,g,x,y):=\mathbf H(S_1f,S_2g,x,y).
\]
If $b\ne c$, then the operator obtained by pairing the two pushed-forward
first chaoses with $\mathbf H$ has, for arbitrary orthonormal bases
$(e_\mu)$ and $(f_\nu)$, the coordinate representation
\begin{equation}
 Z^\sharp
 =\sum_{\mu,\nu}
 \mathbf W_b(e_\mu)\mathbf W_c(f_\nu)H^\sharp_{\mu\nu},
 \qquad
 \langle H^\sharp_{\mu\nu}x,y\rangle
 =\mathbf H^\sharp(e_\mu,f_\nu,x,y).
\end{equation}
If $b=c$ and the two Hilbert spaces are identified with the same
$\mathfrak H_b$, the completely Wick-centered pairing is
\begin{equation}
 Z^{\sharp,\mathrm{Wick}}
 =\sum_{\mu,\nu}
 (H^\sharp_{\mu\nu})^{\mathrm{sym}}
 \bigl(\mathbf W_b(e_\mu)\mathbf W_b(e_\nu)-\delta_{\mu\nu}\bigr).
\end{equation}
These identities are basis independent.  If the four flattenings of
$\mathbf H^\sharp$ lie in $\Sch_r$, they remain valid as identities in the
$L^p(\Omega;\mathcal K(\mathcal C_0,\mathcal E))$ limit supplied by
Theorem~\ref{thm:centered-gaussian-operator}.

Status: proof draft (unaudited); no novelty or general-T362 claim.

Use exactly the common-Hessian two-coordinate model and settled epoch recursion of C001, normalized to mu=1. Fix n>=2, deterministic x0!=0 and y0, fixed zero-sum component linear terms with mean squares s1>=0 and s2>0. Fresh independent uniform permutations are shared across coordinates. Set T=nK and suppose

    kappa_T*log(T)/T -> c,   0<c<4.

For 0<q<2 put a=1-q and

    W_n(q)=sum_{0<=i<j<n}(a^i-a^j)^2,
    J_n(q)=q^2 W_n(q)/[2(n-1)(1-a^(2n))].

Let P_T(eta) be the exact expected final-epoch function error. Then

    kappa_T * min_{eta>=0} P_T(eta)
        -> s2 * min_{c/2<=q<2} J_n(q).                    (1)

The right minimum is attained. Every sequence of globally optimal steps has

    dist(kappa_T*eta_T, argmin_{[c/2,2)} J_n) -> 0.        (2)

No assertion that J_n is increasing or has a unique minimum is required. In particular (1) is a finite-dimensional exact variational limit, not an elementary expression for its roots. Only the critical range 0<c<4 and s2>0 is covered.

## Proof

1. Write q=kappa*eta. For the stiff coordinate, the settled epoch recursion gives its variance contribution R_T exactly as

    kappa R_T = [s2*q^2*W_n(q)/(2(n-1))]
                  *sum_{r=0}^{K-1}(1-q)^(2nr).           (3)

Its deterministic contribution, after multiplication by kappa, is kappa^2*y0^2*(1-q)^(2T)/2. The flat deterministic contribution is A*(1-eta)^(2T), A=x0^2/2>0. All contributions are nonnegative. The objective is a continuous coercive polynomial: the pair (0,1) of any noisy coordinate yields a positive quartic lower bound. Thus global minimizers exist for each T.

2. First choose any fixed q in (c/2,2) and eta=q/kappa. Since kappa~c*T/log T, eta->0 and T/kappa~log T/c. Hence

    log[kappa*A*(1-q/kappa)^(2T)]
      = log kappa + log A - 2q*T/kappa + O(T/kappa^2)
      = (1-2q/c+o(1))*log T -> -infinity.

Here T/kappa^2->0. On compact subsets of (0,2), the stiff deterministic term tends uniformly to zero, and (3) tends uniformly to s2*J_n(q). The flat variance is O(eta^3) by the fixed-n flat-coordinate variance estimate in C001, so kappa times that contribution is O(kappa^-2). This proves a finite constant upper bound kappa*min P_T<=M for all sufficiently large T. It does not yet establish recovery at the boundary q=c/2.

3. Let eta_T be ANY global minimizer and q_T=kappa*eta_T. From the pair (0,1) and the last epoch in (3),

    kappa P_T(eta_T) >= s2*q_T^4/[2(n-1)].               (4)

The upper bound in step 2 makes q_T bounded. Consider any subsequential limit q_bar>=0. If q_bar>=2, the geometric sum in (3) tends to infinity: for every fixed m, K>=m eventually and its first m summands tend to numbers each >=1. Its prefactor stays bounded away from zero by W_n(q)>=q^2 and q_bar>=2. Thus the bounded scaled objective excludes all q_bar>=2. This argument includes approach to 2 from below; no uniform stationary approximation at the endpoint is used.

4. If q_bar<c/2, bounded q_T and eta_T=q_T/kappa->0 give

    log[kappa*A*(1-eta_T)^(2T)]
       = (1-2q_T/c+o(1))*log T -> +infinity,

contradicting the same upper bound. In particular q_bar=0 is excluded. Therefore every subsequential limit belongs to [c/2,2). Boundedness plus exclusion of 2 and larger limits shows that all minimizers lie eventually in a fixed compact subset of (0,2). These statements can be made uniform over minimizers: a failure would select a contrary sequence of global minimizers, to which the preceding argument applies.

5. On that compact subset, (3) converges uniformly to s2*J_n(q_T), because K->infinity and |1-q_T| is bounded below 1. Nonnegativity of all other terms gives

    liminf kappa*min P_T >= s2*min_{[c/2,2)} J_n.         (5)

Formally take a subsequence realizing the liminf, then a convergent subsequence of its bounded q_T. Step 4 puts its limit in the constraint set and uniform convergence gives (5). The objective is nonnegative, so no integrability or interchange of a random minimum is involved: P_T is already an expectation and eta is deterministic.

6. J_n is continuous on (0,2). As q->2 from below, W_n(q)>=q^2 remains bounded away from zero while 1-(1-q)^(2n)->0 positively. Thus J_n(q)->infinity, so its minimum on [c/2,2) is attained at some q_star<2. If q_star>c/2, the fixed candidate from step 2 gives recovery with scaled error s2*J_n(q_star).

If q_star=c/2, a fixed q=c/2 need not suppress the flat transient: the hypothesis allows subleading errors in kappa~c*T/log T. Use instead

    q_T^rec = kappa*[log kappa + sqrt(log kappa)]/(2T),
    eta_T^rec = [log kappa + sqrt(log kappa)]/(2T).

Then q_T^rec->c/2 in (0,2), and

    kappa*A*(1-eta_T^rec)^(2T)
        <= A*exp(-sqrt(log kappa)) ->0.

The other terms converge as in step 2, uniformly near c/2. Hence this boundary recovery sequence gives the same scaled limit s2*J_n(c/2). Together with (5), this proves (1).

7. For (2), suppose a sequence of optimal q_T remains a positive distance from the minimizing set. Its compactness from steps 3-4 gives a subsequence converging to q_bar in [c/2,2). Equation (3), nonnegativity, and (1) imply J_n(q_bar)<=min J_n, so q_bar is a minimizer, a contradiction. This proves (2).

## Scope and unpaid step

This is the next named-target-1 minimization regime after C003; it does not change C003 or re-prove its recursion. It covers an infinite critical condition-number family with nonzero stiff-coordinate noise. It does not settle general last-iterate RR, growing n, x0=0, s2=0, c>=4, or a minimax bound over all finite sums. No finite numeric checks are offered as an asymptotic certificate.

Least-trusted audit points: exclusion of the endpoint q=2 by finite partial sums, and the boundary recovery sequence in step 6. Both are essential; merely substituting growing kappa into C003 is invalid here. [Theorem 1 of arXiv:2606.24090, 'Sparsity-adaptive concentration inequalities for random polynomials'] Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a polynomial of degree $D$. 
Let $X_1,\cdots,X_n$ be a sequence of independent random variables such that $X_i=\delta_i\cdot\xi_i$, where the variables $\{\delta_i, \xi_i: i\in [n]\}$ are mutually independent, $\delta_{i}\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_i)$, and $\xi_i$ is an $\alpha$-sub-exponential random variable satisfying $\Vert \xi_i\Vert_{\Psi_\alpha}\le 1$.  Assume $0<\alpha\le 1$. Then, for any $r\ge 1$,
\[
\|f(X)-\mathbb E f(X)\|_{L_r} \lesssim_{D, \alpha}
\sum_{d=1}^D \sum_{I\subseteq[d]} \sum_{\mathcal J\in\Pi([d]\setminus I)}
r^{|\mathcal J|/2+|I|/\alpha} M_{d,I,\mathcal J}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let A_n (n = 1, 2, ...) and A be self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space H, each on its own dense domain; the domains are not assumed equal or even comparable. One says A_n -> A in the STRONG RESOLVENT SENSE if for every psi in H and every z in C with nonzero imaginary part, (A_n - z)^(-1) psi converges in norm to (A - z)^(-1) psi. Because each operator is self-adjoint, the resolvent (A_n - z)^(-1) is bounded with norm at most 1 / |Im z|, so the family is uniformly bounded and it is enough to verify the convergence for a SINGLE non-real z: one z in the upper half plane suffices, the conjugate point following by taking adjoints and the remaining z by the resolvent identity together with the uniform bound. The NORM RESOLVENT SENSE is the same statement with convergence in operator norm; it implies the strong resolvent sense and is strictly stronger. Practical criterion: if all the A_n and A are essentially self-adjoint on a common core D and A_n psi -> A psi for every psi in D, then A_n -> A in the strong resolvent sense. Without such a hypothesis convergence on a dense subspace says nothing, which is precisely why the resolvent formulation, and not naive pointwise convergence of unbounded operators, is the notion that interacts with the spectral theorem.
H is a complex Hilbert space
every A_n and A is self-adjoint (so the resolvent set contains C minus R and the resolvent norm bound 1/|Im z| holds)
no relation between the domains of the A_n and of A is assumed
convergence is of the resolvents, applied to a fixed vector (strong) or in operator norm (norm)
title: Strong and norm resolvent convergence of self-adjoint operators

[Proposition 18 (Count-chain transition) of arXiv:2605.14511, 'Clumsy and Careless:\\ Stationary-Entry Flux in Non-monotone Coupon Collectors'] The process $K_t$ is a Markov chain on $\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$. Its transition rule is
\[
K_{t+1}\mid K_t=k\sim
\begin{cases}
\Bin(k,q),&\text{with probability }k/n,\\[1mm]
\Bin(k+1,q),&\text{with probability }(n-k)/n.
\end{cases}
\]
In particular, the chain is irreducible and aperiodic and therefore has a unique stationary law $\nu_n$.

A measurable function f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty) is regularly varying at infinity with index \rho \in \mathbb{R} (written f \in RV_\rho) if for every x > 0, \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{f(t x)}{f(t)} = x^\rho. When \rho = 0, f is called slowly varying at infinity (f \in SV). Every regularly varying function can be factored as f(x) = x^\rho L(x) where L is slowly varying.
f: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty) is measurable

body: In mathematics, specifically group theory, Cauchy's theorem states that if G is a finite group and p is a prime number dividing the order of G, then G contains an element of order p. That is, there is x in G such that p is the smallest positive integer with xp = e, where e is the identity element of G. It is named after Augustin-Louis Cauchy, who discovered it in 1845.
title: Cauchy's theorem (group theory)

[Theorem thm:convergence of arXiv:2609.03264, 'Certified Spherical MUSIC for 3D Localization under Adversarial Subspace Perturbations'] Assume all the hypotheses and numerical inequalities in the statement
of (thm:certified-music-landscape of the paper), and define
\[
    m:=C_0^-\kappa^2,
    \qquad
    M:=C_0^+\kappa^2.
\]
For a fixed step size \(h\) satisfying
\begin{equation}

    0<h\leq\frac{2}{(C_0^-+C_0^+)\kappa^2}
    =\frac{2}{m+M},
\end{equation}
let
\[
    T_h({\bm z}):={\bm z}-h\nabla\widetilde q({\bm z}).
\]
Then, for every \(j=1,\ldots,s\),
\[
    T_h\left(\overline{B_\rho({\bm x}_j)}\right)
    \subset B_\rho({\bm x}_j).
\]
Moreover, \(T_h\) is a contraction on
\(\overline{B_\rho({\bm x}_j)}\) with contraction factor
\[
    r_h:=1-hm=1-hC_0^-\kappa^2\in[0,1).
\]
Consequently, every initialization
\({\bm z}^{(0)}\in\overline{B_\rho({\bm x}_j)}\) generates iterates
\[
    {\bm z}^{(n+1)}=T_h({\bm z}^{(n)})
\]
that remain in \(B_\rho({\bm x}_j)\) and converge to the unique local
minimizer \(\widetilde{\bm x}_j\). More precisely,
\begin{equation}

    |{\bm z}^{(n)}-\widetilde{\bm x}_j|
    \leq
    r_h^n|{\bm z}^{(0)}-\widetilde{\bm x}_j|,
    \qquad n\geq0,
\end{equation}
and

[Theorem 11 (Uniform Gr\"obner-basis construction) of arXiv:2608.25725, 'Gr\"obner Bases for Alexander Fitting Ideals of Links'] Define
\[
\mathcal B:=
\{\Pi_0(x),\ y^g-h(x)\}
\cup
\{\Pi_j(x)Q_j(x,y):\,j\in\mathcal S\setminus\{0,g\}\}.
\]
Then \(\mathcal B\) is a Gr\"obner basis of \(I\) with respect to
\(\lex(y>x)\), and
\[
\inop_{\lex}(I)=
\ideal{x^{\deg\Pi_j}y^j:\,j\in\mathcal S}.
\]
Consequently, \(\AG_2(L)\) is the reduced Gr\"obner basis obtained
by monic normalization and interreduction of \(\mathcal B\).
The displayed at-most-four-element Gr\"obner basis may contain redundant
elements before this interreduction.

Let Omega in R^n be a connected open set (bounded or not) and let Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + sum b^i D_i u + c u be uniformly elliptic with bounded coefficients on each open subset with compact closure in Omega (lambda > 0 there). Let u be in C^2(Omega) with Lu >= 0 in Omega. (a) If c = 0 and u attains its supremum over Omega at an interior point, then u is constant. (b) If c <= 0 and u attains a nonnegative maximum over Omega at an interior point, then u is constant. Dually, a supersolution (Lu <= 0) attaining an interior infimum (a nonpositive minimum when c <= 0) is constant.

[Thm 8 of arXiv:2609.00598, 'Supercritical mean--field limit for magnetized Hamiltonian dynamics'] Fix $T>0$. Suppose that $\omega^{\mathrm{in}}\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2})$ and
$\int_{\mathbb T^2}\omega^{\mathrm{in}}\,\dd x=0.$
Assume also that
$
B\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}_{+};W^{2,\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{2})).
$
Then
\begin{enumerate}
   \item[{\rm(i)}]There exists a unique solution $(\omega,v)\in W^{1,\infty}([0,T]\times \mathbb{T}^{2})\times W^{1,\infty}([0,T]\times \mathbb{T}^{2})$ of the Cauchy problem \eqref{vorticity formulation intro} with initial data $\omega^{\mathrm{in}}$. 
Consequently, there exists a unique solution $v\in W^{1,\infty}([0,T]\times \mathbb{T}^{2})$ of 
the Cauchy problem \eqref{magnetized Euler} with initial data $v^{\mathrm{in}}=-\nabla_{x}^{\perp}V\ast \omega^{\mathrm{in}}$. 
 \item[{\rm(ii)}]For any $r\in [1,\infty)$,
 \begin{align}
D^{2}_{x}v\in L^{\infty}([0,T];L^{r}(\mathbb{T}^{2})), \qquad 
\partial_{t}D_{x}v\in L^{\infty}([0,T];L^{r}(\mathbb{T}^{2})).     
\end{align}
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition 12 of arXiv:2606.16164, 'A Low-Regularity Semigroup Sewing Lemma via Quotient Structures'] Let $h\in Z\hat C(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)$, $R\in  C(\Delta_T^2;B_\alpha)$ and $\hat\delta R = h$. For $\tau\in[0,T]$, define $r^\tau := \Theta_\tau R$.
Then $(r^\tau)_{\tau\in[0,T]}$ is a compatible frozen increment family over $h$.
Moreover, if $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and $R\in E^{\gamma}(\Delta_T^2; B_\alpha)$, then for every
$0<\varepsilon<\gamma$,
\[
\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r^\tau\|_{\gamma-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon;\tau}\le M_{\alpha+\varepsilon,T}\|R\|_{\gamma-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon};
\]
if $R\in E_{\log}^{1}(\Delta_T^2; B_\alpha)$, then for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$,
\[
\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r^\tau\|_{1-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon;\tau}\le M_{\alpha+\varepsilon,T} \|R\|_{1-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon},
\]
and $ \sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r^\tau\|_{1,\log;\tau,\alpha}\le M_{\alpha,T}\|R\|_{1,\log;\alpha}$.

[Lemma lem:prop_of_bessel_space of arXiv:2609.01984, 'Instantaneous shrinking of supports for stochastic PDEs\footnote{JY was supported by a KIA'] Let $p>1$ and $\eta\in\mathbb{R}$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 
 
The space $C_c^\infty$ is dense in $H_p^\eta$. 
\item 
 
Let $\eta-\frac1p=n+\nu$ for some $n=0,1,\ldots$ and $\nu\in(0,1]$. Then, for every
$i\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$,
\begin{equation}
    \|D^i u\|_{C(\mathbb{R})}
    +
    \|D^n u\|_{\mathcal C^\nu(\mathbb{R})}
    \le
    N\|u\|_{H_p^\eta},
\end{equation}
where $N=N(p,\eta)$, and $\mathcal C^\nu$ is the Zygmund space.
\item 

For every integer $i\ge0$, the operator $D^i:H_p^\eta\to H_p^{\eta-i}$ is bounded. Moreover, for every $u\in H_p^{\eta+i}$,
\[
    \|D^i u\|_{H_p^\eta}
    \le
    N\|u\|_{H_p^{\eta+i}},
\]
where $N=N(p,\eta,i)$.

\item 

Let $p\in(1,\infty)$ and $\mu\le\eta$. If $u\in H_p^{\eta}$, then $u\in H_p^{\mu}$ and
\[ \|u\|_{H_p^{\mu}}\le\|u\|_{H_p^{\eta}}. \]
Moreover, if $q\in(1,\infty)$ satisfies $\eta-\frac{1}{p}=\mu-\frac{1}{q}$, then
\[ \|u\|_{H_q^{\mu}}\le N\|u\|_{H_p^{\eta}}, \]
where $N=N(\eta,\mu,p,q)$.

\item 

Let
\[
\varepsilon\in[0,1],
\qquad
p_i\in(1,\infty),
\qquad
\eta_i\in\mathbb{R},
\qquad i=0,1,
\]
and suppose
\[
    \eta=\varepsilon\eta_0+(1-\varepsilon)\eta_1,
    \qquad
    \frac1p=\frac{\varepsilon}{p_0}+\frac{1-\varepsilon}{p_1}.
\]
Then 
\[
    \|u\|_{H_p^\eta}
    \le
    \|u\|_{H_{p_0}^{\eta_0}}^\varepsilon
    \|u\|_{H_{p_1}^{\eta_1}}^{1-\varepsilon}.
\]
In particular, for every $\delta>0$,
\[
    \|u\|_{H_p^\eta}
    \le
    \delta\|u\|_{H_{p_0}^{\eta_0}}
    +
    N(\delta)\|u\|_{H_{p_1}^{\eta_1}} .
\]

\item  If $u\in H_p^\eta$, $a\in B^{|\eta|+\alpha}$ and $b\in B^{|\eta|+\alpha}(\ell_2)$, then
\[
    \|au\|_{H_p^\eta}
    \le
    N\|a\|_{B^{|\eta|+\alpha}}\|u\|_{H_p^\eta},
\]
and
\[
    \|bu\|_{H_p^\eta(\ell_2)}
    \le
    N\|b\|_{B^{|\eta|+\alpha}(\ell_2)}\|u\|_{H_p^\eta},
\] 
where $N=N(\alpha,\eta,p)$. 
\item

Let $\Theta\in C_c^\infty$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\Theta(x)\,\mathrm{d} x=1$, and set $\Theta_k(x):=k\Theta(kx)$ for
$k\ge1$. Then, for every $u\in H_p^\eta$,
\[
    \|u*\Theta_k\|_{H_p^\eta}
    \le
    \|u\|_{H_p^\eta}.
\]

\end{enumerate}

Let Omega be a compact full-dimensional polytope in R^din and g:R^din -> R^dout a continuous finite piecewise affine map. For width n, take networks F=fu composed with (id+fL) composed with ... composed with (id+f1) composed with fe, with affine embedding fe and unembedding fu, and fl(z)=Wl,2 ReLU(Wl,1 z+bl,1)+bl,2. Define C(L,n,lambda;g) as the infimum, over parameters computing g exactly on Omega, of (||Wu||_F^2+||We||_F^2)/2 + (lambda/2) sum_{l=1}^L (||Wl,1||_F^2+||Wl,2||_F^2); all biases are unpenalized. Let rJ be the maximum rank of Jg(x) at differentiability points in the interior of Omega, and let rBN be the least integer k admitting a finite continuous piecewise affine factorization g|Omega=h2 composed with h1 through R^k. For every sufficiently large fixed n depending on g and Omega, rJ <= liminf_{lambda->0+} liminf_{L->infinity} C(L,n,lambda;g)/(lambda log(1/lambda)) and limsup_{lambda->0+} limsup_{L->infinity} C(L,n,lambda;g)/(lambda log(1/lambda)) <= rBN. These bounds do not assert rJ=rBN or that either normalized limit equals rBN. They concern residual connections, unpenalized biases, and an ordered depth-then-lambda limit; they do not determine the plain-network depth-normalized cost R_infinity of a branching tripod. This is a restricted-domain, liminf/limsup formulation of Boix-Adsera Theorem 3.3, equations (3.1)-(3.2), arXiv:2501.19149v1, Section 3, printed pp.6-8.
Omega compact full-dimensional polytope
g continuous finite piecewise affine
fixed width sufficiently large depending on g and Omega
two-layer residual blocks; affine external embedding and unembedding
biases unpenalized
L tends to infinity before lambda tends to zero

\right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2604.23133, 'High-Precision Framework for Expected Hitting Times Analysis in the Dice-Sum Process'] Let $p_n$ denote the probability of ever hitting $n$, and let $q_n = 1 - p_n$ denote the probability of skipping (or missing) $n$.  
Then
\[
\frac{2}{7} - \varepsilon_n \le p_n \le \frac{2}{7} + \varepsilon_n,
\qquad
\frac{5}{7} - \varepsilon_n \le q_n \le \frac{5}{7} + \varepsilon_n,
\]
where $\varepsilon_n := \tfrac{5}{7}\,|w_+|^{\,n}$ and $|w_+| = 0.7302499667.$

[Theorem 32 of arXiv:2605.02002, 'Glauber dynamics for random field Ising models on bounded degree graphs and MLSI'] Suppose that the graph $G=(V,E)$ has $\alpha$-stretched exponential growth for some $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Suppose that the RFIM measure $\mu_G$ on $G$ satisfies $\operatorname{WSM}(C)$ for some $C>0$. Then we can find $C_0=C_0(\alpha,C_\alpha,C)>0$ such that for any $p\geq 1$,
$$
\mathbb{E}_h\left[\sup_{t\geq 0}\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Cov}(\nu_t)^p)\mid h]\right]\leq (C_0p)^p|V|
.$$
    In particular, for any $R\geq 0$, by Markov's inequality, 
    $$
\mathbb{E}_h\left[\sup_{t\geq 0}\mathbb{P}\left(\|\operatorname{Cov}(\nu_t)\|_{op}\geq R\mid h\right)\right]\leq |V|e^{-c_0R},
    $$with $c_0=(eC_0)^{-1}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Defn 27 (Similarity) of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] We say that two multicycles $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ are similar and write $\gamma \sim \gamma'$ if the following holds: for any nodes $i$ and $j$, $m^\gamma_{ij} > 0$ iff $m^{\gamma'}_{ij} > 0$, and the difference of the multiplicities $|m^\gamma_{ij} - m^{\gamma'}_{ij}|$ is even.

[Definition 19 of arXiv:2608.26953, '2608.26953'] Let \(\widehat{\mathsf{DG}}_n\) be the full subcategory of \(\mathsf{DG}_n\) whose objects \((\Omega^\bullet,\wedge,d)\) satisfy the following conditions.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{(D\arabic*)},ref=D\arabic*,nosep,labelsep=.5em,align=left]
\item There exist a finite set \(X\) and an algebra isomorphism
\(\iota\colon\Bbbk(X)\cong\Omega^0\) such that, writing again \(\delta_x\) for \(\iota(\delta_x)\), the DGA \(\Omega^\bullet\) is exterior.

\item For \(p>1\) and \(x,y\in X\),
\( \Omega^p_{x,y}=0 \ \text{whenever}\ \Omega^1_{x,y}=0.\)
\item For \(x,y\in X\), put
\[ \omega_{[x,y]}:=
\begin{cases}
\delta_xd(\delta_y),&x\neq y,\\ 
0,&x=y.
\end{cases}
\]
For \(1 \leq p \leq n\), define \[ P_p(x,y) := \Bigl\{ (v_0, \ldots, v_p) \ \Big|\ v_0 = x,\ v_p = y,\  (v_i,v_{i+1})\in \overline{E}_\Omega \text{ for } 0 \leq i < p \Bigr\}.\] For \(v=(v_0,\ldots,v_p)\in P_p(x,y)\), put \( m(v):= \omega_{[v_0,v_1]}\wedge\ldots\wedge \omega_{[v_{p-1},v_p]} \in \Omega^p_{x,y}, \) and \[ S_p(x,y) := \{ v \in P_p(x,y) \mid m(v)\neq 0\}.\] Then \((m(v))_{ v\in S_p(x,y)}\) is a \(\Bbbk\)-basis of \(\Omega^p_{x,y}\).
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition 19 of arXiv:2608.26953

  where $\mathbf{m}_1, \mathbf{m}_2$ are two probability measures and the
  above convergence is weak. Moreover, let $\pi (N) = \pi^{\lambda_1 (N)}
  \otimes \pi^{\lambda_2 (N)}$. Then, for $\lambda (N) \in \hat{U}
  (N)$ chosen at random with respect to $\varrho^{\pi (N)}$, the random
  measures $\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{m}}_N [\lambda (N)]$ converge, as $N \rightarrow

[Proposition prop:dual-flatness of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Each leaf is an exponential family whose sufficient statistics are
		the separable functions $u(x_{1}) + v(x_{2})$, hence e-flat in the
		sense of information geometry; each Fr\'echet fiber is convex, hence
		m-flat; the transport of Theorem~(thm:flat-transport of the paper) is the
		e-projection onto the m-flat fiber, the dual transport is the
		m-projection onto the e-flat leaf, and both Pythagorean identities
		hold~[csiszar1975,amari2016]. The $\alpha = \pm1$ connections
		of this dually flat pair are torsion-free and curvature-free; the
		tensor of Theorem~(thm:frame-torsion of the paper) is the torsion of the
		\emph{frame}, a structure finer than the $\alpha$-connections, and
		it alone sees dependence.

The Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind are defined on [-1, 1] by T_n(cos theta) = cos(n theta), n = 0, 1, 2, ...; equivalently T_0 = 1, T_1 = x and T_{n+1}(x) = 2 x T_n(x) - T_{n-1}(x). Facts: (1) T_n is a polynomial of degree n with leading coefficient 2^{n-1} for n >= 1, and T_n(x) = ((x + sqrt(x^2 - 1))^n + (x - sqrt(x^2 - 1))^n) / 2 for all real x (cosh(n arccosh x) for x >= 1); (2) |T_n(x)| <= 1 on [-1, 1], with T_n(cos(k pi / n)) = (-1)^k at the n + 1 extremal points and zeros at cos((2k - 1) pi / (2n)), k = 1..n, all in (-1, 1); (3) orthogonality: integral_{-1}^{1} T_m(x) T_n(x) dx / sqrt(1 - x^2) = 0 for m != n, pi for m = n = 0, pi/2 for m = n >= 1; (4) MINIMAX (Chebyshev): among all monic polynomials of degree n, 2^{1-n} T_n has the smallest maximum absolute value on [-1, 1], namely 2^{1-n}, and it is the unique minimiser; equivalently x^n is best approximated in the sup norm on [-1, 1] by polynomials of degree < n with error 2^{1-n}; (5) Chebyshev interpolation at the zeros of T_{n+1} has Lebesgue constant O(log n) and the Chebyshev series of a Lipschitz function converges uniformly, which is why Chebyshev nodes replace equispaced nodes (Runge's phenomenon) in numerical analysis. The polynomials of the second kind U_n are defined by U_n(cos theta) sin theta = sin((n+1) theta) and satisfy the same recurrence with U_1 = 2x.

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2607.11773, '2607.11773'] A family $\Phi =
                           \left\{\Phi(t, \tau): t \in \mathbb{R}^+, \tau \in \mathbb{R}
                           \right\}$
  of mappings from $\left( \mathcal{P}_m(D_{\rho}), d_{\mathcal{P}(D_{\rho})} \right)$
  to itself 
  is called a non-autonomous cocycle on $\left( \mathcal{P}_m(D_{\rho}), d_{\mathcal{P}(D_{\rho})} \right)$
  if $ \Phi $ satisfies 
  the following conditions:
   for all $\tau \in \mathbb{R}$ and $t,s \in \mathbb{R}^+$:

  (i) $\Phi(0, \tau) = I$,
      where $ I $ is the identity operator on $\left( \mathcal{P}_m(D_{\rho}), d_{\mathcal{P}(D_{\rho})} \right)$;

  (ii) $\Phi(t+s, \tau) = \Phi(t,s+\tau) \circ \Phi(s,\tau)$.

  In addition, if for every bounded subset $\mathscr{B}$ of $ \mathcal{P}_m (D_{\rho}) $,
  $ \Phi $ is continuous from  $\left( \mathscr{B} , d_{\mathcal{P}(D_{\rho})} \right)$
  to $\left( \mathcal{P}_m(D_{\rho}),  d_{\mathcal{P}(D_{\rho})} \right)$,
  then   $\Phi$ is 
  said to be continuous on bounded subsets of $ \mathcal{P}_m(D_{\rho}) $.

[Lem 7 of arXiv:2607.03360, 'Smoluchowski-Kramers Approximation Meets Khasminskii Averaging Principles in Nonequilibriu'] For each $\e>0$ and any fixed $R>0$, let $e_1, e_2: \rr^{d_1} \times \rr^{d_2} \to \rr$ be continuous functions satisfying $|e_1(x,y)| \leq C_{e_1}(1+|x|)$ and $|e_2(x,y)| \leq C_{e_2}$ for some constant $C_{e_1}, C_{e_2} > 0$.  Then,  for each $i,j, \iota =1,\dots, d_1$ and $\ell=1,\dots, d_2$, we have
\beq{inner-mv}
\lim_{\e \to 0} \EE \bigg[ \bigg( \sup_{t\in [0,T]} \Big|\int_0^t \big[M^{-1}_{R,n} \big]_{ij}(x_s^m, y_s^\e) e_1(x_s^m, y_s^\e) m (v_s^m)_i ds \Big|\bigg)^2 \bigg]=0,
\eeq
\beq{mv-W}
\lim_{\e \to 0} \EE \bigg[\bigg(\sup_{t \in [0,T]} \bigg| \int_0^t  \big[M^{-1}_{R,n} \big]_{ij}(x_s^m, y_s^\e) e_1(x_s^m, y_s^\e) m (v_s^m)_i d(W_s)_j \bigg| \bigg)^2 \bigg]=0,
\eeq
and 
\beq{ev-B}
\lim_{\e \to 0} \EE \bigg[\bigg(\sup_{t\in [0,T]} \bigg| \sqe \int_0^t \big[M^{-1}_{R,n} \big]_{ij}(x_s^m, y_s^\e) e_2(x_s^m, y_s^\e) \sqrt{m} (v_s^m)_\iota d(B_s)_\ell \bigg|\bigg)^2 \bigg]=0.

body:
[Theorem kpartW1 of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let Assumption~(ass:w1-normalized-matern of the paper) hold and suppose the joint initial law of the particles is exchangeable. For fixed \(k\ge1\), define
the random \(k\)-fold empirical occupation measure
\[
        \widehat\mu_T^{N,k}
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T (\mu_t^N)^{\odot k}\,dt,
        \qquad
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T \mu_t^{\otimes k}\,dt,
\]
where
\[
(\mu_t^N)^{\odot k}
:=
\frac{1}{(N)_k}
\sum_{\substack{1\le i_1,\ldots,i_k\le N\\
i_1,\ldots,i_k\ {\rm distinct}}}
\delta_{\bigl(x_{i_1}^N(t),\ldots,x_{i_k}^N(t)\bigr)},
\qquad
(N)_k:=N(N-1)\cdots(N-k+1).
\]
Let \(W_1^{(k)}\) be the Wasserstein distance on \((\mathbb R^d)^k\)
associated with the product cost
\(
        d_k(x,y):=\sum_{\ell=1}^k \|x_\ell-y_\ell\| .
\)
Then, with $\gamma$ as in Theorem~(prop:uniform-time-averaged-w1 of the paper),
\begin{equation}
\lim_{M \to \infty} \, \limsup_{N \to \infty}\,\sup_{T>0}
\mathbb P\left(
W_1^{(k)}
\left(
\widehat\mu_T^{N,k},
\overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
\right)
>
M(\log \log N)^{-\gamma/2}
\right)=0.
\end{equation}
Moreover, suppose the initial distributions satisfy (equation Gaussexp of the paper). 
Define, for $k \ge 1$,
\[
        \bar\mu_T^{N,k}
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T
        \mathcal L(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))\,dt,
        \qquad
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        :=
        \frac1T\int_0^T \mu_t^{\otimes k}\,dt ,
\]
where $L(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))$ denotes the joint law of $(x_1^N(t),\ldots,x_k^N(t))$.
Then there is \(C_k<\infty\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(N\),
\begin{equation}
        \sup_{T>0}
        W_1^{(k)}
        \left(
        \bar\mu_T^{N,k},
        \overline{\mu^{\otimes k}}_T
        \right)
        \le
        C_k(\log\log N)^{-\gamma/2}.

[Lemma quotient-we of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let $G$ be a compact Lie group, and let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a $G$-equivariant map of $G$-free Hausdorff spaces. Then $f$ is a (non-equivariant) weak homotopy equivalence if and only if the induced map $f/G\colon X/G\to Y/G$ on orbits is so.
    \begin{proof}
        By Lemmas~(lemma:quotient-map-is-fib of the paper) and~(lemma:quotient-pb of the paper), the commutative square
        \[
            \begin{tikzcd}
                X\arrow[d,"f"']\arrow[dr,pullback]\arrow[r] & X/G\arrow[d,"f/G"]\\
                Y\arrow[r] & Y/G
            \end{tikzcd}
        \]
        is a pullback in $\textbf{\textup{Top}}$ and the horizontal maps are Serre fibrations. Thus, this square defines a homotopy pullback in the $\infty$-topos $\Spc$. As $Y\to Y/G$ is surjective on $\pi_0$, i.e.\ an effective epimorphism, the claim follows from [HTT]*{Lemma 6.2.3.16}.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
