{"artifact_digest":"sha256:ebe4bd36ade091b992520698d91281b9388a07f6d144ef589a2db55d847fb656","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/eb/ebe4bd36ade091b992520698d91281b9388a07f6d144ef589a2db55d847fb656.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:954195ca0ea5fbedb34d3515cee6ee4ed30a69adfb4e177323269a4b8125cfec","bundle_entry_key":"claim-013","bundle_id":"population.adam-global-critical-cap-and-uncorrected-tracking-obstruction-005","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"deterministic adaptive optimization","draft":"w706/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.adam:adam-uncorrected-small-epsilon-uniform-curvature-tracking-obstruction","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"T421-W706-013 v2; target1; kind special; proof (unaudited).

Statement. There exist rho0>0 and delta>0 depending only on b=.9,d=.999
such that for every uncorrected scalar Adam run, epsilon outside sqrt,
standard m0=v0=0, with 0<rho=epsilon/(eta lambda)<=rho0, all but countably
many x0 satisfy
 limsup_(t->infinity) |eta C_t-38| >=delta.                    (1)
Here C_t=lambda/(sqrt(v_(t+1))+epsilon). The constants are existential,
not numerical bounds. For every p>1, fixed lambda>0, and any countable
eta_n->0, absolutely continuous random initialization almost surely
satisfies (1) for all sufficiently large n with epsilon_n=eta_n^p.
No choice of finite burn-in can give eventual o(1/eta) tracking along
this sequence for uncorrected scalar Adam.

In a positive two-eigenvalue diagonal quadratic, the same conclusion
holds for ACTIVE curvature on the invariant standard-initialization
family (x1,0), with x1 absolutely continuous. The second coordinate is
exactly dormant. This is not a full-dimensional random initialization
theorem, and does not cover ordinary time0 bias correction. Those are
explicit remaining gaps for the full dossier target. The result records
a rigorous tracking obstruction in a stated variant; it is not a generic
two-dimensional solution or a claim that every Adam convention fails.

Hardest remaining step: exclude capture in the higher-dimensional
clock-augmented stable set from standard starts under bias correction,
and control genuine two-coordinate averaging.

Proof. Work in claim009's normalized variables X,M,V with map
 M'=bM+(1-b)X, V'=dV+(1-d)X^2,
 X'=X-M'/(sqrt(V')+rho).
Choose, for definiteness, rho0=1/1000, which is strictly below
rho_*=358811/13673160. At rho in [0,rho0] the nonzero cycle has
 a(rho)=1/38-rho>=1/38-1/1000>0,
 p_s(rho)=(s a,-s a/19,a^2), s in {+1,-1}.
By claims003 and009 its two-step derivative has one simple real stable
eigenvalue and two unstable eigenvalues, uniformly separated from the
unit circle on this compact interval. At rho=0 the count follows from
the exact negative discriminant and real-root bounds in claim009; the
no-unit-root argument of claim003 excludes crossings throughout.

UNIFORM LOCAL STABLE CAPTURE
Claim009 constructs the analytic stable curve of each phase directly
by the power-series coefficient equation
 w_n=(mu(rho)^n I-A(rho))^(-1)[N_rho(v_rho s+w)]_n.
That proof can be made uniform on [0,rho0]. The simple stable spectral
projection and its complement vary continuously; choose continuous
local bases and norms, or use finitely many such choices on this compact
parameter interval. The stable eigenvalue has a uniform upper bound<1,
all unstable eigenvalues have a uniform lower modulus>1, and the linear
operators are invertible. Thus the inverses in the coefficient equation
are uniformly bounded for all n>=2 and all rho: large n are handled by
mu(rho)^n->0 uniformly, and finitely many small n by compactness.
The nonlinear maps are analytic on a fixed complex neighborhood of the
cycle branches, since their variances are bounded below by a(rho0)^2.
Their Taylor majorants are therefore uniformly bounded. One contraction
radius works on each of a finite cover and their minimum is positive.
Graph-relative unstable expansion also has a uniform factor>1 in the
chosen norms after shrinking. Since all these finitely many norms are
uniformly equivalent to the Euclidean norm, there is a single radius
r>0 with this property: an orbit of F_rho^2 staying within the Euclidean
r-neighborhood of a phase forever lies on its local stable curve and
converges to that phase. Smaller r may be chosen so neighborhoods of the
two phases are disjoint, uniformly in rho.

AN EVENTUAL CURVATURE BAND FORCES SUCH CAPTURE
Put k_t=eta C_t=1/(sqrt(V_(t+1))+rho). Suppose that eventually
 |k_t-38|<delta, where delta will be chosen sufficiently small below.
For delta<=1, the map k->1/k is uniformly Lipschitz on [37,39], so
 sqrt(V_(t+1))=a(rho)+O(delta),
 V_(t+1)=a(rho)^2+O(delta).
Every O(delta) here and below has a constant uniform for rho in
[0,rho0]. Subtracting dV_t in the exact variance update gives
 X_t^2=a(rho)^2+O(delta)/(1-d).
Since 1-d is a fixed positive number and a(rho) is uniformly positive,
 |X_t|=a(rho)+O(delta).                                    (2)
In particular X_t is nonzero for all sufficiently large t if delta
is small. Let s_t=sign(X_t).

Eliminate momentum exactly:
 X_(t+1)=[1+b k_t/k_(t-1)-(1-b)k_t]X_t
              -b k_t/k_(t-1)X_(t-1).
Using k_t=38+O(delta), (2), and b=.9, this yields
 s_(t+1)=-(1+b)s_t-b s_(t-1)+O(delta).                      (3)
For a sign triple that is not alternating, the absolute residual of
the exact relation in (3) is at least 2b=1.8: if the two preceding
signs coincide, the residual is at least1.8; if they differ, the wrong
next sign has residual2. Thus delta can be chosen uniformly so that
the error in (3) is smaller than0.9, forcing sign alternation at every
sufficiently late step. The exact preceding update also gives
 M_t=(X_(t-1)-X_t)/k_(t-1)=-s_t a(rho)/19+O(delta).
Together with (2) and the variance estimate, this puts every sufficiently
late state within C delta of p_(s_t)(rho), with uniform C. Choose delta
smaller still so C delta<r. Alternating signs then ensure each parity
subsequence remains in one local stable neighborhood forever. By uniform
local capture it converges to the alternating cycle.

COUNTABLE EXCEPTIONS AND THE SMALL-ETA CONSEQUENCE
For each fixed rho>0, claim009 proves that only countably many standard
initial X0 can converge to this cycle. The previous paragraph shows that
every orbit with limsup|k_t-38|<delta belongs to that countable set.
Scaling X0=x0/eta preserves countability. Therefore all other starts
satisfy (1). For p>1 and eta_n->0,
rho_n=eta_n^(p-1)/lambda eventually lies in (0,rho0]. For each such n
the exceptional x0 set is countable, and their countable union is null
for any absolutely continuous initialization law. Thus (1) holds almost
surely simultaneously along the specified sequence. This order of
quantifiers does NOT claim one null set for an uncountable eta family.

For the diagonal invariant-coordinate family, g2=m2=v2=0 at all times,
and the active quotient equals the scalar channel's curvature whenever
g1!=0. The eventual-band assumption itself forces g1!=0, so no undefined
quotient enters the capture implication. One may state the scalar bound
using the always-defined scalar C_t to avoid isolated zero-gradient times.

Scope/novelty: this strengthens claim009's noncap-limit obstruction to
a positive, eta-uniform limsup gap. It is a consequence of the local
analytic cycle argument, not a numerical attractor calculation. The
literature already observes default-beta cycle instability; instability
alone is not the argument. Bias-corrected and full-dimensional diagonal
claims remain open. No bound on a time average or invariant distribution
is asserted. Independent audit of uniform local capture is required.


VERSION2: FULL-DIMENSIONAL RANDOM INITIALIZATION FOR RANK ONE
Consider H=diag(lambda,0), lambda>0, with ordinary coordinatewise
uncorrected Adam and standard zero moments. The flat coordinate has
zero gradient and stays fixed for arbitrary x2,0. Thus active curvature
equals the scalar first-channel curvature whenever x1,t!=0. For an
absolutely continuous law on R^2, its first-coordinate marginal is
absolutely continuous, so the scalar exceptional set is null.

We also exclude exact zero iterates without an added assumption. For
fixed rho>0 and n>=1, the finite-time function X_n(X0) is real analytic
on each of (0,infinity),(-infinity,0), since V_1>0 and all later V stay
positive. It is not identically zero on either branch: the moment bound
gives |X_n-X0|<=nK, so X_n is unbounded as X0 tends to either infinity.
The real-analytic identity theorem makes its zeros isolated on each
branch and therefore countable. Union over n is countable. Outside
this extra null set all active quotients are defined, and the scalar
limsup bound transfers literally. The same countable-eta argument
already given proves the result simultaneously along any chosen
eta_n->0 for absolutely continuous random initial positions in R^2.

This is a full-dimensional random-initialization obstruction for the
RANK-ONE uncorrected quadratic, which is in the repaired row statement.
It is not a full-rank two-positive-eigenvalue result and is recorded
as special for target1. body:
Let B[u,v] be the bilinear form of a second-order elliptic operator in divergence form, B[u,v] = integral over Omega of ( sum a^{ij} u_{x_i} v_{x_j} + sum b^i u_{x_i} v + c u v ), with a^{ij} in L^infinity satisfying the uniform ellipticity condition sum a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j >= theta |xi|^2 for some theta > 0 and all xi, and with b^i, c in L^infinity. Then there are constants beta > 0 and gamma >= 0 such that B[u,u] >= beta ||u||^2_{H^1(Omega)} - gamma ||u||^2_{L^2(Omega)} for every u in H_0^1(Omega). That is, the form is coercive only AFTER subtracting a multiple of the L^2 norm; equivalently B[u,v] + gamma (u,v)_{L^2} is coercive, so Lax-Milgram applies to the shifted operator.
Uniform ellipticity and bounded coefficients.
The subtracted term gamma ||u||^2_{L^2} cannot in general be removed - it vanishes only when the zeroth-order coefficient is large enough (for example c >= 0 with b = 0 gives gamma = 0 by Poincare).
Forgetting the gamma term and asserting plain coercivity is the standard error, and it is exactly what makes the Dirichlet problem solvable only away from the spectrum.

[Theorem thm:inter clt of arXiv:2512.17747, 'On exponentially height-penalized random trees'] Let $\mu=\mu_n$ be such that $1/\sqrt{n}\ll\mu\ll n^{1/4}$.
    Let $\mathbf{T}_n$ be a $\mu$-height-biased tree of size $n$.
    Then
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{h(\mathbf{T}_n)-\left(\frac{2\pi^2n}{\mu}\right)^{1/3}}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{2\pi^2n}{\mu^4}\right)^{1/3}}}\overset d\longrightarrow\mathcal{N}(0,1)\,,
    \end{align*}
    where $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let Omega(t) be a family of bounded domains in R^n moving with a C^1 velocity field, whose boundary points move with normal speed V_n, and let f(x,t) be C^1. Then the derivative in t of the integral over Omega(t) of f equals the integral over Omega(t) of the partial derivative of f in t, plus the boundary integral of f times V_n with respect to surface measure. If the domain is transported by a flow with velocity field w then the boundary term is the integral of f (w dotted with nu), and the divergence theorem turns the identity into the integral over Omega(t) of ( partial f in t plus the divergence of f w ). In one dimension this is the classical Leibniz rule with the two endpoint terms f(b(t),t) b'(t) minus f(a(t),t) a'(t).
C^1 regularity of both the integrand and the motion of the domain;
ONLY the NORMAL component of the boundary velocity appears, since tangential motion does not change the region.
Forgetting the boundary term - differentiating under the integral sign as if the domain were fixed - is the standard error when a domain depends on the parameter.

[Thm quenched of arXiv:2607.00311, 'Thermal Concentration and Poisson--Dirichlet Edge Statistics for Random-Lattice Gibbs Ense'] Let $L_n$ be distributed according to $\mu_n$ on $\mathbb X_n$.
Assume $0<c<1$.
Then
$$
\frac{1}{n}\log B_{n,c}(L_n)\to F(c)
$$
in probability.
Moreover, for every fixed real number $a$ with $a\ne y_c$,
$$
\Pi_{n,c}((-\infty,a],L_n)\to
\begin{cases}
0, & a<y_c,\\
1, & a>y_c,
\end{cases}
$$
in probability.

body:
[Theorem thm:exact-interval-formula-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Assume that the dyadic vector-weight law is energy-admissible.  Let \(\mu\) be
the limiting dyadic vector cascade measure on \([0,1]\), and set
\(M=\mu([0,1])\).  Then, almost surely on \(\{M>0\}\),
\begin{equation}
    \dim_{\mathrm F}(\mu)
    =
    \dim_{\mathrm E}(\mu)
    =
    \dim_2(\mu)
    =
    D_{\mathrm E}(X).
\end{equation}
In particular, on the same event, if \(D_{\mathrm E}(X)>0\), then for every
\(0<\sigma<D_{\mathrm E}(X)\) there is a finite random constant
\(C_\sigma(\omega)<\infty\) such that
\begin{equation}
    |\widehat{\mu}(\xi)|
    \le
    C_\sigma(\omega)|\xi|^{-\sigma/2}
\end{equation}
for all sufficiently large \(|\xi|\).  If \(D_{\mathrm E}(X)=0\), the decay
assertion is vacuous, and all three dimensions in
(equation eq:exact-interval-vector-theorem-paper of the paper) are equal to \(0\).

body:
[Lemma 11 of arXiv:2603.28093, 'Random Stability of Random Variables'] Under the condition~\eqref{eq:ln-N}, a nonnegative $N$-stable $X$ has Laplace transform 
$$
\mathbb E\left[e^{-uX}\right] = L(\beta u^{\alpha})
$$
for the Laplace transform $L$ of the standard $N$-stable random variable $Y$, and for some $\alpha \in (0, 1]$ and $\beta > 0$. This $X$ can be represented as $X \stackrel{d}{=} Y^{1/\alpha}Z$, where $Z$ is the stable positive random variable of index $\alpha$, independent of $Y$, defined via Laplace transform
\begin{equation}

body: For a discrete random variable X taking values in a finite or countable set with probability mass function p(x) = Pr(X=x), the Shannon entropy is H(X) = - sum_{x: p(x)>0} p(x) * log p(x), using the convention 0*log 0 = 0. H(X) is measured in bits when the logarithm has base 2 (or nats for natural log). H(X) >= 0 always, H(X) = 0 exactly when X is deterministic (a single outcome has probability 1), and among distributions on a fixed set of m outcomes, H(X) is maximized, at value log m, by the uniform distribution.
title: Shannon Entropy

body: For Y = (1/3) sum_{k>=0} B_k (2/3)^k with fair independent bits B_k, the Fourier transform of its law mu (the Bernoulli-2/3 measure) has the exact closed form hat_mu(xi) = prod_{k>=0} (1 + exp(-2 pi i xi (2/3)^k / 3))/2, agreeing with an independent stationary-density solver's Fourier coefficients to 1e-11 at xi = 1,2,3,5,8,16,32. Writing mu_n for the law of frac(2^n Y), hat_mu_n(k) = hat_mu(2^n k) for every integer k, so every level of a 'fibre-bias' deficit ladder is the same measure evaluated at a doubled frequency; an explicit Fourier lower bound (Cauchy-Schwarz against a unimodular test function, the k=0 term vanishing by the Y -> 1-Y symmetry) reproduces 14-39 pct of the numerically measured fibre bias at ladder levels n=0..6 using 20,000-term sums, independently of any density solver. Along the lacunary orbit 2^n, |hat_mu(2^n)| reduces to the exact arithmetic product prod_{k>=0} |cos(pi 2^{n+k}/3^{k+1})|, each factor depending only on 2^{n+k} mod 2 * 3^{k+1} (verified digit-for-digit against the direct Fourier product for n=0..16), with only k up to about 1.71n contributing; because 2 is a primitive root mod every 3^j, the exact period-average of log|cos(pi u/3^{k+1})| over units u equals -log 2 for every k, predicting an average decay of about 1.185 per level n, while the MEASURED slope of log|hat_mu(2^n)| over n=0..16 is about 1.0 per level - the decay itself is bursty (0.31 at n=0, 4.1e-8 at n=7, back up to 1.7e-5 at n=10, 4.3e-9 at n=15), the small factors being exactly the k where 2^{n+k+1} lands near an odd multiple of 3^{k+1}, though the trend matches the prediction; the exchange of sums behind the prediction is rigorous only for k up to about log_3 n, where the window covers the period 2 * 3^k. For the rational, non-Pisot ratio lambda=2/3, the currently PROVED decay rate of hat_mu is only logarithmic in the frequency (giving deficits of order n^{-c}, not summable - the family a related paper bound n^{-13/25} belongs to), while the measured/predicted decay is vastly faster; the gap between the proved logarithmic rate and the faster measured rate is exactly the missing ingredient - a lacunary Fourier estimate for the 2/3 Bernoulli convolution better than logarithmic - and closing it requires simultaneous equidistribution of 2^{n+k} mod 3^{k+1} across k up to about 1.71n, an unproved, Erdos-Kahane-barrier-type statement (a literature check found proved Fourier decay for rational lambda=p/q is logarithmic-power in general, and known absolute-continuity results for algebraic parameters reach down to about lambda=0.7995, above 2/3=0.667). The chain end to end: such simultaneous equidistribution would give geometric decay of |hat_mu(2^n)|, which would give a stated two-level contraction target, which would give summability of the deficit ladder (that implication is Lean-checked), which would give a finite-entropy density; only the first link is unproved.

[Defn def-ct of arXiv:2607.25567, 'Random Trees in Hyperbolic FPP'] Let $(X, d_X)$ and  $(Y, d_Y)$  be  hyperbolic metric spaces and let $i: (Y,y_0) \to (X,x_0)$ denote a proper embedding. Let $\partial X, \, \partial Y$ be their (Gromov) boundaries.
	Also, let $\widehat X$ and $\widehat Y$ denote their Gromov compactifications.
	We say that the triple $(X,Y,i)$ admits a Cannon-Thurston map, if
	$i$ extends continuously to 
	$\widehat i: \widehat Y \to \widehat X$. The continuous extension, if it exists, is referred to as a \emph{Cannon-Thurston map} for 
	$i: Y \to X$.

body:
[Lemma 16 (Haar measure on $\ASim(V)$) of arXiv:2607.05219, 'Random free semigroups of affine groups'] The group $K:=\ker c=\Isom(V)$ is compact, and the sequence
\[
1\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow\Sim_{\lin}(V)\xrightarrow{\;c\;}\Lambda\longrightarrow1
\]
is exact, where $\Lambda:=c(\Sim_{\lin}(V))$. For any measurable section
$s:\Lambda\to\Sim_{\lin}(V)$, the map $(r,k)\mapsto s(r)k$ is a measurable
bijection $\Lambda\times K\to\Sim_{\lin}(V)$, and $dm_{\lin}$ disintegrates as
\[
dm_{\lin}(T)=dk\,d\nu(r),\qquad r=c(T),\quad k=s(r)^{-1}T,
\]
independently of the choice of $s$. Consequently,
\[
dm(b,T)=c(T)^{-d}\,db\,dk\,d\nu(r)
\]
is a left Haar measure on $\ASim(V)$, where $dk$ is the Haar probability measure
on $K$, and $d\nu$ is a Haar measure on the abelian group $\Lambda$.

body:
Let P be a product measure on a finite product of finite sets and let A and B be arbitrary events, not necessarily increasing. Then P(A box B) <= P(A) P(B), where A box B is the disjoint occurrence of A and B, witnessed by disjoint coordinate sets (Reimer 2000). This extends the van den Berg-Kesten inequality, which required both events to be increasing; the general statement had been conjectured by van den Berg and Kesten and by van den Berg and Fiebig. The proof is combinatorial (a butterfly lemma on pairs of subcubes) and does not go through monotonicity. The inequality still needs a product measure.
P is a product measure on a finite product of finite sets
A and B are arbitrary events (no monotonicity)
A box B is the disjoint-occurrence event

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The Lindeberg exchange (swapping) principle proves distributional limit theorems by replacing the summands or matrix entries of a random object one at a time with Gaussian (or other reference) analogues, bounding the resulting change in E[F] for a sufficiently smooth test function F via a Taylor expansion at each swap, provided the relevant moments, typically up to third or fourth order depending on the smoothness assumed of F, agree between the original and replacement distributions. In random matrix theory, the Tao-Vu four-moment theorem states that for Wigner matrices, local eigenvalue statistics such as gap distributions at a fixed bulk location are universal, independent of the specific entry distribution, provided the first four moments of the off-diagonal entries match those of the Gaussian (GOE/GUE) case up to a small, quantified error, with a weaker three-moment matching sufficing for some global statistics; this is the primary technical engine behind Wigner-Dyson-Mehta universality results beyond the exactly solvable Gaussian ensembles. It does not apply directly to test functions or statistics that are insufficiently smooth, requiring a separate regularization step, typically via a local relaxation flow or Dyson Brownian motion argument, to pass from smooth test functions to eigenvalue counting functions or individual eigenvalue locations, and it requires the specific moment-matching order assumed, with fewer matched moments giving correspondingly weaker conclusions. Typical failure: Applying the four-moment theorem's universality conclusion directly to a non-smooth statistic, such as the exact location or gap of a specific eigenvalue or an indicator-type event, without the additional Green's function comparison or local relaxation machinery needed to pass from smooth test functions to such statistics; the raw Lindeberg swapping argument by itself only controls E[F(eigenvalues)] for smooth F, and asserting the full local universality conclusion from moment matching alone skips this substantial extra step. Canonical reference: Lindeberg, 1922, Mathematische Zeitschrift; Tao and Vu, 2011, Acta Mathematica; Erdos and Yau, A Dynamical Approach to Random Matrix Theory, 2017, American Mathematical Society (Courant Lecture Notes).

[Proposition 107 (Uniform phase constants on separated parameter classes) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Fix a class $\mathfrak P(\underline c,\overline c,
\underline m,\overline m,\delta_*)$.  The constants in
Lemma~\ref{lem:explicit-phase-gap} may be chosen uniformly on that class.  One
may take, after changing the fixed Littlewood--Paley constants,
\[
  \delta_0=\min\left\{\frac14,
  \frac{\delta_*}{8\overline c}\right\},
  \qquad
  c_{\mathrm{sp}}
  \ge \kappa_{\mathrm{ann}}
      \min\{\delta_*,\underline c\}>0,
\]
and
\[
  N_{\mathrm{sp}}
  \le C_{\mathrm{ann}}\left(1+
  \frac{\overline m}{\sqrt{\underline c\,\delta_*}}\right),
\]
where $\kappa_{\mathrm{ann}},C_{\mathrm{ann}}>0$ depend only on the fixed
annular support constants.
The radial derivative lower bounds used in the continuous phase-layer
arguments and the scalar wave/Klein--Gordon Strichartz constants are likewise
uniform on the class.  These constants are independent of the forcing orders
and profiles.

[Pron 3 of arXiv:2506.18834, '\large\bf On the random-time and finite-time ruin probability for widely dependent claim s'] $(1)$ Let $\xi_i,i\geq1$ be WLOD (or WUOD) with common distribution $V$ on $(-\infty,\infty)$. If $f_i(\cdot),i\geq1$ are nondecreasing,
then $f_i(\xi_i),i\geq1$ are still WLOD (or WUOD);
if $f_i(\cdot),i\geq1$ are nonincreasing, then $f_i(\xi_i),i\geq1$ are WUOD (or WLOD).

$(2)$ If $\xi_i,i\geq1$ are nonnegative and WUOD with common distribution $V$ and finite mean,
then for each $n\geq1$,
$$E\prod^{n}_{i=1}\xi_{i} \leq g_{U,V}(n)\prod^{n}_{i=1}E\xi_{i}.$$
Therefore, if $\xi_i,i\geq1$ are WUOD with common distribution $V$ on $(-\infty,\infty)$ satisfying $Ee^{s {\xi_i}}<\infty$
for some $s>0$, then for each $n\geq1$,
$$Ee^{s \sum^{n}_{i=1}\xi_{i}} \leq g_{U,V}(n)\prod^{n}_{i=1}Ee^{s {\xi_i}}.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system. For a finite (or countable, with finite entropy) measurable partition $\xi = \{A_1, \dots, A_k\}$ put $H_\mu(\xi) = -\sum_i \mu(A_i) \log \mu(A_i)$ (with $0 \log 0 = 0$), and $\xi^n_0 = \bigvee_{j=0}^{n-1} T^{-j}\xi$, the partition into sets $A_{i_0} \cap T^{-1}A_{i_1} \cap \dots \cap T^{-(n-1)}A_{i_{n-1}}$ (the $n$-step itineraries). The entropy of $T$ relative to $\xi$ is $h_\mu(T, \xi) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n H_\mu(\xi^n_0)$ (the limit exists because $n \mapsto H_\mu(\xi^n_0)$ is subadditive; it also equals $\inf_n \frac1n H_\mu(\xi^n_0)$ and $\lim_n H_\mu(\xi \mid \xi^n_1)$). The Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is $h_\mu(T) = \sup_\xi h_\mu(T, \xi)$ over finite partitions, in $[0, \infty]$. Facts used constantly: $h_\mu(T, \xi) \le H_\mu(\xi) \le \log k$; $h_\mu(T, \xi) \le h_\mu(T, \eta) + H_\mu(\xi \mid \eta)$ for partitions $\xi, \eta$; $h_\mu(T^m) = m\, h_\mu(T)$ for $m \ge 1$; the Kolmogorov-Sinai generator theorem: if $\xi$ is a generator ($\bigvee_{j \ge 0} T^{-j}\xi$ generates $\mathcal{B}$ mod $\mu$, or $\bigvee_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}$ for invertible $T$) then $h_\mu(T) = h_\mu(T, \xi)$; and if $\xi_m$ is an increasing sequence of partitions generating $\mathcal{B}$ then $h_\mu(T, \xi_m) \uparrow h_\mu(T)$. On a compact metric space, partitions of diameter $< \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \to 0$ are such a sequence. The map $\mu \mapsto h_\mu(T)$ on invariant measures is affine, but it is NOT in general continuous or even upper semicontinuous in the weak* topology; upper semicontinuity holds when $T$ is expansive (and for $C^\infty$ maps of compact manifolds by Newhouse), which is what guarantees measures of maximal entropy exist in those cases.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check which steps of the d = 2 proof are dimension-dependent. Result: The source's d = 1+1 proof establishes superconcentration of the free energy (variance o(n)) via hypercontractivity and then chaos from superconcentration through the general equivalence theorem; the dimension-dependent step is the variance bound Var(log Z_n) = O(n/log n), obtained from the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm influence inequality applied to the free energy with the influence of a single site bounded by the expected overlap of two polymers at that site, whose sum over sites is the expected overlap, of order n in the strong disorder regime. The BKS argument is dimension-free provided the polymer is in the strong disorder phase (positive overlap); in d >= 3 the strong disorder phase exists at low temperature (Comets-Yoshida), so the variance bound O(n/log n) transfers and superconcentration follows; the equivalence theorem then gives chaos at the level of the overlap between the polymers at slightly perturbed environments. So the obstruction the source mentions ('certain parts do not work in higher dimensions') must be in the identification that the overlap in the strong-disorder phase is of order n (needed for the influence sum to be order n and the BKS gain to be meaningful): in d >= 3 at low temperature the overlap is positive but the known lower bounds are only qualitative (positive limit of the overlap along the endpoint), not quantitative along the whole path. Rigorous partial: superconcentration (Var log Z_n = o(n)) in d >= 3 at low temperature follows from BKS if the expected path overlap is of order n, which is a consequence of the strong disorder characterisation via the endpoint overlap only if the overlap is positive at a positive fraction of times; this last step is plausible but I found no reference proving it in d >= 3. Reduction recorded. Obstruction: Quantitative (order n) path overlap in the strong disorder phase for d >= 3.

[Lemma 2 (The viewing
angle) of arXiv:2608.06591, 'Random Triangles on Concentric Circles'] \protect\hypertarget{lem-omega}{}

Let \(\psi = \angle O P_i P_k\) and let
\(h = r_k \sin\omega = r_i \sin\psi\) be the distance from the center to
the line \(P_kP_i\). Then

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  if \(r_k \leq r_i\), the folded angle \(\min(\omega, \pi - \omega)\)
  is uniform on \((0, \pi/2)\);
\item
  if \(r_k \geq r_i\), the acute branch
  \(\psi_0 = \min(\psi, \pi - \psi)\) is uniform on \((0, \pi/2)\). (The
  line meets the circle twice, and \(\psi\) is obtuse at the far point,
  so \(\psi\) itself is not confined to \((0, \pi/2)\).)
\end{itemize}

In both cases \(h = \min(r_i, r_k)\sin\mu\) for a \(\mu\) uniform on
\((0, \pi/2)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:edge-spacing of arXiv:2507.12502, 'Quantitative Edge Eigenvector Universality for Random Regular Graphs: Berry-Esseen Bounds '] For random $d$-regular graphs with fixed $d \geq 3$, the eigenvalue spacing near the edge satisfies:
\[
\lambda_i - \lambda_{i+1} = \Theta(N^{-2/3}) \quad \text{for } |\lambda_i - 2| = O(N^{-2/3})
\]
This compressed spacing limits the convergence rate of eigenvector statistics to at most $N^{-1/6+o(1)}$.

Let u be harmonic and nonnegative in the open ball B_R(x0) in R^n, n >= 2. Then for every x with |x - x0| = r < R, R^{n-2} (R - r)/(R + r)^{n-1} u(x0) <= u(x) <= R^{n-2} (R + r)/(R - r)^{n-1} u(x0). In particular, taking r = R/2 in both bounds, sup over B_{R/2}(x0) of u <= 3^n inf over B_{R/2}(x0) of u. More generally, if Omega is a connected open set and K is a compact subset of Omega, there is C = C(n, K, Omega) such that sup over K of u <= C inf over K of u for every nonnegative harmonic u on Omega. Corollaries: Liouville's theorem for harmonic functions bounded below on R^n, and Harnack's convergence theorem for monotone sequences of harmonic functions.

[Prop 35 of arXiv:2609.02261, 'Quantization and process'] Let $A$ be a bounded   operator  in 
      $L^2( \R^n)$. Fix  a   probability measure $\nu$  on $\R^{2n}$. 
We define  an operator  $\Pi(\nu) (A) $ by, 
    
    $$ \Pi(\nu) (A)= \int _{ \R^{2n}} W_h (-X) A W_h (X) d\nu (X), $$
    
   where $ W_h (X)$ are the Weyl translation operators in (\ref{trans-Weyl}). Then, the following three points hold true.
    
    
    i) The map $ \Pi(\nu)$ 
    is bounded from ${\cal L} ( L^2( \R^n))$ into itself and from $C_h$ 
  into itself.
    
    ii) We have,
    
    $$ \Pi (\mu) \Pi (\nu) = \Pi (\mu \star \nu).$$
    
   iii) We also have,
   
    $$ \Pi (\mu) (A \circ B) =  \Pi (\mu) (A) \circ   \Pi (\mu) (B).$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 13 (Finite-time decay of the non-invariant part) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Given \(0<\alpha<1\), \(K\geq0\), \(\lambda>0\), an integer \(N\geq2\), and
\(\sigma\in(0,1)\), there are constants
\(\beta_{\mathrm{orb}}>0\) and \(\beta_{\mathrm{pert}}>0\) with the following
property.  Let \(h(t)\) be an invariant Ricci-flow solution on \(M\), defined
for \(t\in[1,100]\), such that \(|\sec_{h(t)}|\leq K\) and such that, for every
\(t\in[1,100]\), the quotient circle for the chosen local \(\TT^2\)-structure
has length at least \(\lambda\), while every local \(\TT^2\)-orbit has
\(h(t)\)-diameter less than \(\beta_{\mathrm{orb}}\).  Let \(g_\RDT(t)\) be a
solution of the Ricci--DeTurck equation relative to \(h(t)\), defined for
\(t\in[1,100]\), and assume
\[
        \|g_\RDT-h\|_{X_h^N[1,100]}<\beta_{\mathrm{pert}}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
        \|g_\RDT^\perp\|_{X_h^N[10,100]}
        \leq \alpha\,\bigl\|g_\RDT^\perp(1)\bigr\|_{C^{N,\sigma}(M,h(1))}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2608.08242, 'Bang--bang representation of $3\times 3$ embeddable stochastic matrices'] The set $R_n\subseteq\mathcal M_+$ consists of the matrices $A$ for which
	\[
	A\sim
	X_{i_nj_n}(t_n)\cdots X_{i_1j_1}(t_1)
	\]
	for some $i_\ell\neq j_\ell$ and some $t_\ell\geq0$. Put
	$R_\infty=\bigcup_nR_n$.
	
	The threshold region $\T$ consists of matrices $A\in R_\infty$ with at least one zero entry.
	
	
	The vestibule $\V$  consists of the matrices $A>0$ such that $A\sim B X_{ij}(t)$
	for some $B\in\T$, some $i\neq j$, and some $t>0$.

	for some $B\in\V$, some $i\neq j$, and some $t>0$.

body: Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space, let g be a nonnegative mu-integrable function on X, and let f_1, f_2, ... be measurable functions with |f_n| <= g pointwise almost everywhere for every n. Then liminf_n f_n and limsup_n f_n are integrable, and the integral over X of liminf_n f_n dmu <= liminf_n of the integral of f_n dmu <= limsup_n of the integral of f_n dmu <= the integral over X of limsup_n f_n dmu. This chain follows from applying Fatou's lemma to g - f_n and to g + f_n, and it yields the dominated convergence theorem whenever f_n converges pointwise a.e.
title: Fatou-Lebesgue theorem

[Proposition 3 (\cite{Mitoma1983}, Mitoma's criterion) of arXiv:2607.01629, 'Quadratic fluctuations of speed-change Kawasaki dynamics'] The sequence of processes \(\left\{ (X_t^N)_{t\in [0,T]} \right\}_{N \in \mathbb{N}}\) is tight in

body: [Corollary 2.4 of arXiv:2512.19517, 'Spiking and Resetting'] For any $t>0$ and any $0<a\leq b\leq 1$, the probability distribution $P^{\varepsilon}_{c}(\cdot\,:\,t,a,b)$ over $\mathbb{N}_{0}$ converges in law to a Poisson distribution with parameter $f(0)\,t\,\lambda_{*}([a,b])=f(0)\,t\,\int_{a}^{b}\cfrac{dx}{x^{2}}=f(0)\,t\,(a^{-1}-b^{-1})\ .$ Furthermore, we have that, for any $n\geq 0$, the function $\Phi_{n}^{\varepsilon}:r\in[0,\infty)\mapsto\mathbb{P}(e_{1}^{\varepsilon}\geq r,N^{\varepsilon}_{(0,r]}([a,b])=n)\in[0,1]$ converges uniformly on any compact interval $[0,t]$, $t>0$, as $\varepsilon$ vanishes to $\Phi_{n}:r\in[0,\infty)\mapsto e^{-rf(0)}e^{-rf(0)\lambda_{*}([a,b])}\frac{(rf(0)\lambda_{*}([a,b]))^{n}}{n!}\in[0,1]\ ,$ where $\lambda_{*}([a,b])=\int_{a}^{b}dx/x^{2}=a^{-1}-b^{-1}$ as in the first part. [The paper prints this limit as $e^{-rf(0)}e^{-r\lambda_{*}([a,b]}\frac{(r\lambda_{*}([a,b]))^{n}}{n!}$; the factor $f(0)$ and the closing parenthesis are restored here: the limit is forced by Proposition 2.2, whose generating function $Z(z,\sigma:a,b)=\sum_{n}z^{n}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\sigma r}\Phi_{n}(r)\,dr=1/(\sigma+f(0)+(1-z)f(0)(1/a-1/b))$ inverts to it, and the paper derives the first part, Poisson with parameter $f(0)\,t\,(a^{-1}-b^{-1})$, from it.] Notation from the paper: $e_{1}^{\varepsilon}=\inf\{t\geq 0:X_{t}^{\varepsilon}>y_{*}^{\varepsilon}\}$ is the first jump time; $N^{\varepsilon}_{(0,r]}([a,b])$ is the number of pre-spikes in $(0,r]\times[a,b]$; and $P^{\varepsilon}_{c}(n,t:a,b)$ is the probability of exactly $n$ pre-spikes in $(0,t)\times[a,b]$ given no jump in $(0,t)$, i.e. the no-jump probability of that event divided by $\mathbb{P}(e_{1}^{\varepsilon}\geq t)$.

[Proposition 125 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] In the setting of Theorem~\ref{proposition_FFF_conditioning}, let $\mu^X$ be the equilibrium measure of the ensemble $X$, $\mu^Y$ the equilibrium measure of $Y$. Let $h \in [H]$ and set $\amsmathbb{A}_h^{Y} = \amsmathbb{A}^Y \cap [\hat{a}_h',\hat{b}_h']$. For any $\delta > 0$, there exists constants $C_1,C_2 > 0$ depending only on $\delta$ and the constants in the assumptions such that, for any $z \in \amsmathbb{C}$ at distance at least $\delta$ from $\amsmathbb{A}_h^Y$, we have
\[
\bigg|\int_{\amsmathbb{A}^{Y}_h} \frac{\mu_h^X(x) - \mu^{Y}_h(x)}{z - x} \dd x \bigg| \leq \frac{C_1}{\N}.
\]
The upper bound is actually
\[
\bigg|\int_{\amsmathbb{A}^{Y}_h} \frac{\mu_h^X(x) - \mu^{Y}_h(x)}{z - x} \dd x \bigg| \leq \frac{C_2}{\N^2}.
\]
in case the following three conditions hold simultaneously
\begin{itemize}
\item the endpoints $\hat{a}_h'$ and $\hat{b}'_h$ are in a void, or $\theta_{h,h} = 1$;
\item $\iota_h^{-,X} = 0$, or $\rho_{h,j}^{-,X} = \theta_{h,h}$ for every $j \in [\iota_h^{-,X}]$;
\item $\iota_h^{+,X} = 0$, or $\rho_{h,j}^{+,X} = \theta_{h,h}$ for every $j \in [\iota_h^{+,X}]$.
\end{itemize}
Similar results hold in the setting of Theorem~\ref{proposition_fluct_conditioning}, provided we take $\mu^X$ to be the measure obeying fixed filling fractions constraints and compare it with $\mu^Y$ corresponding to the same constraints. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] Suppose $c\colon \mathbb R\to \cN_{\mathrm{ne}}(E)$ is a continuous curve which is smooth away from a finite set $D\subset \mathbb R$ of the domain. 
Thus, for $t\notin D$, the velocity $\frac{dc}{dt}$ is a complete $\mathbb R$-filtration $\cF_\lambda^{t}$ of $\operatorname{gr}(E,c(t))$.
The \textbf{support} of $c$ is the closure, $\mathcal W(c)$, of the set of pairs $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2$ such that $\operatorname{gr}_{\lambda(x,t)}\cF^t\neq 0$.
We restrict to curves $c$ where $\cW(c)$ is topologically a graph with finitely many vertices.
Each edge of the graph comes with a label, the object $\operatorname{gr}_{\lambda(x,t)}\cF^t\in\mathbf{Rep}(Q,\mathbf k)$.
The path is said to be \textbf{harmonic} if every edge of $\mathcal W(c)$ is labeled by a $Z$-semistable object in $\mathbf{Rep}(Q,\mathbf k)$, and the edge is a straight line with direction $\pm\overline{Z(A)}$. (See Figure~(fig:specnetdeform of the paper), right.)
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'

[Proposition prop:COntractionkappap of arXiv:2603.00773, 'Long-time $L^p$ Wasserstein contraction for diffusion processes without global dissipativi'] Under Assumption~(Assum:basic of the paper),  for all $p\geqslant 1$ and $t\geqslant 0$,
\[\kappa_p^p(t) = \sup_{x,y\in\mathbb R^d,x\neq y} \frac{\mathbb E_{(x,y)}\left( |X_t-Y_t|^p \right)}{|x-y|^p}\,,\]
where, in the right hand side, $(X_t,Y_t)_{t\geqslant 0}$ are two solutions of~(equation eq:EDS_X of the paper) (driven by the same Brownian motion $B$) with $(X_0,Y_0)=(x,y)$. In particular, for any $t\geqslant 0$, given two solutions of~(equation eq:EDS_X of the paper) (with the same Brownian motion),
\[\mathbb E \left( |X_t-Y_t|^p\right) \leqslant \kappa_p^p(t) \mathbb E \left( |X_0-Y_0|^p\right)\,.\]
As a consequence, for all $p\geqslant 1$ and $t\geqslant 0$,  $\beta_p(t) \leqslant \kappa_p(t)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited), claim T381-C002 v1. Let n(lambda) be polynomial, efficiently computable and positive. A stateless polynomial-time watermark for the n-bit uniform binary model yields a secret-key zero-bit PRC for exactly the same binary channel C if it has (i) undetectability for polynomially many samples under one key, (ii) uniformly negligible key-averaged acceptance of every fixed key-independent string, and (iii) negligible robust-completeness error on outputs whose original-model empirical entropy exceeds b_lambda(n), with b_lambda(n)<=n. Encode by watermark sampling and decode by keyed detection. With a deterministic termination token use b_lambda(n+1)<=n, strip that token on encoding and restore it on detection. Malformed outputs can be replaced by 0^n, adding only their negligible probability to completeness error. For independent fair-bit refresh rate s the exact inherited bit-flip rate is s/2. This gives no unconditional impossibility from one-way functions; only applicable black-box separation classes transfer.

Let W be a real symmetric n by n matrix whose entries W_{ij} for i <= j are independent standard Gaussians, and let H = W / sqrt(n) with eigenvalues lambda_1, ..., lambda_n. Let f be Lipschitz with constant ||f||_L. Then for every t > 0, P( | (1/n) sum_{i=1}^n f(lambda_i) - E (1/n) sum_i f(lambda_i) | >= t ) <= 2 exp( - n^2 t^2 / (4 ||f||_L^2) ). The exponent scales like n^2 t^2, not n t^2: linear eigenvalue statistics are FAR more concentrated than an average of n independent samples would be, and their fluctuations are of order 1/n rather than 1/sqrt(n). This is a consequence of the eigenvalue repulsion built into the matrix model, and it is one of the few places where a naive independence heuristic gives the wrong exponent by a whole power of n. The result needs only Lipschitz f - no smoothness, no boundedness - and it is a statement about concentration around the MEAN, not about identifying the mean, which is the separate content of Wigner's theorem. The constant 4 in the denominator is tied to the stated normalisation (independent standard Gaussians for the free entries, then divided by sqrt(n)); a different convention rescales it. [standard; the argument is Hoffman-Wielandt plus Gaussian Lipschitz concentration, e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Theorem 2.3.5]
free entries independent standard Gaussian, H = W/sqrt(n)
f Lipschitz; no other regularity
the bound is around the mean, which is not identified here

body:
[Thm 3 of arXiv:2608.30554, 'Strong law of large numbers for generalized operator means II'] Assume that \(\varphi: \mathbb{P} \times \mathbb{P} \rightarrow \mathbb{S}\) is Lipschitz continuous on any bounded \(d_\infty\)-metric ball. Furthermore, for each \(x \in \mathbb{P}\), there exists an \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that the family of functions
    $$ \mathcal{F}_{x, \varepsilon} = \left\{ \left\| s^{-1/2} \varphi(s, y) s^{-1/2} \right\| \colon d_\infty(s,x) < \varepsilon \right\} $$
admits a common $L^1$-dominating function. In addition, for every \(y \in \mathbb{P}\), we have \(\alpha(\varphi(\: \cdot \:, y)) \geq \alpha > 0\). Let \(Y_1, Y_2, \ldots\) be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with law \(\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{P})\). Then, for any initial point \(S_0 \in \mathbb{P}\), the stochastic resolvent iteration defined by
$$
S_{n+1} = J_{\frac{1}{n+1}}(Y_{n+1}, S_n)
$$
almost surely converges to \(\Lambda_\varphi(\mu)\) in the Thompson metric.

[Proposition prop:two-example of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $B:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<1\}$ be the unit disk centered at the origin
and, for $\tau>0$, set
\[
  F_\tau(z):=z+\tau z^3,
  \qquad D_\tau:=F_\tau(B).
\]
Then
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] For every $\tau\in(0,1/3)$, the domain $D_\tau$ is a bounded,
simply connected, noncircular domain with analytic boundary.
\item[(ii)] There exist $\tau_0\in(0,1/3)$ and a family
$\{r_\tau\}_{0<\tau<\tau_0}\subset(0,1)$ such that
\[
  r_\tau\longrightarrow r_0:=\sqrt{\sqrt5-2}
  \quad\text{as }\tau\to0,
\]
and, for every $\tau\in(0,\tau_0)$ and every $\mu>0$, the function
$W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}$ corresponding to
$\kappa_1=\mu=-\kappa_2$ has a strict nondegenerate local minimum point at
\[
  \bigl(F_\tau(r_\tau),F_\tau(-r_\tau)\bigr).
\]
\end{itemize}

body: Let W_t be a standard Brownian motion on [0,T] under a probability measure P, and let theta_t be an adapted process satisfying Novikov's condition E[exp((1/2) integral_0^T theta_t^2 dt)] < infinity. Define Z_t = exp(-integral_0^t theta_s dW_s - (1/2) integral_0^t theta_s^2 ds) and a new measure Q with dQ/dP = Z_T. Novikov's condition makes Z_t a true martingale, and Girsanov's theorem states that under Q the process W~_t = W_t + integral_0^t theta_s ds is again a standard Brownian motion. So an equivalent change of measure removes or adds a drift theta. Due to Igor Girsanov.
title: Girsanov theorem

[Theorem 12 of arXiv:2512.01483, 'Scaling Limits of Line Models in Degenerate Environment'] For $T>0$, let $\hat{X}^{(T)}(t) := (\hat{X}^{(T)}_1(t), \hat{X}^{(T)}_2(t))$, $t \geq 0$, where 
\[ \hat{X}^{(T)}_1(t) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{T}} \hat{X}^T_1(Tt), \quad \hat{X}^{(T)}_2(t) := T^{-\frac{1}{2\delta}} \hat{X}^T_2(Tt), \qquad t \geq 0. \]
Then, for $\mathbb{P}$-a.e. $\omega$, as $T \to \infty$, the process $(\hat{X}^{(T)}(t))_{t \geq 0}$ converges in distribution, in $D \times D$, to

[Definition 18 (Weak and logarithmic Schatten ideals) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Let $1<r<\infty$.  We use
\begin{align}
 \norm{T}_{r,\infty}^{*}
 &:=\sup_{n\ge1}n^{1/r}s_n(T),
 \\
 \norm{T}_{\Sch_{r,\infty}}
 &:=\sup_{n\ge1}n^{1/r}s_n^{**}(T).
 
\end{align}
The first is the standard weak quasi-norm and the second is an equivalent
fully symmetric Banach norm:
\begin{equation}

 \norm{T}_{r,\infty}^{*}
 \le\norm{T}_{\Sch_{r,\infty}}
 \le\frac r{r-1}\norm{T}_{r,\infty}^{*}.
\end{equation}
For $\alpha\ge0$, define
\begin{equation}

 \norm{T}_{\Sch_{r,\infty}(\log\Sch)^{-\alpha}}
 :=
 \sup_{n\ge1}
 n^{1/r}(\log(e+n))^{-\alpha}s_n^{**}(T).
\end{equation}
For Hilbert spaces $E,F$, the notation
$\Sch_{r,\infty}(E,F)$ denotes the compact operators $T:E\to F$ for which
\eqref{eq:weak-schatten-fully-symmetric} is finite, and
$\Sch_{r,\infty}(\log\Sch)^{-\alpha}(E,F)$ is defined analogously by
\eqref{eq:weak-logarithmic-schatten}.  The standard weak quasi-norm
\eqref{eq:weak-schatten-standard} defines the same first class.

Indeed, $n s_n^{**}(T)=\sum_{j=1}^n s_j(T)$ is the $n$th Ky Fan norm, so
\eqref{eq:weak-logarithmic-schatten} is a supremum of positive multiples of
unitarily invariant, fully symmetric norms.  It is therefore a fully
symmetric Banach ideal norm; monotone convergence of the finite Ky Fan sums
gives the Fatou property.  Moreover, $s_n\le s_n^{**}$ and
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^n j^{-1/r}\le\frac r{r-1}n^{1-1/r},
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:weak-norm-equivalence}.
All these spaces are the full, or maximal/Fatou, ideals.  In particular,
finite-rank operators need not be dense in
\eqref{eq:weak-schatten-fully-symmetric}; the proof below does not assume
such density.
title: Weak and logarithmic Schatten ideals

[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2608.27450, 'Koszul duality and Morita categories'] Let $\sA$, $\sB$, and $\sC$ be stable presentable categories, and let $\sQ$, $\sR$, and $\sS$ be strongly positive coalgebras in the categories $\SSeqnu(\sA,\sA)$, $\SSeqnu(\sB, \sB)$ and $\SSeqnu(\sC, \sC)$ respectively.
    Suppose we are given bicomodules
    \[
    M \in \BcoMod_{(\sS, \sR)}(\SSeqnu(\sB, \sC)) \quad \text{and} \quad N \in \BcoMod_{(\sR, \sQ)}(\SSeqnu(\sA, \sB)).
    \]

    \[
    \SSeqnu(\sA, \sC) \times \SSeqnu(\sD, \sA) \to \SSeqnu(\sD, \sC) \quad \text{and} \quad \SSeqnu(\sC, \sD) \times \SSeqnu(\sA, \sC)  \to \SSeqnu(\sA, \sD)
    \]
    preserve the limit defining the relative cobar construction $M \Box_{\sR} N$.

body:
Recall that a real function g on a topological space Z is of BAIRE CLASS ONE if it is the pointwise limit of a sequence of continuous real functions on Z. THEOREM (Baire for R x R; Rudin in this generality): let X be a METRIC space, let Y be a topological space (in particular a metric space), and let f: X x Y -> R be SEPARATELY CONTINUOUS, i.e. for each fixed y the map x -> f(x,y) is continuous on X and for each fixed x the map y -> f(x,y) is continuous on Y. Then f is of Baire class one on X x Y: there is a sequence of continuous functions f_n: X x Y -> R with f_n(x,y) -> f(x,y) for every (x,y). CONSEQUENCE (Baire's theorem on functions of the first class): if in addition X x Y is a Baire space - for instance if X and Y are both complete metric, or both locally compact Hausdorff - then the set of points at which f is JOINTLY continuous is a dense G_delta subset of X x Y, and its complement is meagre. So a separately continuous function is jointly continuous at 'most' points, in the sense of category. CLASSICAL EXTENSION: a function of n variables that is separately continuous in each variable is of Baire class n - 1 (Lebesgue); the case n = 2 is the theorem above. SHARP EDGES. (a) Separate continuity does NOT give joint continuity: f(x,y) = xy/(x^2 + y^2) with f(0,0) = 0 is separately continuous on R^2, indeed continuous on each line through the origin, and is discontinuous at the origin (it equals 1/2 on the diagonal). The theorem therefore cannot be strengthened to continuity anywhere in particular, only to a residual set of continuity points. (b) The metric structure of the first factor is essential to the proof, which builds a locally finite partition of unity on X; for arbitrary topological factors the statement requires extra hypotheses and should not be quoted in that generality. (c) The consequence about continuity points needs X x Y to be a Baire space; on a non-Baire domain 'dense G_delta' carries no information, and the conclusion is vacuous. (d) Baire class one is a statement about POINTWISE limits; it gives no uniform convergence, and the limit functions f_n constructed in the proof are not monotone in n. (e) The converse is false and is not being claimed: plenty of Baire class one functions on a product are not separately continuous.
X is a metric space
Y is a topological space (metric suffices, and is the usual case)
f: X x Y -> R is separately continuous: continuous in each variable with the other held fixed

Let D_d be the closed span of the psi_j and P_<=M its orthogonal projection onto the first M modes. Define the feature kernel U_d(theta,thetaprime)=E_x~nu_d sigma_d(x,theta)sigma_d(x,thetaprime), its spectral tail U_>r=sum_(j>r) mu_j phi_j phi_j^T, and kappa_r=sum_(j>r)mu_j>0 for each cutoff used. Draw theta_1,...,theta_N independently from tau_d and let K_ij=U_d(theta_i,theta_j). All stochastic rates below are as d->infinity. (H) There is one sequence u(d)>=M(d) such that, for every fixed real q>=1, all g in span{phi_1,...,phi_u} satisfy ||g||_(L2q(tau_d))<=C_q||g||_(L2(tau_d)), with C_q independent of d and g. (E) For the same u there is a fixed delta_E>0 such that N^(2+delta_E)<=kappa_u^2/sum_(j>u)mu_j^2 eventually. (Sa) There is a fixed delta_a>0 with N^(1+delta_a)<=kappa_M/mu_(M+1) eventually. With Lambda=diag(U_>M(theta_i,theta_i)/kappa_M), Proposition2 gives K>=kappa_M(Lambda+Delta) in positive-semidefinite order, where Delta is symmetric and E||Delta||_op=O(N^(-delta_prime)) for some fixed delta_prime>0. If in addition (Dlower) For every epsilon>0, min_i U_>M(theta_i,theta_i)/kappa_M=Omega_P(N^(-epsilon)), where Omega_P means that the reciprocal divided by N^epsilon is stochastically bounded. then K is invertible with probability tending to1 and kappa_M||K^(-1)||_op=O_P(N^epsilon) for every fixed epsilon>0. Let (X, Y) be a jointly Gaussian random vector in R^a x R^b with means mu_X, mu_Y and covariance blocks A = Cov(X), B = Cov(X, Y), C = Cov(Y), so its covariance matrix is M = [[A, B], [B^T, C]], possibly singular; A^+ is the Moore-Penrose inverse, and a value x is compatible when x - mu_X lies in the range of A (the support of X). For every compatible x, the support of the conditional law of Y given X = x is an affine subspace of dimension rank K = rank M - rank A, where K = C - B^T A^+ B; it does not depend on x.

[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2607.19873, 'Local limit theorem for the operator norm of products of random matrices'] Let $B$ be a compact metric space and let $\pi: E \to B$ be a 
Lipschitz vector bundle of dimension $d$ over $B$. 
Let $G$ be a locally compact group acting on $E$ by an isometric Lipschitz bundle action. 
Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $G$. 
For any continuous section $s: B \to E$, define the operator $P_\mu$ by
\begin{align*}
P_{\mu} s (b) = \int_{G}  g^{-1} s (g b) \mu(dg), \quad b \in B. 
\end{align*}
Then $P_{\mu} s: B \to E$ is again a continuous section, and the operator $P_{\mu}$ is bounded on $\bf \Gamma^{0}(E)$. 

Assume furthermore that there exists a constant $\alpha >0$ such that $\bb E ({\rm Lip}_E(g_1)^{\alpha} ) < \infty$. 
Then, for any $\gamma \in (0, \alpha)$, 
the operator $P_{\mu}$ is bounded on $\bf \Gamma^{\gamma}(E)$. 
Moreover, if $(G, \mu)$ satisfies the contraction property \eqref{contraction-property-on-B} on $B$,
then for any $\gamma \in (0, \min \{ \delta, \alpha \})$, 
the operator $P_{\mu}$ has essential spectral radius strictly less than $1$ on $\bf \Gamma^{\gamma}(E)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3 of arXiv:2607.19873

[Defn 6 of arXiv:2605.25762, 'Brownian Convergence of Planar Domains and Stability of the Planar Skorokhod Embedding Pro'] The Hilbert transform of a real valued $2\pi$- periodic function
$f$ is defined by 
\[
H\{f\}(x):=PV\left\{ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int^{\pi}_{-\pi}f(x-t)\cot(\frac{t}{2})dt\right\} =\lim_{\eta\rightarrow0}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\eta\leq|t|\leq\pi}f(x-t)\cot(\frac{t}{2})dt
\]
where $PV$ denotes the Cauchy principal value. The Hilbert transform
does exist a.e whenever $p\geq1$. However, it is a bounded operator
on $L^{p}_{2\pi}$ only when $p>1$. The case $p=1$ is irregular,
and $H$ becomes unbounded. For all proofs and properties of the Hilbert
transform, we refer the reader to \cite{butzer1971hilbert,king2009hilbert}.

body: In mathematics, the Mordell–Weil theorem states that for an abelian variety A over a number field K, the group A(K) of K-rational points of A is a finitely-generated abelian group, called the Mordell–Weil group. The case with A an elliptic curve E and K the field of rational numbers Q is Mordell's theorem, answering a question apparently posed by Henri Poincaré around 1901; it was proven by Louis Mordell in 1922. It is a foundational theorem of Diophantine geometry and the arithmetic of abelian varieties.

Let lambda be the security parameter and let lambda<=n(lambda)<=poly(lambda). Start with a binary secret-key zero-bit PRC: polynomial-time KeyGen, randomized Enc and Dec, uniformly negligible false acceptance of every fixed key-independent input, and computational indistinguishability against probabilistic polynomial-time oracle adversaries of fresh encodings under one fixed key from fresh independent uniform n-bit strings. There exist absolute constants C0,Crob>=1 such that the following holds. Fix0<p0<1/(10*Crob), and assume the base code is robust to every(1/2-p0)-substitution-bounded channel: for each randomized channel C satisfying d_H(x,C(x))<=(1/2-p0)*n almost surely for every x, decoding the corrupted fresh encoding accepts except with negligible probability in lambda, averaged over key, encoder, channel and decoder coins. Fix an integer rho>=C0/p0. Put q=rho*n and m=ceil(n*ln2). The new secret key is(k,psi), where k is the base key and psi:[q]->[n] is an independent uniform map with exactly rho preimages per label. To encode, draw b from the base encoder, draw U uniformly from[n]^m, and let S0={i:b_i=1},S1=Unique(U). If |S0 minus S1|>=|S1 minus S0|, choose a uniform injection from S1 minus S0 into S0 minus S1 and relabel its domain in U by its image. Otherwise choose a uniform injection tau:S0 minus S1->S1 minus S0 and replace each occurrence of tau(a) by a. Call the result Y, and independently lift each Y_j to a uniform Z_j in psi^{-1}(Y_j). Decode any received q-ary word w by applying the base decoder to the binary occupancy vector D_psi(w), whose ith bit is1 iff some symbol of w maps to i. This is a zero-bit PRC on[q] with block length m<=n. It is robust to every polynomial-time sampleable channel E that, for every input x, changes x by a total of at most(1-Crob*p0)*|x| insertions, deletions and substitutions almost surely. The channel receives the input word, not the secret balanced map. This is the zero-bit, fixed integer-rho implementation of Theorem4.1.
Binary secret-key zero-bit PRC with repeated-encoding oracle security, soundness and the stated substitution robustness; lambda<=n<=poly(lambda).
Fixed p0>0 below1/(10*Crob); fixed integer rho>=C0/p0. All fresh encoder and lift coins are independent.
Uniform balanced psi is secret and independent of the base key. Edit channels are efficiently sampleable and see the word alone.

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2609.01996, 'Baumslag--Solitar Subgroups Obstruct Model Companions for Fields with Group Actions'] Let \(\pi:\Gamma\twoheadrightarrow Q\) be a surjective group homomorphism and let \(K\) be a \(Q\)-field.
  Let \(K_\pi\) denote the \(\Gamma\)-field with the same underlying field and action
  \[
    \gamma\cdot a:=\pi(\gamma)(a).
  \]
  Then:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
    \item \(K\) is \(\aleph_0\)-saturated as a \(Q\)-field if and only if \(K_\pi\) is \(\aleph_0\)-saturated as a \(\Gamma\)-field;
    \item \(K\) is p.e.c. as a \(Q\)-field if and only if \(K_\pi\) is existentially closed in every regular \(\Gamma\)-field extension of \(K_\pi\) on which \(\ker(\pi)\) acts trivially.
  \end{enumerate}

[Proposition 25 (Pointwise detection of the weak logarithmic scale) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Fix \(0<p<2\), \(r\geq1\), and set
\[
 \varphi_{p,r}(N)
 :=N^{-1/p}\bigl(\log(e+N)\bigr)^{(r-1)/p}.
\]
For a compact \(T\), the following are equivalent:
\begin{align}
 s_N(T)&=O(\varphi_{p,r}(N)),\\
 \mathcal N_T(R)&=O(e^{pR}(1+R)^{r-1}),\\
 \mathfrak F_T(a)&=O(a^p(\log(e+a))^{r-1}).
 
\end{align}
The same equivalence holds with every \(O\) replaced by \(o\).
Thus the positive determinant detects both the weak and little
logarithmic ideals, even when no asymptotic equivalent exists.

[Lemma 20 (Antidiagonal orthogonality for links) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Let $(K_k)_{k\ge0}$ and $(L_\ell)_{\ell\ge0}$ be finite-rank operators of
the shapes in \eqref{eq:link-definition}.  Suppose that the initial
projections
\[
 q_k:=\supp(K_k^*K_k)\in\cL(X)
\]
are pairwise orthogonal and that the terminal projections
\[
 p_\ell:=\supp(L_\ell L_\ell^*)\in\cL(Y)
\]
are pairwise orthogonal.  Set
\[
 T_{k,\ell}:=\operatorname{Link}_Z(L_\ell,K_k),
 \qquad
 U_j:=\sum_{k+\ell=j}T_{k,\ell}.
\]
Then, for every $j\ge0$, the nonzero singular values of $U_j$, counted with
multiplicity, are the disjoint union
\begin{equation}

 s(U_j)=\bigsqcup_{k+\ell=j}s(T_{k,\ell}).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 \norm{U_j}_{\Sch_p}^p
 &=\sum_{k+\ell=j}\norm{T_{k,\ell}}_{\Sch_p}^p,
 &&1\le p<\infty,
 \notag\\
 \norm{U_j}_{\Sch_\infty}
 &=\max_{k+\ell=j}\norm{T_{k,\ell}}_{\Sch_\infty}.
 
\end{align}

[Definition 21 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Given an equilibrium measure $\boldsymbol{\mu}$, we will use the following terminology for each $h \in [H]$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[$\bullet$] A \emph{void} is a maximal (for the inclusion) and closed interval in $[\hat{a}'_h,\hat{b}'_h]$ where
$\mu_h(x) =0$.
\item[$\bullet$] A \emph{saturation} is a maximal closed interval in
$[\hat{a}'_h,\hat{b}'_h]$ where $\mu_h(x) = \frac{1}{\theta_{h,h}}$.
\item[$\bullet$] A \emph{band} is a maximal open interval in $[\hat a'_h,\hat b'_h]$ where $0<\mu_h(x)<\frac{1}{\theta_{h,h}}$.
\end{itemize}
We denote by $\amsmathbb{V}_{h}$ (respectively $\amsmathbb{S}_{h}$, $\amsmathbb{B}_{h}$) the union of voids (respectively saturations, bands) in $[\hat{a}'_{h},\hat{b}'_{h}]$. If we speak of a \emph{saturated segment} (respectively, a \emph{void segment}), we mean a segment included in a saturation (respectively, in a void) but not necessarily maximal.

body:
In the spiked covariance model with noise level $\sigma^2$ and ratio $\gamma = p/n$, let $\hat\lambda$ be a sample eigenvalue lying above the bulk edge, $\ell := \hat\lambda / \sigma^2 > (1 + \sqrt{\gamma})^2$. Then the unique $\theta > \sqrt{\gamma}$ with $(1 + \theta)(1 + \gamma/\theta) = \ell$ is $$\hat\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}\Big( (\ell - 1 - \gamma) + \sqrt{(\ell - 1 - \gamma)^2 - 4\gamma} \Big),$$ and $\sigma^2 (1 + \hat\theta)$ is the consistent estimate of the population eigenvalue behind $\hat\lambda$. The discriminant is nonnegative exactly when $\ell \ge (1 + \sqrt{\gamma})^2$, so the formula is defined precisely for eigenvalues at or above the edge. The population value $\sigma^2(1 + \hat\theta)$ is always strictly less than $\hat\lambda$ (a sample spike is debiased downward), by the amount $\sigma^2 \gamma (1 + 1/\hat\theta)$.
the spiked covariance model with a detected spike, i.e. a sample eigenvalue above the Marchenko-Pastur edge
gamma = p/n in (0, 1]

[Theorem contracted of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Suppose $\mathcal{E} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{X}$ is a smooth irreducible Cartier divisor, where $\mathcal{X}$ is a smooth, separated Deligne--Mumford stack of dimension $n > 1$.
    Suppose also that there exists a contraction $\pi : \mathcal{X} \to Z$ to a smooth irreducible variety of dimension $n$ such that $\pi(\mathcal{E}) = p \in Z$ and $\pi : \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{E} \xrightarrow{\sim} Z \setminus p$ is an isomorphism. 
    Then, $\mathcal{E}$ is algebraically simply-connected, i.e., $\pi_1^{\text{\'et}}(\mathcal{E}) \simeq 1$.

DRAFT author-derived material; independent review pending; no novelty or parent-solved claim. For N independent fair signs, let S=a_N sum_{i=1}^N sigma_i with a_N>0. Its MGF is cosh(a_N h)^N, variance V=N a_N^2, and first imaginary zero y_1=pi/(2a_N). Thus r=sqrt(V)y_1=pi sqrt(N)/2, while 3-E(S/sqrt(V))^4=2/N and S/sqrt(V) converges to N(0,1). Choosing a_N=N makes y_1 tend to zero even though normalized zeros escape and the limit is Gaussian. This refutes the generic inference from axis location or raw zero collapse to non-Gaussian scaling. It is not a counterexample to critical nearest-neighbor 3D Ising.

[Lemma 4 (Markov branching property) of arXiv:2605.11264, 'Uniform sampling of multitype continuous-time Bienaym\'e-Galton-Watson trees'] Assume $j\in \na\cup\{0\}$ and $k\in\na$ such that $j\leq k$ and $t\in (0,T)$.
Suppose that a vertex $v$ in $\mathcal{N}_{t}$, of type $c(v)$, carries $j$ marks at time $t$. 
Then, under $\Q^{(k),\bm \theta}_{T,r}$, the subtree generated by $v$ after time $t$ is independent of the rest of the system and behaves as if under $\Q^{(j),\bm \theta}_{T-t,c(v)}$. In particular, if $j=0$ then $\Q^{(0),\bm \theta}_{T-t,c(v)}=\p^{\bm \theta}_{T-t,c(v)}$.

body:
[Theorem thm:gen-frag-pos-recurrent of arXiv:2511.10223, 'Stochastic Reaction Networks Within Interacting Compartments with Content-Dependent Fragme'] Let $N$ be the coarse-grained model associated to (equation eq:general-content-dependent-fragmentation of the paper):
\begin{equation*}
\begin{tikzcd}
    \mathcal I_\mathcal K & &
    0\arrow[yshift=.5ex]{r}{\kappa_I}& C\arrow[yshift=-.5ex]{l}{\kappa_E} \arrow[yshift=.5ex]{r}{\kappa_FS_C}& 2C\arrow[yshift=-.5ex]{l}{\kappa_C} & &
    \mu.
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
Let $\mathcal A$ denote the generator of the associated chemistry $\mathcal I_\mathcal K$. Suppose there exists a linear function $f:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^d\to\mathbb R$ of the form $f(x)=w\cdot x$ for some $w\in\mathbb R_{>0}^d$, such that $\sup_x\mathcal Af(x)<\infty$, 
and that condition~(con:lambda finite of the paper) holds; that is, $\lambda<\infty$.
If $\kappa_C>0$ and $\kappa_E>0$, then the state with no compartments is positive recurrent for $N$, all states reachable from it are also positive recurrent for $N$, and all other states are transient with finite expected time to reach the set of positive recurrent states.

\begin{remark}
    If $f$ were a Lyapunov function witnessing (via Corollary (cor:lyapunov-positive-recurrence of the paper)) that $\mathcal I_\mathcal K$ was positive recurrent, we would have $\mathcal Af(x)\le-1$ outside some finite set. Similarly, if $f$ were witnessing that $\mathcal I_\mathcal K$ was recurrent, we would have $\mathcal Af(x)\le0$ outside some finite set. Either of these conditions would imply the assumption $\sup_x\mathcal Af(x)<\infty$ from the theorem. 
    
    The assumption $\sup_x\mathcal Af(x)<\infty$ is in fact \emph{strictly} weaker than having a Lyapunov function for recurrence, as we will see in Corollary (cor:spec-frag-pos-recurrent of the paper), when we apply it with the transient chemistry $0\to S$. However, the assumption $\sup_x\mathcal Af(x)<\infty$ is stronger than having a Lyapunov function for non-explosivity. Indeed, if $\sup_x\mathcal Af(x)<\infty$ and $f\to\infty$, then a suitable shift $g$ of $f$ will satisfy $\mathcal Ag(x)\le g(x)$.\hfill $\triangle$
\end{remark}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem (thm:gen-frag-pos-recurrent of the paper)]

Let $V(n)=C(n)+\alpha\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^d} n_x (w\cdot x)$, for some constant $\alpha>0$ to be chosen later. 
The assumption that every coordinate of $w$ is strictly positive means that $V\to\infty$ in the sense of Corollary~(cor:lyapunov-positive-recurrence of the paper). 
Our goal is to show that $\mathcal L V(n)\le -1$ outside a finite set of states, which will then allow us to conclude positive recurrence via Corollary~(cor:lyapunov-positive-recurrence of the paper).

We next compute $\mathcal L V(n)$, the generator of $V$, and bound its growth term by term.
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal LV(n)
    &=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^d} \bigg[ \kappa_FS(x)n_x+\kappa_I\mu(x)(1+\alpha w\cdot x)+\alpha\sum_{\nu\to\nu'}n_x\lambda_{\nu\to\nu'}(x)\big(w\cdot(x+\nu'-\nu)-w\cdot x\big)\\

[Definition of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] We say $\mathfrak{F} = (W, \sqsubset)$ is a \emph{Kripke frame (k-frame)} if $W$ is a non-empty set and $\sqsubset$ is a binary relation on $W$,
  and $\mathfrak{M} = (\mathfrak{F}, V)$ is a \emph{Kripke model (k-model)} if $\mathfrak{F}$ is a k-frame and $V: \mathord{\mathrm{PropVar}} \to \mathcal{P}(W)$.
  Such $\mathfrak{M}$ is said to be \emph{based on} $\mathfrak{F}$.
  For $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \sqsubset, V)$, we define a \emph{satisfaction relation} $\Vdash_\mathfrak{M}$ on $W \times \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}$ by:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item $x \nVdash_\mathfrak{M} \bot$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} p \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} x \in V(p)$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \land \psi_2 \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} (x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \mathrel{\text{\&}} x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_2)$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \lor \psi_2 \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} (x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \mathrel{\text{or}} x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_2)$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \to \psi_2 \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} (x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \mathrel{\Rightarrow} x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_2)$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \Box \varphi \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} \forall y \sqsupset x \, (y \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \varphi)$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \varphi \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} \exists y \sqsupset x\, (y \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \varphi)$
  \end{enumerate}

Fix N>=1 data points, output dimension K>=1, real offsets b_i in R^K, and fixed matrices G_ij in R^(m by n). Define h(D)=N^(-1) sum_i ell_i(b_i+(<G_ij,D>)_(j=1..K)), where each ell_i:R^K->R is convex, nonnegative and twice continuously differentiable. This is the exact affine/NTK model, not an error bound for a nonlinear network. Let lambda>=0 and suppose h(D)+lambda||D||_* has a global minimizer. Let r>=1 satisfy r(r+1)/2>KN. For U in R^(m by r), V in R^(n by r), Q=[U;V], and P in S_+^(m+n), set F_P(U,V)=h(UV^T)+(lambda/2)(||U||_F^2+||V||_F^2)+<P,QQ^T>. For Lebesgue-almost every nonzero P in the full PSD cone (with ambient symmetric-matrix Lebesgue measure), every second-order stationary point of F_P is a global minimizer of F_P. The same almost-sure conclusion holds for any perturbation law absolutely continuous with respect to that measure, including laws supported in an arbitrarily small PSD ball. The conclusion does not cover deterministic P=0, a measure supported on a lower-dimensional face, or finite-iteration convergence of GD.
Same exact affine/NTK model and nonnegative convex C2 losses as Theorem3.1
lambda>=0 and existence of an unperturbed nuclear-regularized global minimum
Strict rank threshold r(r+1)/2>KN
Nonzero P is generic with ambient symmetric Lebesgue measure; distributional form requires absolute continuity
Unconstrained U,V and exact gradient zero / Hessian positive semidefinite

Before a harmonic fluctuation calculation can support a low-temperature Riesz crystal argument, the chosen lattice must have a nonnegative displacement Hessian in the relevant directions. Force balance alone is insufficient, as the density-one simple cubic lattice has a finite-support negative second variation for every s>3. Even a valid finite infrared fluctuation integral in dimension three leaves the nonlinear control of defects, competing phases and a symmetry-breaking infinite-volume Gibbs limit open. This is a proof-route guard, not a solution of P0309.
Classical three-dimensional continuum Riesz crystal proof route
Reference to the counterexample at s>3 only

[Thm conditional-rank-one-bound of arXiv:2607.21428, 'Subcritical percolation and network archaeology on random recursive tree substrate network'] Assume the rank-one comparison setup satisfies the edge bound, the
		maximum-weight bound, and the susceptibility bound.  Then, for every
		\(r>0\), there is \(C_r<\infty\) such that, for every \(L\geqslant0\), every
		\(t>0\), and all sufficiently large \(n\),
		\begin{equation}
			
			\mathbb P\left(
			\max_{\mathcal{D}:\,\mathcal{D}\cap[L]=\varnothing}w(\mathcal{D})>t
			\right)
			\leqslant
			C_r t^{-r}\sum_{i>L}w_{n,i}^r.
		\end{equation}
		In particular, if, for a fixed \(L\) with \(L+1\leqslant N_n\) eventually and
		some \(r_L>0\),
		\[
		\sum_{i>L}
		\left(\frac{w_{n,i}}{w_{n,L+1}}\right)^{r_L}
		\leqslant C_L
		\qquad\text{for all large }n,
		\]
		then
		\[
		\max_{\mathcal{D}:\,\mathcal{D}\cap[L]=\varnothing}w(\mathcal{D})
		=O_{\mathbb P}(w_{n,L+1}).
		\]
		Finally, suppose the weights are random.  Assume there are events \(E_n\),
		measurable with respect to the weights, with \(\mathbb P(E_n)\to1\), such that on
		\(E_n\), conditional on the realized weights, the deterministic rank-one
		comparison setup above holds with the same constants \(p,\beta,\nu\) and with
		a deterministic error sequence \(\varepsilon_n\to0\) in the edge bound.  If,
		for some \(r>1/p\),
		\begin{equation}
			
			\lim_{L\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}
			\mathbb P\left(
			n^{-pr}\sum_{i>L}w_{n,i}^r>\varepsilon
			\right)=0
			\qquad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.
		\end{equation}
		then
		\[
		\lim_{L\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}
		\mathbb P\left(
		n^{-p}
		\max_{\mathcal{D}:\,\mathcal{D}\cap[L]=\varnothing}w(\mathcal{D})>\varepsilon
		\right)=0
		\]
		for every \(\varepsilon>0\).

body:
[Defn contFV of arXiv:2608.06500, 'Free energy of Ising models under a spectral condition'] For $\alpha>0$, an \emph{$\alpha$-good potential} is a
    function $V:\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$,  $(h,\varphi)\mapsto V_h(\varphi)$ 
    which is twice continuously differentiable 
    
    with 
    \[
        \sup_{\substack{|h|\le C \\ \varphi\in\mathbb{R}}}
        \left| \frac\partial{\partial h} V_h'(\varphi)\right| < \infty
    \]
    for all $C>0$ and $V_h''(\varphi)\in[\alpha,\alpha^{-1}]$
    for all $h,\varphi\in\mathbb{R}$ (where  $V_h'$ and $V_h''$ are the first and
     second  derivatives of $V_h$ with respect to $\varphi$). In other words, this family of potential
    functions is smooth and uniformly strongly convex with Lipschitz
    gradient, and furthermore $V_h'$ is Lipschitz in $h$. For
    $\text{\boldmath $h$}\in\mathbb{R}^N$, we define the potential

    \begin{align*}
V_\text{\boldmath $h$}(\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}):=\sum_{i=1}^NV_{h_i}(\varphi_i)\, .
\end{align*}

    Given an $\alpha$-good potential $V$ and
    a weighted graph $G=(\text{\boldmath $B$},\text{\boldmath $h$})$ on $[N]$ with $\text{\boldmath $B$}\succ-\alpha\text{\boldmath $I$}$,
    we consider the Gibbs measure on $\mathbb{R}^N$ with base measure
    $e^{-V_\text{\boldmath $h$}(\text{\boldmath $\varphi$})}{\rm d}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}$ and quadratic Hamiltonian
    $-\frac12\<\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}, \text{\boldmath $B$}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}\>$ and denote its free energy density
    by

    \begin{align*}
F_V(G)=F_V(\text{\boldmath $B$},\text{\boldmath $h$})=\frac1N \log \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \exp\left( -\frac12
\<\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}, \text{\boldmath $B$}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}\> \right) e^{-V_\text{\boldmath $h$}(\text{\boldmath $\varphi$})} {\rm d}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}.
\end{align*}
title: Defn contFV of arXiv:2608.06500

[Definition def:languages-formulas of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] Let $\mathord{\mathrm{PropVar}}$ be the set of all propositional variables, and let:
  \begin{align*}
    \mathscr{L}_p  &= \mathord{\mathrm{PropVar}} \cup \set{ \land, \lor, \to, \bot },
      & \mathscr{L}_\Box &= \mathscr{L}_p \cup \set{ \Box }, \\
    \mathscr{L}_\Diamond &= \mathscr{L}_p \cup \set{ \Diamond },
      & \mathscr{L}_{\Box\Diamond}  &= \mathscr{L}_p \cup \set{ \Box, \Diamond },
  \end{align*}
  where $\bot$ is nullary, $\Box, \Diamond$ are unary, and $\land, \lor, \to$ are binary.
  We use $\top$ and $\neg \varphi$ as abbreviations for $\bot \to \bot$ and $\varphi \to \bot$, respectively.
  The formulas of each language are built from $\mathord{\mathrm{PropVar}}$ and $\bot$ in the usual inductive way using these connectives.
  For a language $\mathscr{L}$, by abuse of notation, we also write $\mathscr{L}$ for the set of all formulas in $\mathscr{L}$.
title: Definition def:languages-formulas of arXiv:2608.29708

[Lemma app-L-1 of arXiv:2608.30548, 'Finite speed of propagation and waiting time phenomena for stochastic porous media equatio'] Let $ 1 \le r \le \infty$, $0< q <p$, $ m \in \mathbb{N}_+$
such that
\[
\frac 1r - \frac mN < \frac 1p \,.
\]
If $\mathcal{O} \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ is bounded with piecewise smooth boundary,
then positive constants $c_1$ and $ c_2$ depending only on $\mathcal{O},
r, p, m$ and $q$ exist such that for any $u \in L^q (\mathcal{O})$
satisfying $ D^m u \in L^r (\mathcal{O})$, the following inequality holds:
\begin{equation}
\| u \|_p \le c_1 \|D^m u\|^a_r \| u \|^{1-a}_q + c_2 \| u \|_q

\end{equation}
where $a = \frac{\frac 1q - \frac 1p}{\frac 1q + \frac m N - \frac
1r}$.

Especially, if $\mathcal{O}=\mathbb{R}^N$,  then ((eq-GN of the paper)) holds
with constant $c_1=c(r,p,m,q)$ and $c_2=0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma app-L-1 of arXiv:2608.30548

[Theoremb 2 (Positive-time heat-flow Schur convexity) of arXiv:2605.11451, '2605.11451'] Let $1\le p<2$ and $t>0$. The map
\[
 \theta\mapsto \widetilde A_{p,n,t}(\theta)
\]
is strictly Schur-convex as a function of $s(\theta)$. In particular, with
\[
 \diag=\frac1{\sqrt n}(1,\ldots,1),
\]
one has
\[
 \widetilde A_{p,n,t}(\diag)
 \le \widetilde A_{p,n,t}(\theta)
 \le \widetilde A_{p,n,t}(e_1),
 \qquad \theta\in\sphere,
\]
with equality only for the corresponding signed-permutation orbits. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Positive-time heat-flow Schur convexity

 +C \left(\dfrac{a^2}{\epsilon}+|a|\right)\Delta^2.

body:
[Definition 9 of arXiv:2609.01965, 'A logarithmic Bogomolov--Sommese vanishing theorem on compact K\"ahler manifolds'] Let $(X,\omega)$ be a compact K\"ahler manifold of dimension $n$ and $\{\alpha\}\in H^{1,1}(X,\mathbb{R})$ a $(1,1)$-class on $X$. Let $L$ be a line bundle on $X$.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(1)] $\{\alpha\}$ is said to be nef if for every $\varepsilon>0$, 
        there exists a smooth function $\varphi_\varepsilon$ on $X$ such that $\alpha+\ddbar \varphi_\varepsilon\geq-\varepsilon\omega$.
        One defines the numerical dimension of $\{\alpha\}$ to be
        $$\nd(\{\alpha\})=\max\{k=0,\ldots,n~|~\{\alpha\}^k\neq0 \text{ in } H^{2k}(X,\mathbb{R})\}.$$
        $L$ is said to be nef if $c_1(L)$ is a nef class.
        In this case, we define its numerical
        dimension by $\nd(L)=\nd(c_1(L))$.
        A vector bundle $E$ is called nef if the line bundle $\mathcal{O}_E(1)$ on $\mathbb{P}(E)$, the projective bundle of hyperplanes in the fibres of $E$, is nef.
        \item[(2)] $\{\alpha\}$ is said to be pseudo-effective if there is a quasi-psh function $\varphi$ such that $\alpha+\ddbar\varphi\geq 0$ in the sense of currents.
        One defines the numerical dimension of $\{\alpha\}$ to be
        $$\nd(\{\alpha\})=\max\{k=0,\ldots,n~|~\langle \{\alpha\}^k \rangle\neq0 \}.$$
        Here $\langle \{\alpha\}^k \rangle:=\lim\limits_{\delta\to0}\{\langle T^k_{\min,\delta\omega} \rangle\}$ 
        where $T^k_{\min,\delta\omega}$ is the positive current with minimal singularity in the class $\{\alpha+\delta\omega\}$ and $\langle T^k_{\min,\delta\omega} \rangle$ is the non-pluripolar product.
        We refer to \cite{BEGZ10} for more precise argument.
        $L$ is said to be pseudo-effective if $c_1(L)$ is a pseudo-effective class. 
        In this case, we define its numerical
        dimension by $\nd(L)=\nd(c_1(L))$, and there is a singular Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ such that $\image\Theta_{L,h}\geq 0$ in the sense of currents.
        \item[(3)] $\{\alpha\}$ is said to be big if there is a quasi-psh function $\varphi$ such that $\alpha+\ddbar\varphi\geq \varepsilon\omega$ for some positive continuous function $\varepsilon$ in the sense of currents.
        $L$ is said to be big if $c_1(L)$ is a big class. 
        In this case, there is a singular Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$ such that $\image\Theta_{L,h}\geq \varepsilon\omega$ in the sense of currents. 
        Note that a nef line bundle is big if its numerical dimension is $n$.
    \end{itemize}

[Theorem 1 (Degree--parameter envelope) of arXiv:2608.30304, '2608.30304'] For all $n\in\Nzero$, all $\alpha,\beta\ge-1/2$ and all $x\in[-1,1]$,
\begin{equation}
 F_{n,\alpha,\beta}(x)\le C_*\,\mathcal E_n(\alpha+\beta+1),
 \qquad C_*=1.2\cdot10^5.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\[
 F_{n,\alpha,\beta}(x)^2\le C_*^2
 \max\left\{1,S^{1/3},\frac{S^{1/2}}{(n+1)^{1/6}}\right\},
 \qquad S=\alpha+\beta+1.
\]
No attempt is made to optimise the numerical constant. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Mainthm t:1.2i of arXiv:2602.21277, 'A Limit in Law for the Cover Time and Last Visited Vertex of Wired Planar Domains'] There exists a coupling between
$\eta_{\rm D}$ from~(equation e:1.10i of the paper), $\mathcal Z_{\rm D}$ from~(equation eq:deflqgm of the paper) and $\overline{h}_{\rm D}$ from~(equation e:1.7p of the paper), such that $\eta_{\rm D}$ and $\mathcal Z_{\rm D}$ 
are related as in~(equation e:1.10i of the paper), $\mathcal Z_{\rm D}$ is measurable w.r.t. $\eta_{{\rm D}}$ and $\eta_{\rm D}$ is conditionally independent of $\overline{h}_{\rm D}$ given  $\mathcal Z_{\rm D}$. Under this coupling, if $(r_N)_{N \geq 1}$ satisfies~(equation e:1.11i of the paper) then
\begin{equation}

\big(\eta_{N,r_N},\, \overline{h}_N\,\big)
\underset{N \to \infty}\Longrightarrow \big(\eta_{\rm D},\, \overline{h}_{\rm D} \big) \,,
\end{equation}
with the underlying space for the first component taken as in~(equation e:1.10i of the paper). In particular, the joint law of $\eta_{\rm D}$, $\mathcal Z_D$ and $\overline{h}_{\rm D}$ in any such coupling is the same. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2511.14757, 'A weak convergence approach to the large deviations of the dynamic Schr\"odinger problem'] Assume Assumptions \ref{ass:b-sigma-local-properties}-\ref{ass:log-gradient-convergence} hold and fix $x,y$. For $F$ bounded and continuous, the sequence $\{ X^{\eta, xy} \} _\eta $ of bridge processes satisfies 
\begin{align*}
    \lim _{\eta \to 0} -\eta \log \mathbb{E} \left[ \exp\left\{ -\frac{1}{\eta} F(X^{\eta, xy}) \right\} \right] = \inf _{\varphi \in \calC _1} \left[ F(\varphi) + \inf _{\calU _\varphi} \frac{1}{2} \int _0 ^1 | \nu _s | ^2 ds  \right].
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:Plancherel-Polya of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact and let $r>0$. There is a
constant $C=C(K,r)$ such that
\[
    \sum_{p\in P}|f(p)|^2
    \leq
    C\|f\|_2^2
\]
for every $r$-separated set $P\subset\mathbb R^d$ and every
$f\in PW_K$.
