[Lemma lem:uniform_bound of arXiv:2609.01984, 'Instantaneous shrinking of supports for stochastic PDEs\footnote{JY was supported by a KIA'] Let $\tau\le T$ be a bounded stopping time. Recall the parameters $\gamma$ and $p$ from Assumption (asp:sigma of the paper) and (equation eq:asp_initial_regularity of the paper), respectively. Assume in addition that one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm (a)]
$p\gamma\ge1$ and
\[
    \mathbb{E}\int_{\mathbb{R}}u_0(x)\,\mathrm{d} x<\infty;
\]

\item[\rm (b)]
$p\gamma<1$, and for some $q>0$,
\[
    p\gamma>\frac1{q+1},
    \qquad
    \mathbb{E}\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+x^2)^{q/2}u_0(x)\,\mathrm{d} x<\infty .
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then there exists a constant $N>0$, independent of $n$, such that
\[
\sup_{n\ge1}
\mathbb{E}\left[
\sup_{\substack{0\le t\le\tau\\x\in\mathbb{R}}}v_n(t,x)
+
\sup_{\substack{0\le t\le\tau\\x\in\mathbb{R}}}w_n(t,x)
\right]
\le N .
\]
title: Lemma lem:uniform_bound of arXiv:2609.01984

body:
[Definition 3 of arXiv:2608.30089, 'On the Coefficients of Hurwitz-Type Matrix Polynomials'] Let \(\kappa\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}\), and let
\((\widetilde s_j)_{j=0}^{2\kappa}\) be a sequence of complex
\(q\times q\) matrices. For each \(n\in\mathbb N_0\), define the
block Hankel matrix
\[
H_n^{(\widetilde s)}
:=
(\widetilde s_{j+k})_{j,k=0}^{n}.
\]

The sequence
\((\widetilde s_j)_{j=0}^{2\kappa}\)
is called \emph{Hankel positive definite} if
\(H_n^{(\widetilde s)}\) is Hermitian positive definite for every
\(n\le\kappa\).

A sequence \((P_k)_{k=0}^{\kappa}\) of complex
\(q\times q\) matrix polynomials is called a
\emph{monic left orthogonal system of matrix polynomials with respect
to \((\widetilde s_j)_{j=0}^{2\kappa}\)} if the following conditions
are fulfilled:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(I)]
\(\deg P_k=k\) for all \(k\in\mathbb Z_{0,\kappa}\).
\item[(II)]
The leading coefficient of \(P_k\) is \(I_q\).
\item[(III)]
\[
Z_n^{[P_j]}
H_n^{(\widetilde s)}
\bigl(Z_n^{[P_k]}\bigr)^*
=
0_{q\times q},
\]
for all \(j\neq k\), where
\(n=\max\{j,k\}\).
\end{itemize}

[Defi kesten of arXiv:2607.01877, 'Coupling some conditioned L\'evy trees with the Kesten tree'] Let  $\psi$   be  a   branching  mechanism  satisfying~(equation eq:hyp-param of the paper)-(equation eq:grey of the paper).   Let
  $(h_i, {\mathcal T}_i)_{i\in  I}$ be the  atoms of  a Poisson point  measure on
  $\llbracket 0, \infty  \rrparenthesis \times  {\mathbb T}$ with intensity  ${\rm d} h \, {\mathbf N}^\psi[{\rm d}  {\mathcal T}]$ (and
  ${\mathbf N}^\psi$ given in~(equation eq:def-bN of the paper)).  The  Kesten tree ${\mathcal K}$, whose
  distribution is  denoted ${\mathbb P}^\psi$,  is a ${\mathbb T}$-valued  random variable
  defined as the infinite branch (or  spine) $\llbracket 0, \infty  \rrparenthesis$, on which the ${\mathcal T}_i$ are
  grafted at height $h_i$, that is:
\[
  {\mathcal K}= \llbracket 0, \infty  \rrparenthesis  \circledast_{i\in
    I}( {\mathcal T}_i,h_i).
\]

[Lemma lm:predual and ideal of arXiv:2609.00970, 'The unique predual problem for Lipschitz spaces, revisited'] Let $Y\subset\Lip_0(M)^*$ be a predual of $\Lip_0(M)$. Let $N\subset M$ be such that $0\in N$ and suppose that
\begin{enumerate}[label={\upshape{(\roman*)}}]
\item $\mathcal{I}({N})$ is closed in the weak topology $\sigma(\Lip_0(M),Y)$ induced by $Y$, and
\item $\mathcal{F}({N})$ is the strongly unique predual of $\Lip_0(N)$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\mathcal{F}_M(N)\subset Y$.

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The all-one, or flat matrix, diagonalizes according to
$$\frac{1}{N}\begin{pmatrix}
1&\ldots&1\\
\vdots&&\vdots\\
1&\ldots&1\end{pmatrix}=\frac{1}{N}\,F_N
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
&0\\
&&\ddots\\
&&&0\end{pmatrix}
F_N^*$$

body: A U-statistic U_n with symmetric kernel h is said to be degenerate (or degenerate of order 1) if \zeta_1 = \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[h(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_m) \mid X_1]) = 0, so that h_1(x) = 0 almost surely. body:
[Lem subcritical-maximal-bound of arXiv:2607.21428, 'Subcritical percolation and network archaeology on random recursive tree substrate network'] Let \(\Gamma_n\) denote the contracted shortcut graph on blob labels.  If
		\(D\) is a component of \(\Gamma_n\), write
		\[
		\mathcal{C}(D):=\bigcup_{j\in D}\mathcal{B}_{n,j},
		\qquad
		|\mathcal{C}(D)|=\sum_{j\in D}W_{n,j},
		\]
		for the corresponding full component.  All maxima over \(D\) below are over
		components of \(\Gamma_n\).  Then
		\[
		\lim_{L\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}
		\mathbb P\left(
		n^{-p}
		\max_{D:\,D\cap[L]=\varnothing}
		|\mathcal{C}(D)|>\varepsilon
		\right)=0
		\]
		for every \(\varepsilon>0\).

[Prop 34 of arXiv:2609.02261, 'Quantization and process'] We have the following properties.
 
 i) For every bounded  operator  $A$ in $L^2(\R^n)$
 and for any   $f\in {\cal S}(\R^n)$,  
  
  $$ ( T_h Af) (X) = \int _{\R^{2n} }  \  {\cal P}_h (Y , X) \ 
   (\sigma_h ^{\rm ext}A) (Y, X)  (T_hf) (Y)  d\mu_h (Y) $$
   
where

   $$ {\cal P}_h (Y , X) = e^{ \frac {1}  {2h}
  < Y , X>_{\rm C}  } . $$
   
We denoted by $\sigma_h ^{\rm ext}A$  the Berezin symbol of $A$, 
   by $T_hf$  the  Bargmann transform of $f$ defined  by (\ref{Barg}), 
   and we set
  
  $$  d\mu_h (Y) = (2 \pi h)^{-n} e^{ - \frac {1}  {2h} | Y | ^2  } dY .$$
  
   
   ii) If a function   $\Psi (X , Y)$ 
  satisfies  $(\partial  _{x_j } + i \partial _{\xi_j }) \Psi  = 0$ 
and 
   
   \be  ( T_h Af) (X) = \int _{\R^{2n} }  \  {\cal P}_h (Y , X) \ 
  \Psi  (Y, X)  (T_hf) (Y)  d\mu_h (Y), \ee 
   
for all $f\in {\cal S}(\R^n)$, then
 $\Psi =  \sigma_h^{\rm ext} A $. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:C_bdds of arXiv:2605.15545, 'Crossover from subcritical to critical decay: \\ random walk, self-avoiding walk, percolat'] Let $d \ge 1$,
$x,\eta\in \mathbb{R}^d$, and let $\Lambda \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ be symmetric and positive-definite.
Suppose $\hat{b} = \sqrt{ \hat x \cdot \Lambda^{-1} \hat x} \asymp 1$ for all $\hat x$.
Then, for $d > 2$ we have
\begin{equation} 
\mathbb{C}(x;\abs \eta \hat x,\Lambda)    \asymp	B(x;\abs \eta \hat x)
\quad \text{with} \quad
B(x;\eta)=
\frac{ ( \abs \eta  \vee \abs x^{-1} )^{(d-3)/2} }{ \abs x^{(d-1)/2} }
\end{equation}
uniformly in $\eta$ and in $x\ne 0$.
If $d \le 2$ and $s_0 > 0$ is a given constant,
(equation eq:C-combo of the paper) still holds subject to the condition that $\abs \eta \abs x \ge s_0$, with constants that depends on $s_0$.
title: Lemma lem:C_bdds of arXiv:2605.15545

body:
Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T in B(X,Y). Then T is Fredholm if and only if T is invertible modulo compact operators, i.e. there is S in B(Y,X) with I_X - S T in K(X) and I_Y - T S in K(Y). Moreover, if T is Fredholm one may choose S (a Fredholm regularizer, or parametrix) so that I_X - S T and I_Y - T S have finite rank, namely the projection onto ker T along a closed complement and the projection onto a finite-dimensional complement of ran T along ran T; any such S is itself Fredholm with ind S = -ind T. For X = Y this says: T is Fredholm if and only if its class in the Calkin algebra B(X)/K(X) is invertible.
X and Y are Banach spaces
T is a bounded linear operator X -> Y
compactness of I - ST and I - TS (not merely boundedness) is what makes the criterion work

body:
[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Consider the setup described just above where we let $\Gamma^\C$ be a nested whole-plane~\clekp{}. There exists a unique (up to a deterministic factor) collection of resistance forms $\rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = ((\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C}))_{k \in \N}$ that is measurable with respect to $\Gamma^\C$ and satisfies the following properties. There is a further collection of resistance forms $((\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^\C}))_{V \in \metregions}$ such that the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[I.]
 \item For each $k \in \N$ we have that $(\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C})$ is a local, regular resistance form on $\Upsilon_k$. Its associated resistance metric $\rmetres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}$ is topologically equivalent to $\dpathY[\Upsilon_k]$.
 \item Let $V_1,\ldots,V_n \in \metregions[k]$, $n \in \N$, such that $V_i \cap V_j = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$ and $\bigcup_i \ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k = \Upsilon_k$. Then
 \begin{align*}
  \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C} &= \{ f : f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k} \in \rfdomainres{V_i}{\Gamma^\C} \text{ for each } i \} ,\\
  \text{and}\quad
  \rformres{k}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} &= \sum_i \rformres{V_i}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{\Gamma^\C} .
 \end{align*}
\item If $V,V' \in \metregions[k]$, $V \subseteq V'$, and $f\colon \ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \to \R$ is a continuous function that is constant on each $\dpathY$-connected component of $\ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \setminus \ol{V}$, then
\begin{align*}
 & f \in \rfdomainres{V'}{\Gamma^\C} \text{ if and only if } f|_{\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_k} \in \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^\C} \\
 \text{and}\quad & \rformres{V'}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} = \rformres{V}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} .
\end{align*}
 \item For each open set $U \subseteq \C$, the collection of forms $(\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C})_{V \in \metregions[U]}$ is a.s.\ a measurable function of $\Gamma^\C|_U$.
\item For each $z \in \C$, we have
\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = \rform{T_{z}\cdot}{T_{z}\cdot}{\Gamma^\C+z} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $T_{z} f = f(\cdot -z)$ denotes translation by $z$.
\item There exists a constant $\resexp > 0$ so that for each $\lambda > 0$, we have
\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = \lambda^{\resexp}\rform{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{\lambda\Gamma^\C} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $S_{\lambda} f = f(\lambda^{-1}\cdot)$.
\end{enumerate}
The analogous statement holds for the \clekp{} Brownian motion. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let Omega be open in R^n and let u belong to H^1(Omega) (or W^{1,p}_{loc}). Then for every real k the truncation (u - k)^+ = max(u - k, 0) also belongs to H^1_{loc}(Omega), with gradient equal to the gradient of u almost everywhere on the set {u > k} and equal to 0 almost everywhere on {u <= k}. In particular the gradient of u VANISHES almost everywhere on every level set {u = k}, and |u|, u^+, u^- and min(u,v), max(u,v) of Sobolev functions are again Sobolev with the expected gradients. If u is in H_0^1(Omega) and k >= 0 then (u-k)^+ is again in H_0^1(Omega), which is what makes it a legitimate test function in the weak formulation.
u in H^1 (no continuity or boundedness needed).
Membership of (u-k)^+ in H_0^1 needs k >= 0 together with u in H_0^1;
for k < 0 the truncation need not vanish on the boundary and is not an admissible test function - a common oversight in De Giorgi-Nash-Moser and Stampacchia iterations.

Set $\epsilon=D_{\mathscr T^{\alpha,\mathscr C_+}_\tau}(M_{\tau_0}).$ Assume that $|\alpha|,\epsilon,T^{-1}\leq\epsilon_0, \tau+1\leq T_\alpha$, and $\tau_0\geq T$.

If $\epsilon>e^{-\frac{\tau_0}{8}}$, then
$$\left(\int_{M_{\tau_0+1}\cap B_{(1+\theta)R_\epsilon}(0)} d_{\mathscr T^{\alpha,\mathscr C_+}_{\tau+1}}^{2p}
e^{-\frac{|x|^2}{4}}\,d\mathcal H^n \right)^{\frac{1}{2p}} \leq C\epsilon,$$

e^{-\frac{|x|^2}{4}}\,d\mathcal H^n \right)^{\frac{1}{2p}}\leq Ce^{-\frac{\tau_0}{8}},$$
and $M_{\tau_0+1}$ is an $\frac{\eta}{4}$-graph over $\mathscr T^{\alpha,\mathscr C_+}_\tau$ on $B_{(1+\theta) \sqrt{\tau_0}}(0)$.

[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2606.07839, 'Bounds on Spectral Gaps for Non-Reversible Markov Chains with Applications to Temporal Dif'] Say that the system $(F,G)$ is controllable and all eigenvalues of $F$ have magnitude less than $1$. 
  \begin{enumerate}
      \item  $P$ is irreducible.
    \item  The unique invariant distribution for $P$, $\mu$, is a Gaussian with mean $0$ and covariance $S$, where $S\succ 0$ solves the linear Lyapunov equation:
\begin{equation}
  
  S=GG^\top +FSF^\top.
\end{equation}
\item 
  For all integers $m$ sufficiently large (in particular, for $m\ge n$) the matrix
  $$
  W = \sum_{i=0}^{m-1}F^i G G^\top (F^i)^\top
  $$
  is positive definite.
\item  For $m$ as above, let $A=F^m$. Then $S$ also satisfies the Lyapunov equation:
  $$
  S = W+ASA^\top.
  $$

\item   If $\tilde A =   S^{-\frac{1}{2}}F^{m}S^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $W$ is positive definite, then $\|\tilde A\|_2 <1$.
  \end{enumerate}

[Theorem 30 (Doubly exponential approach to one) of arXiv:2604.09933, 'Explicit cutoff profiles for colored top-\texorpdfstring{$m$}{m}-to-random shuffles'] Fix \(p\ge1\). As \(c\to-\infty\), equivalently \(\lambda\to\infty\),
\[
1-f_p(c)=\exp\bigl(-\lambda+o(\lambda)\bigr)
=\exp\bigl(-(1+o(1))\lambda\bigr)
=\exp\bigl(-(1+o(1))e^{-c}\bigr).
\]
In particular, \(f_p(c)\to1\) doubly exponentially fast as \(c\to-\infty\).

[Coro 15 of arXiv:2606.16164, 'A Low-Regularity Semigroup Sewing Lemma via Quotient Structures'] Let $\gamma\in(0,1]$, $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, and $h\in Z\hat C^{\gamma}(\Delta_T^3; B_\alpha)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every $\tau\in[0,T]$, the frozen defect $h^\tau$ defined in \eqref{eq:frozen-defect} satisfies $h^\tau\in ZC^{\gamma}(\Delta_\tau^3;B_\alpha)$. 

\item In order to construct a semigroup increment $R$ solving \eqref{eq:semigroup-sewing-eq}, it is enough to construct a compatible frozen increment family
$(r^\tau)_{\tau\in[0,T]}$ over $h$ such that the bounds in \eqref{eq:frozen-equivalence-subcritical-target} hold when $\gamma\in(0,1)$, or the bounds in \eqref{eq:frozen-equivalence-critical-target} hold when $\gamma=1$. 

\item Once such a family is available, the formula $ R_{ts}=r^t_{ts}$ defines a semigroup increment with
\[
R\in
\begin{cases}
E^{\gamma}(\Delta_T^2; B_\alpha), & 0<\gamma<1,\\[0.3em]
E_{\log}^{1}(\Delta_T^2; B_\alpha), & \gamma=1,
\end{cases}
\ \text{\, and\, }\ \hat\delta R=h.

body:
Let X be a Banach space over R or C, let K in K(X) be compact, let lambda be a nonzero scalar and set T = lambda I - K. Then: (i) ker T is finite-dimensional; (ii) ran T is closed; (iii) dim ker T = dim ker T' = dim(X / ran T) < infinity, where T' = lambda I - K' on the dual X'; in particular T is Fredholm with ind T = 0; (iv) ran T = {y in X : f(y) = 0 for every f in ker T'}. Consequently exactly one of the following holds: either lambda x - K x = y has a unique solution for every y in X (and the solution depends continuously on y), or the homogeneous equation lambda x - K x = 0 has a nonzero solution, in which case the solution space is finite-dimensional of dimension d, the adjoint homogeneous equation lambda f - K' f = 0 also has a d-dimensional solution space, and lambda x - K x = y is solvable exactly for those y annihilated by every solution f of the adjoint homogeneous equation (solutions then form an affine space of dimension d). In a Hilbert space H with K compact, the adjoint condition reads: lambda x - K x = y is solvable iff y is orthogonal to ker(conj(lambda) I - K*).
X is a Banach space over R or C
K: X -> X is compact
lambda is a nonzero scalar (for lambda = 0 every assertion can fail)
in the Hilbert-space form, H is a Hilbert space and K* is the Hilbert adjoint, so the relevant homogeneous adjoint equation uses the complex conjugate of lambda

[Lemma 19 (Growing-scale Fermi form comparison) of arXiv:2608.30211, '2608.30211'] Assume $\partial\Omega\neq\varnothing$.  There are $c_0,C,c>0$ such that,
whenever $1\leq R\leq c_0\kappa$, the following statements hold uniformly in
$\varrho\in[0,1]$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item If $G$ is a connected component of $D_\kappa\cap B_R(z)$, with the
original boundary carrying $\varrho$ data and the artificial boundary carrying
Dirichlet data, then
\begin{equation}
 \lambda\bigl(-\Delta-f'(\Phi_{\kappa,\varrho}),G,\varrho\bigr)
 \geq\mu_\varrho-C\left(\frac{R}{\kappa}+e^{-cR}\right).
\end{equation}
\item For every $p\in\partial\Omega$ and every half-space form function
$\Psi$ supported in $B_{3R}\cap\overline{\Hh^d}$ with, for some $C_1\geq1$,
\[
 \|\Psi\|_2=1,
 \qquad
 \int_{\Hh^d}|\nabla\Psi|^2
 +\beta_\varrho\int_{\partial\Hh^d}\Psi^2\leq C_1,
\]
where the boundary term is omitted at $\varrho=0$, there is an admissible
function $T_{\kappa,p}\Psi$ on $D_\kappa$ such that
\begin{equation}
 \frac{Q_{\kappa,\varrho}(T_{\kappa,p}\Psi)}
      {\|T_{\kappa,p}\Psi\|_2^2}
 \leq Q_\varrho(\Psi)+CC_1\frac{R}{\kappa}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

[Definition Xi of arXiv:2411.06089, '{\Large \bf Averaging principle for semilinear slow-fast rough partial differential equati'] Let $\mathbf B= ( B, B^2) $ be a $\mathscr{C}^\gamma([0,T];\mathbb{R}^d)$-valued random variable for $\gamma \in (1/3, \gamma_0)$ and $\{W_t\}_{t\in [0,T]}$ is a $m$-dimensional BM.
Define the ``enhancement" of $W$ by
$$W_{t,s}^2:= \int_s^t \delta W_{r,s} \otimes dW_r,  ~~~~ \delta W_{r,s}=W_r-W_s,$$
where the stochastic integration is understood in the sense of It\^{o} integral.
Sometimes we indicate this by writing $W_{t,s}^{It\hat{o}}$.
Then $\mathbf W=(W,W^2)$ is an It\^{o}-type Brownian rough path
and for any $\gamma \in (1/3, 1/2)$, $\mathbf W=(W,W^2) \in \mathscr{C}^\gamma ([0,T]; \mathbb R^m)$, $\mathbb P$-a.s..
Moreover, we define
$$I[B,W]_{t,s}=\int_s^t \delta B_{r,s} \otimes dW_r$$
as an It\^{o} stochastic integral, and then it holds that
$$I[W,B]_{t,s}=\int_s^t \delta W_{r,s} \otimes dB_r=\delta W_{t,s} \otimes \delta B_{t,s} -\int_s^t dW_r \otimes \delta B_{r,s} $$
by imposing integration by parts.
By now we have set all components of the random rough path $\mathbf \Xi=(\Xi, \Xi^2)$.

A shallow (two-layer) neural network functional $F_M: \mathbb{R}^d \times \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ with hidden width $M$, activation function $\sigma: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, and random Gaussian weights is defined by $F_M(x) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}} \sum_{m=1}^M a_m \sigma(\langle w_m, x \rangle + b_m)$, where $(a_m, w_m, b_m)_{m=1}^M$ are i.i.d. Gaussian random variables. Regarded as a function of the input $x \in \mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, $F_M$ is a random element taking values in the Hilbert space $K = L^2(\mathcal{X}, \mu)$ provided $\int_{\mathcal{X}} \mathbb{E}[\sigma(\langle w, x \rangle + b)^2]\,d\mu(x) < \infty$, for instance when $\sigma$ grows at most polynomially, of order $q$, and $\mu$ is a finite measure with $\int |x|^{2q}\,d\mu(x) < \infty$. Without such a condition it can fail: for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ and $\sigma(t) = t$, $F_1$ is a nonzero affine function, which is not square integrable.

If 
		$\theta (\eta^\ast) |\widetilde{\Delta}(\eta^{\ast})| \leq \mathcal C \widetilde{\psi}_w(\eta^\ast)  $

		\[

		\right\}

[Lemma lem:oco-lb-gadget of arXiv:2608.24731, 'Optimal Alternating Regret for Online Learning and Games\thanks{Authors are alphabetically'] The common loss $\ell_{\boldsymbol{u}}$ and the rare loss $ h_{\boldsymbol{u}, \alpha}$ are continuous and convex and take values in $[0,1]$. Moreover, $h_{\boldsymbol{u},\alpha}(\boldsymbol{u})=1$, and $h_{\boldsymbol{u},\alpha}(\boldsymbol{v})=0$ whenever $\langle\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v}\rangle\leq\cos\alpha$. For every $\boldsymbol{x}\in B_2(1)$, we have
\[
  (1-p_\alpha)\ell_{\boldsymbol{u}}(\boldsymbol{x})
  +p_\alpha h_{\boldsymbol{u},\alpha}(\boldsymbol{x})
  \geq p_\alpha.
\]
Finally,
$
  \alpha^2/9\leq p_\alpha\leq\alpha^2/4
$

body: For an m by n random matrix with iid mean-zero variance-one entries having finite fourth moment, with m/n converging to a fixed aspect ratio, the extreme singular values converge almost surely after sqrt(n)-normalization: the largest to 1 + sqrt(m/n) and (for m <= n) the smallest to 1 - sqrt(m/n), matching the edges of the Marchenko-Pastur support. The fourth moment is necessary for the largest singular value's convergence.

body:
[Theorem thm:n2 of arXiv:2607.08551, 'Weighted-threshold Coupon Collection'] Consider the Zipf family with $N=2$:
\[
w_1(s)=\frac{1}{1+2^{-s}},
\qquad
w_2(s)=\frac{2^{-s}}{1+2^{-s}},
\qquad s\ge 0.
\]
Fix $\theta\in(1/2,1)$ and set
\[
s_\theta:=\log_2\!\left(\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}\right).
\]
Then the expected quorum time has the explicit form
\[
\mathbb{E}[\tau_{2,\theta}^{(s)}]
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{w_1(s)}+\dfrac{1}{w_2(s)}-1\right), & 0\le s\le s_\theta,\\[1.0em]
\dfrac{1}{\lambda\, w_1(s)}, & s>s_\theta.
\end{cases}
\]
Moreover:
\begin{itemize}
\item the map $s\mapsto \mathbb{E}[\tau_{2,\theta}^{(s)}]$ is strictly increasing on $[0,s_\theta]$;
\item the map $s\mapsto \mathbb{E}[\tau_{2,\theta}^{(s)}]$ is strictly decreasing on $(s_\theta,\infty)$.
\end{itemize}
Hence global monotonicity in the aligned heterogeneity parameter is false.

If moreover \(M\) is a smooth manifold and

the category of rank-\(r\) smooth \(\Bbbk\)-vector bundles equipped
with flat connections.

 \begin{equation}

 \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

		{\mathbb E}\big[\big(|\bm{U}|_2-\sqrt{n}\big)_+^2\big]
		&\leq 2\mathrm{Var}(U_1^2) \leq 2\,{\mathbb E}\,U_1^4.
	\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 4 (Properties of the limit process) of arXiv:2606.27117, 'Occupation-Time Fluctuations of an Age-Dependent Branching System Driven by Poisson Immigr'] $\,$  
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item The limit process $\X$ is self-similar with self-similarity index
$\frac{3+\gamma-d/\alpha}{2}$, that is, for every $a>0$,
\[
\{\X(at),\ t\ge0\}
\stackrel{d}{=}
\left\{a^{\frac{3+\gamma-d/\alpha}{2}}\X(t),\ t\ge0\right\}.
\]
   
   
\item For every $0\le s<t$, we have $C(s,t)>0$. In particular, the covariance functional of $\X$ is strictly positive.
    
       
\item For every $0\le s\le t$,
\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{\gamma}\left(4-2^{3-\frac{d}{\alpha}}\right) s^{\gamma}(t-s)^{3-\frac{d}{\alpha}}
\le
\EE\big(\X(t)-\X(s)\big)^2
\le
\frac{2}{\gamma} (t-s)^{3-\frac{d}{\alpha}}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\X$ is not a semimartingale.
    
    
\item $\X$ has Hölder-continuous sample paths of any order less than
$\frac{3-d/\alpha}{2}$; that is, for every
\(
\varepsilon\in\left(0,\frac{3-d/\alpha}{2}\right)
\)
and every $L>0$, there exists a random variable $K_{\varepsilon,L}\ge0$ such that, almost surely,
\[
|\X(t)-\X(s)|
\le
K_{\varepsilon,L}
|t-s|^{(3-d/\alpha)/2-\varepsilon},
\qquad s,t\in[0,L].
\]

\item $\X$ is not Markovian.

\item $\X$ exhibits long-range dependence  in the sense that, for
$0\le r<v\le s<t$,
\[
\lim_{T\to\infty}
T^{d/\alpha}
\EE\big[(\X(t+T)-\X(s+T))(\X(v)-\X(r))\big]
=
\frac{2-d/\alpha}{\gamma(1+\gamma)}
(t-s)\big(v^{1+\gamma}-r^{1+\gamma}\big).
\]
  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:f.straight.spanning.trees of arXiv:2411.02046, 'Speed of Convergence and Moderate Deviations of FPP on Random Geometric Graphs'] Let $d \geq 2$, $r>r_c(\lambda)$, and~$\epsilon\in (0,1/4)$. Consider  FPP with i.i.d.\ random variables
    defined on edges of the infinite component $\Hh$ of  $\G$; assume (equation A1 of the paper) and (equation A2 of the paper) are satisfied. For any~$x \in \R^d$, there almost surely exists a finite set~$\mathscr F_x \subseteq \mathcal H$ such that the following holds. If~$u \in \mathcal H \backslash \mathscr F_x$ and~$\upgamma=(q_0,\ldots,q_n)$ is a geodesic started at~$q(x)$ with~$q_i = u$ for some ${i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}}$, then for all~$j \in \{i,\ldots, n\}$ we have~$\uptheta(u-x,q_j-x) \le \|u-x\|^{-\frac14+\epsilon}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Thm 14 of arXiv:2609.00723, 'An integral Hyodo--Kato isomorphism'] Put $(\sR/p)_{\red}:=(R/\sqrt{pR},N)$
 and let $\DA_R^{\str}$ be the category of strict Dieudonn\'e algebras over $R$ from \cite{BLM}.
There is a functor
\[
\mathcal W\uomega^*_{-/\sR}\colon
\mathrm{lPoly}_{(\sR/p)_{\red}}
\longrightarrow
\DA_R^{\str}
\]
characterized as follows. For
$\sP_0=(P_0,L_P)\in\mathrm{lPoly}_{(\sR/p)_{\red}}$, let $\sP$ be its
standard $p$-complete polynomial $F$-lift over $\sR$, and put
\[
\mathbf W_{\sR}(\sP_0)
:=
\WSat\bigl(\widehat{\uomega}^*_{\sP/\sR}\bigr)
\in(\DAlogSs)^{\str}.
\]
Then $\mathcal W\uomega^*_{\sP_0/\sR}$ is the underlying strict
Dieudonn\'e algebra of $\mathbf W_{\sR}(\sP_0)$.

Let
\[
q_{\sP}\colon
\widehat{\uomega}^*_{\sP/\sR}
\longrightarrow
\mathbf W_{\sR}(\sP_0)
\]
be the  unit map, and let
\[
e_{\sP_0}\colon
\sP_0
\longrightarrow
\left(
 (\mathbf W_{\sR}(\sP_0)^0/p)_{\red},L_P
\right)
\]
be its reduction on degree zero. For a morphism
$u\colon\sP_0\to\sQ_0$, the morphism
$\mathbf W_{\sR}(u):\mathbf W_{\sR}(\sP_0)\to \mathbf W_{\sR}(\sQ_0) $ 
is the unique strict logarithmic Dieudonn\'e
algebra morphism satisfying
\begin{equation}
(\mathbf W_{\sR}(u)^0/p)_{\red}\circ e_{\sP_0}
=
e_{\sQ_0}\circ u.
\end{equation}
Precomposing with reduction gives, in particular, a functor on
$\mathrm{lPoly}_{\sR/p}$.

[Prop IGgoup of arXiv:2604.12963, 'Shocks, instability, and the twenty networks\\ of infinite geodesics in the Directed Lands'] Let $\omega\in\Omega_0$. There exists a process $\bigl\{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}:\theta\in\Theta^\omega,(x,s)\in\IG\theta,{\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}\bigr\}$ of bi-infinite space-time paths such that the following hold for all $\theta\in\Theta^\omega$ and $(x,s)\in\IG\theta$.
    \begin{enumerate} [label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}] \itemsep=1pt 
    \item For each ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$, $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2$ is a continuous space-time path.
    \item For all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(t)\le \Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(t)$.
    \item For all $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$, $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(t)\in\IG\theta$.
    \item For all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, if $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(t)<\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(t)$, then $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(t)$ is right-isolated and $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(t)$ is left-isolated. Conversely, if $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(t)=\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(t)$, then this point is neither left- nor right-isolated.
    \item $(x,s)\in\{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(s),\,\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(s)\}$.
Moreover, $\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(s)=(x,s)$ if and only if $(x,s)$ is not left-isolated, and
$\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(s)=(x,s)$ if and only if $(x,s)$ is not right-isolated. 
    \item For any $r\in\mathbb{R}$ and ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$, $\Psi_{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(r)}^{\theta-}=\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}$ and $\Psi_{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(r)}^{\theta+}=\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}$.
    \item For any $(x',s')\in\IG\theta$ and ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$, either $\Psi_{(x',s')}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}=\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}$ or $\Psi_{(x',s')}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}\cap\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}=\varnothing$.
    \item For any $s'\in\mathbb{R}$, 
    \begin{align}
    \begin{split}
    &\Gamma\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(s')}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s',\infty)}\prec\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}\big|_{(s',\infty)}\preceq\Gamma\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta-}(s')}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s',\infty)}\quad\text{and}\\
    &\Gamma\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(s')}\dir{L}{\theta}{-}\big|_{(s',\infty)}\preceq\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}\big|_{(s',\infty)}\prec\Gamma\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta+}(s')}\dir{R}{\theta}{+}\big|_{(s',\infty)}.
    \end{split}
    \end{align}
    \item For any $s'\in\mathbb{R}$ and ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$, $\Upsilon\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(s')}\dir{L}{\theta}{+}\preceq\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}\preceq\Upsilon\from{\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(s')}\dir{R}{\theta}{-}$.
    \item For any ${\raisebox{-0pt}{\scaleobj{1.1}{\boxempty}}}\in\{-,+\}$,
$\displaystyle\lim_{|t|\to\infty}t^{-1}\Psi_{(x,s)}^{\theta{\raisebox{1.5pt}{\scaleobj{0.6}{\boxempty}}}}(t)=(\theta,1)$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon optimal unbiased selection, strictly positive-score specialization. Let X take values in a standard Borel space, let Z(X)>0 almost surely be measurable with E Z(X)<infinity, and fix 0<gamma<1. Among nonnegative randomized weights S satisfying E[S|X]=1 and E[P(S>0|X)]=gamma, the minimum of J(S)=E[S^2 Z(X)] is attained by S_star=I/pi_star(X), where I conditional on X is Bernoulli(pi_star(X)) and pi_star(X)=min(1,c*sqrt(Z(X))). There is a unique c>0 such that E pi_star(X)=gamma. The minimum is E[Z(X)/pi_star(X)]=E[max(Z(X),sqrt(Z(X))/c)]<infinity. Every minimizer has this same retention probability almost surely and has constant weight 1/pi_star(X) on its retained observations, conditional on X. Uniform random retention has objective E Z/gamma; the optimal objective is strictly smaller unless Z is almost surely constant. This is the convex allocation problem in Proposition4.2 and AppendixB of Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon, with the strict-positive-score restriction stated explicitly to avoid zero-score conventions. It optimizes an unbiased influence objective; it does not establish the asymptotics of a pruned max-margin estimator.
Standard Borel covariate; strictly positive measurable score almost surely, finite mean score.
Fixed retention fraction strictly between zero and one.
Conditional unbiasedness and the mean positive-weight retention budget; no claim about estimator asymptotics.

[Ppn 1 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix parameters $\alpha, L, r,s, \iota, \epsilon$. As above, let $\omega$ denote a random variable, and let $\bG, \bXi$ be $M\times N$ matrices with i.i.d.\ standard gaussian entries, with rows $\barbg^1,\ldots,\barbg^M$ and $\bmeta^1,\ldots,\bmeta^M$ respectively, such that $\bXi$ is independent of $(\bG,\omega)$. Let $\bar{\bx} = \bar{\bx}(\bG)$ and $\hat{\by} = \hat{\by}(\bG, \bXi)$ be $L$-Lipschitz, $\R^N$-valued functions such that 
\begin{align*}
    &\E \|\bar{\bx}\|^2 = \E \|\hat{\by}\|^2 = N\,, \\ 
    &\E(\hat{\by}\,|\,\bG) = \bzero\,\,\text{almost surely}\,.
\end{align*} As in \eqref{e:fp-partition}, let $ \hat{\cB} = \hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)$ be a random partition of $[M]$ and $[N]$ into $r$ and $s$ parts respectively, with proportions $\lambda(\bG,\omega),\mu(\bG,\omega)$ as in \eqref{e:lambda-mu-random}. Assume these proportions satisfy condition~\eqref{e:def-Lambda}, so that $r,s$ must satisfy condition~\eqref{e:r-s-bd}. Then, for all sufficiently large $N$,  we have
    \beq
        
        \sum_{j=1}^r
        \lambda_j(\bG,\omega) \,
        \Cost(\bbb_j,\uuu_j,\vvv_j)
        \le \frac1\alpha
         \bigg(
            \sum_{j=1}^s
            \mu_j(\bG,\omega)
            (\www_j)^{1/2}
        \bigg)^2
        + \epsilon
    \eeq
with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$, where $c$ is a positive constant depending on the parameters $\alpha, L, \iota, \epsilon$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $\eta>0$, $n,k,d\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge k$, and $d\ge2$. There exists a
constant $C(\eta,k,d,n)>0$, depending only on $\eta,k,d,n$, such that, for
every absolutely continuous log-concave measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^n$ and
every
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\in\mathcal P_d(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^k)$
such that
\[
\sigma_{f_j}^2:=\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f_j)>0
\quad
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\},
\]
and
\[
\det \Sigma_\mu^d(f)\ge \eta,
\]
the following two estimates hold.

First, for every $\psi\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^k)$ satisfying $0\le\psi\le1$,
one has
\[
\bigl(\sigma_{f_1}^2\cdot\ldots\cdot\sigma_{f_k}^2\bigr)^{\frac{1}{2(k(d-1)+1)}}
\int_{\mathbb R^n}\psi(f)\,d\mu
\le
C(\eta,k,d,n)
\|\psi\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^k)}^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+1}}.
\]
Second, for every unit vector $\theta\in\mathbb R^k$, every $t>0$, and every
$\varphi\in C_b^\infty(\mathbb R^k)$ satisfying
\[
\|\varphi\|_\infty\le t,
\quad
\|\partial_\theta\varphi\|_\infty\le 1,
\]
one has
\[
\bigl(\sigma_{f_1}^2\cdot\ldots\cdot\sigma_{f_k}^2\bigr)^{\frac{1}{2(k(d-1)+1)}}
\biggl|
\int_{\mathbb R^n}(\partial_\theta\varphi)(f)\,d\mu
\biggr|
\le
C(\eta,k,d,n)t^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+1}}
\biggl(\sum_{j=1}^k\sigma_{f_j}^2\biggr)^{\frac{k-1}{2(k(d-1)+1)}}.
\]

[Definition of arXiv:2411.09075, 'Weak Poincar{\'e} Inequalities, Simulated Annealing, and Sampling from Spherical Spin Glas'] We say $\pi$ satisfies a \emph{weak \Poincare inequality} if for some error functional $\Error: \R_{>0}^{\Omega} \to \R_{\ge 0}$ and $\CPoi > 0$,
    \[
        \Var_{\pi} [f] \le \frac{1}{\CPoi}\cdot\calE(f, f) + \Error(f)\mper
    \]
    Similarly, we say $\pi$ satisfies a \emph{weak modified log-Sobolev inequality} if for some error functional $\Error : \R_{> 0}^{\Omega} \to \R_{\ge 0}$ and $\MLSI \ge 0$,
    \[
        \Ent_{\pi}[f] \le \frac{1}{\MLSI} \cdot \calE(f, \log f) + \Error(f).
    \]

DRAFT: independent verification pending. On the nearest-neighbor ladder Z x {0,1} with iid Uniform[1,2] edge weights, almost surely a bigeodesic uses one of the two edges across the cut between columns 0 and 1. Every geodesic from (-n,0) to (n,0) crosses that finite cut; an infinite subsequence shares one cut edge, and anchored diagonal compactness yields a bigeodesic. By row symmetry each cut edge has bigeodesic probability at least 1/2. Deleting either cut edge leaves the graph connected. Its conditional deleted-edge capacity therefore exceeds the weight support infimum a=1 with positive probability. This is a control outside Z^2, showing that planarity, atomless iid weights, and properness alone cannot establish support collapse; it does not refute P0117.
Ladder graph Z x {0,1}, not the full Z^2 target
Iid Uniform[1,2] weights

[Proposition prop: poly_internal of arXiv:2512.06640, 'Existence and sharpness of the phase transition for the frog model on transitive graphs'] Let $G$ be a quasi-transitive graph that is of superlinear polynomial growth. Then, there exist positive constants $C = C(\lambda, G)$ and $c = c(\lambda,  G)$ such that, for any $x \in V$, $a > C^{\star}(\lambda,G)>1$, and $A \subseteq B_x(a)$, we have
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb P_{\lambda, a^2} \left( \mathcal{G}_{B_x(a)} \cap A = \varnothing \right) \le C \exp(-c \, |A|) \, . 
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop: poly_internal of arXiv:2512.06640

[Defn def.Stab.Radius of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Given  a marking  function $\xi :
W_n \times\mathbb{K}\times\hat{\mathcal{N}}_{W_n \times \mathbb{K} }\longrightarrow \mathbb{K}'$, 
 $n\in\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$ (as usual for $n=\infty$, we take $W_\infty:=\mathbb{R}^d$) and $(x,u)\in\tilde{\mu} \in\mathcal{N}_{W_n \times \mathbb{K}}$  we 
define the radius of stabilization $R_{W_n}^\xi((x,u);\tilde{\mu})$ 
to be the smallest $r \in \mathbb{N}$    such that
\begin{equation}
\xi((x,u), \tilde{\mu} \cap B_r(x)) = \xi((x,u), (\tilde{\mu} \cap B_r(x)) \cup ( \tilde \nu \cap B^c_r(x))) \,
\end{equation}
for  all $\tilde\nu\in \mathcal{N}_{W_n \times \mathbb{K}}$. The definition is naturally extended to $\tilde{\mu} \in\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}}$ by setting $R_{W_n}^\xi((x,u);\tilde{\mu}) := R_{W_n}^\xi((x,u);\tilde{\mu} \cap W_n)$.
title: Radius of stabilization

body:
Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a standard probability space, let G be a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m, and let phi : X -> G be measurable (the cocycle generator). The G-extension, or skew product, is the transformation

  T_phi(x, g) = (T x, phi(x) g)   on   (X x G, B x Borel(G), mu x m).

It preserves mu x m: for fixed x the fibre map g -> phi(x) g is a left translation, and Haar measure on a compact group is left invariant (compactness is what makes Haar a probability measure, so that mu x m is a probability measure). Iterating, T_phi^n(x, g) = (T^n x, phi_n(x) g) with the cocycle phi_n(x) = phi(T^{n-1} x) * ... * phi(T x) * phi(x), which satisfies the cocycle identity phi_{n+k}(x) = phi_k(T^n x) * phi_n(x).

Two standard obstructions to ergodicity are built into the definition. (i) If phi takes values in a proper closed subgroup H of G, then every set of the form X x (union of right cosets H g) is T_phi-invariant, so T_phi is not ergodic. (ii) More generally if there is a measurable u : X -> G with phi(x) = u(T x)^{-1} h(x) u(x) for h taking values in a proper closed subgroup, the same conclusion holds after the measurable change of coordinates (x, g) -> (x, u(x) g); cocycles differing in this way are called cohomologous, and ergodicity of T_phi depends only on the cohomology class. Note the sides: with the convention above the cocycle acts by LEFT translation and the invariant objects are RIGHT cosets; the opposite convention T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, g phi(x)) swaps them, and mixing the two conventions is the usual source of sign/side errors in the ergodicity criteria.
(X, B, mu, T) is a measure-preserving system on a standard (Lebesgue) probability space
G is a compact metrizable group, m its normalized Haar measure
phi : X -> G is Borel measurable
the fibre action is by left translation, T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, phi(x) g)
title: Group extension (skew product) of a measure-preserving system by a compact group

body:
[Theorem 20 (WUSH: a model-optimal adaptive block transform \citep{chen2025wush}) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Under a stochastic model of the per-group AbsMax block quantizer, block losses
approximated as independent, matrix columns treated as i.i.d.\ samples, and
quantization modeled as \emph{unbiased} noise (multiplicative i.i.d.\ for the
floating-point grid, max-scaled i.i.d.\ for the integer grid), with the bilateral
loss split to first order, there is a closed-form, data-aware blockwise transform
that is \emph{optimal} for the FP-AbsMax model and \emph{$d^{o(1)}$-near-optimal}
for the INT-AbsMax model on zero-mean Gaussian or Laplacian data (within a factor
$d$ for arbitrary distributions), among all invertible block-diagonal
transforms, $d$ here being the transform's block dimension, which the
source sets equal to the quantization group size $G$ of \Cref{tab:notation}. It combines a data-dependent whitening/balancing component with a
Hadamard factor applied \emph{after} it, so the Hadamard acts on the
already-whitened representation rather than as the raw-element flattening of
\Cref{prop:rht}. The optimality is of the \emph{model}; the source paper then
applies the resulting transform to deterministic rounding (both round-to-nearest
and GPTQ error-feedback) and reports that the advantage transfers empirically. Its full construction we give with the
rest of the non-orthogonal family in \Cref{sec:tax-affine}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: WUSH: a model-optimal adaptive block transform \citep{chen2025wush}

For complex matrices A (n by n) and B (m by m), S(X) = AX - XB on n by m matrices X, and the Frobenius separation is sep_F(A, B) = min over ||X||_F = 1 of ||AX - XB||_F. If A(t), B(t), C(t) are differentiable with spec A(t) and spec B(t) disjoint and X(t) solves A X - X B = C, then S(X') = C' - A' X + X B' and ||X'||_F <= (||C'||_F + (||A'||_2 + ||B'||_2) ||X||_F) / sep_F(A, B). With C fixed, the relative rate is at most (||A'||_2 + ||B'||_2) / sep_F.

[Defn 39 of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Define the \textbf{distance} between two SRI chains $\br,\br'\in \mathcal E_{k\times d}^{\mathrm{SRI}}(q,M,F)$ by $$d_{\mathrm{SRI}} (\br,\br'):= \sup_{\x\in I^k} \| \br(\x,\bullet) - \br' (\x,\bullet)\|_{TV}.$$
    We do not impose that $\br,\br'$ have the same base measure $\nu$, though $(q,M,F)$ will always be the same and fixed for any two SRIs that we compare. We say that a sequence of SRI chains $\brn$ \textbf{converges} as $N\to \infty$ to an SRI chain $\br$ if $d_{\mathrm{SRI}} (\br,\brn) \to 0$ as $N\to \infty$.
title: Definition 39 of arXiv:2510.22155

Let 1 <= p, q, r <= infinity satisfy 1/p + 1/q = 1 + 1/r. If f is in L^p(R^n) and g is in L^q(R^n) (Lebesgue measure), then the integral (f * g)(x) = int_{R^n} f(x-y) g(y) dy converges absolutely for almost every x (for every x when r = infinity, i.e. 1/p + 1/q = 1), f * g is measurable, and ||f * g||_r <= ||f||_p ||g||_q. Special cases: p = 1, q = r arbitrary gives ||f * g||_q <= ||f||_1 ||g||_q; 1/p + 1/q = 1 gives ||f * g||_infinity <= ||f||_p ||g||_q with f * g uniformly continuous and (if p, q < infinity) vanishing at infinity. The same statement holds on any locally compact abelian group with Haar measure. The constant 1 is not optimal on R^n: for 1 < p, q, r < infinity the sharp constant (Beckner; Brascamp-Lieb) is (A_p A_q A_{r'})^n < 1, where A_m = (m^{1/m} / (m')^{1/m'})^{1/2}.

1 <= p, q, r <= infinity
1/p + 1/q = 1 + 1/r

Take L^r norms in x and use the case p = q = 1 (Tonelli): ||f^p * g^q||_1 = ||f||_p^p ||g||_q^q. Combining exponents gives ||f*g||_r <= ||f||_p ||g||_q. body:
[Defi ie real of arXiv:2507.20324, 'Non-existence of several random fractals in Brownian motion and Brownian loop soup'] Assume that $d=2,3$. Let $X_{0},X_{1},\ldots,X_{k}$ be independent Brownian motions in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ started uniformly from $\mathcal{C}_0$, and stopped upon reaching $\partial\mathcal{B}(0,e^{r})$.
Write
\[Z_{r,d}=Z_{r,d}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{k}):=\mathbb{P}(X_{0}\cap(\cup_{j=1}^{k}X_{j})=\varnothing|X_{1},\ldots,X_{k}).\]
For all $\lambda>0$, let $a_{r,d}=a_{r,d}(\lambda):=\mathbb{E}[Z_{r,d}^{\lambda}]$. Then, the following limit can be shown to exist.
\[\xi_{[d]}(k,\lambda):=-\log\lim_{r\to\infty}(a_{r,d})^{1/r},\]
which is called the intersection exponent.
title: Defi ie real of arXiv:2507.20324

body:
[Corollary cor:uniform of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] Assume $\pi$ is uniform on $S$, that is, $\pi(x)=1/n$.
Define
\[
  H(P(x,\cdot))=-\sum_{y\in S}P(x,y)\log P(x,y),
  \qquad
  H_{\min}(P):=\min_{x\in S}H(P(x,\cdot)).
\]
Then
\[
  \eta_{\mathrm{KL}}(P)\ge 1-\frac{H_{\min}(P)}{\log n},
  \qquad
  \gamma_{\mathrm{KL}}(P)\le \frac{H_{\min}(P)}{\log n}.
\]

\(
\varepsilon_2=\tfrac{1}{200}\min\{\rho,\lambda,1\}\varepsilon_1, \ \varepsilon_3=\tfrac14\varepsilon_2.
\)

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Connected FMSF on trees of finite cycle blocks Result: Suppose an infinite cactus graph is built from bridges and edge-disjoint finite cycles. Its free minimal spanning forest retains every bridge and removes exactly the unique largest-weight edge of each cycle. Each resulting cycle block remains connected. A finite block path between any two vertices remains connected after these deletions, so the forest is globally connected and acyclic. Check: A simple cycle in a cactus is one of its cycle blocks; there are no additional cycle constraints coupling two blocks. Continuous iid labels make every finite maximum unique almost surely. Obstruction: Uniformly bounded block diameters give a class roughly isometric to trees. General roughly-tree graphs can have overlapping cycles and need not admit this block decomposition.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0062-connectivity-of-minimal-forests-on-graphs-roughly-isometric-to-trees

[Define 5 of arXiv:2506.10522, 'On the Law of the Iterated Logarithm for $m$-dependent stationary random variables under s'] \begin{description}
  \item[ \rm (i)] ({\em Identical distribution}) Let $\bm X_1$ and $\bm X_2$ be two $n$-dimensional random vectors defined
respectively in sub-linear expectation spaces $(\Omega_1, \mathcal{H}_1, \mbE_1)$
  and $(\Omega_2, \mathcal{H}_2, \mbE_2)$. They are called identically distributed, denoted by $\bm X_1\overset{d}= \bm X_2$  if
$$ \mbE_1[\varphi(\bm X_1)]=\mbE_2[\varphi(\bm X_2)], \;\; \forall \varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^n). $$
 A sequence $\{X_n;n\ge 1\}$ of random variables is said to be identically distributed if $X_i\overset{d}= X_1$ for each $i\ge 1$.
\item[\rm (ii)] ({\em Independence})   In a sub-linear expectation space  $(\Omega, \mathcal{H}, \mbE)$, a random vector $\bm Y =
(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)$, $Y_i \in \mathcal{H}$ is said to be independent to another random vector $\bm X =
(X_1, \ldots, X_m)$ , $X_i \in \mathcal{H}$ under $\mbE$  if for each test function $\varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n)$
we have
$ \mbE [\varphi(\bm X, \bm Y )] = \mbE \big[\mbE[\varphi(\bm x, \bm Y )]\big|_{\bm x=\bm X}\big].$
 \item[\rm (iii)] ({\em Independent random variables}) A sequence of random variables $\{X_n; n\ge 1\}$
 is said to be independent, if  $X_{i+1}$ is independent to $(X_{1},\ldots, X_i)$ for each $i\ge 1$.
 \item[\rm (iv)](m-dependence) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be $m$-dependent if there exists an integer $m$ such that for every $n$ and every $j\geq m+1$, $(X_{n+m+1},\cdots,X_{n+j})$ is independent of $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)$. In particular, if $m=0$, $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is an independent sequence.
\item[\rm (v)](stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)\overset{d}{=}(X_{1+p},\cdots,X_{n+p})$.
\item[\rm (vi)](linear stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be linear stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $X_1+\cdots+X_n\overset{d}{=}X_{1+p}+\cdots+X_{n+p}$.
 \end{description}

[Theorem 27 of arXiv:2605.06556, 'Probability of Quota Violations in Divisor Apportionment Methods with Nonzero Allocations'] Let $A$ be a divisor method with divisor function $\delta$ that guarantees nonzero allocations on M seats and $n = 3$ states. Then, under the asymptotic uniform distribution on reduced population vectors $(1, x, y)$, with $1<x<y$,  the probability of a quota violation is the same as the probability of a quota violation caused by states guaranteed nonzero allocations and is calculated by:
$$P(A(1,x,y) \text { has a q.v.}) = \sum_{k = \lceil M/2 \rceil}^{M-1} M\left( \frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k + D(k)} \right)$$
where $k$ indexes the integer values of $\lfloor \tilde{q}_3 \rfloor$, where 
$$\tilde{q}_3 = \frac{2M}{3-3\tau}, \qquad \tau = \frac{\mathrm{mean}(1,x,y)-\mathrm{median}(1,x,y)}{\max(1,x,y)}=\dfrac{1 - 2x + y}{3y}.$$ and 
$$D(k) =\frac{(M-k)\delta(k-1)-k\,\delta(M-k-1)}{\delta(k-1)+\delta(M-k-1)}.$$
title: Theorem 27 of arXiv:2605.06556

Let z_k be an exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain on {1,...,N}, with p_ij=P(z_(k+1)=j|z_k=i). Fix real d-by-d matrices A_i, real d-vectors b_i and a constant alpha. Set H_i=I+alpha A_i and let xi_(k+1)=H_(z_k)xi_k+alpha b_(z_k). Assume xi_0 has finite second moment and that, conditional on z_k, the next chain state is independent of xi_k (in particular deterministic initial xi_0 with the natural chain filtration suffices). Define p_k^i=P(z_k=i), q_k^i=E[xi_k 1_{z_k=i}], Q_k^i=E[xi_k xi_k^T 1_{z_k=i}]. Then p_(k+1)=P^T p_k, q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i q_k^i+alpha p_k^i b_i], and Q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i Q_k^i H_i^T+alpha(H_i q_k^i b_i^T+b_i(q_k^i)^T H_i^T)+alpha^2 p_k^i b_i b_i^T]. For stacked q_k and v_k=(vec(Q_k^1),...,vec(Q_k^N)), columnwise vectorization gives q_(k+1)=H11 q_k+alpha(P^T diag(p_k) tensor I_d)b and v_(k+1)=H22 v_k+H21 q_k+alpha^2(P^T diag(p_k) tensor I_(d^2))b2, where b stacks b_i, b2 stacks b_i tensor b_i, H11_(j,i)=p_ij H_i, H22_(j,i)=p_ij(H_i tensor H_i), and H21_(j,i)=alpha p_ij[b_i tensor H_i+H_i tensor b_i]. In particular H22=(P^T tensor I_(d^2))diag_i(H_i tensor H_i); the update factor uses the departure state i. The raw second moment is sum_i Q_k^i and E||xi_k||^2=sum_i trace(Q_k^i); these Q_k^i are not centered conditional covariances. No irreducibility, stationarity, or zero stationary mean of b is needed for these finite-time identities.
Finite exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain with row-stochastic transition matrix P
Fixed finite real matrices A_i, vectors b_i and constant step alpha
Finite second moment of xi_0
Conditional independence of z_(k+1) and xi_k given z_k
Columnwise vectorization and stacking by chain state

Let V be a real or complex inner-product space and J(y) = <., y>, the functional x -> <x, y>. Then J is an isometry of V into its continuous dual V*, ||J(y)|| = ||y||, additive and conjugate-homogeneous (J(c y) = conj(c) J(y); linear in the real case). It is onto V* if and only if V is complete. On c00, the finitely supported sequences with the l2 inner product, ell(x) = sum over n >= 1 of x_n/n is continuous with ||ell|| = pi/sqrt(6); the supremum of |ell(x)|/||x|| over nonzero x in c00 is not attained, and no y in c00 has ell = J(y), since that would need y_n = 1/n for every n.

body: A linear operator T: X -> Y between Banach spaces is compact if the image T(B_X) of the closed unit ball is relatively compact in Y; equivalently, every bounded sequence (x_k) in X has a subsequence along which (T x_k) converges in Y. A compact operator is bounded. Facts: (1) the compact operators K(X, Y) form a closed linear subspace of the bounded operators B(X, Y), and compositions of a compact operator with bounded operators on either side are compact, so K(X) = K(X, X) is a closed two-sided ideal of B(X); (2) every finite-rank bounded operator is compact, and a norm limit of finite-rank operators is compact; when Y is a Hilbert space (more generally when Y has the approximation property) every compact operator is such a limit - for Banach spaces in general this fails (Enflo, 1973); (3) the identity of an infinite-dimensional Banach space is not compact (Riesz's lemma: the unit ball is not compact), so a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space is never invertible; (4) Riesz-Schauder theory: for compact T on an infinite-dimensional Banach space the spectrum sigma(T) is a countable (possibly finite) set whose only possible accumulation point is 0, 0 belongs to sigma(T), every nonzero spectral value is an eigenvalue with finite-dimensional generalised eigenspace, and for lambda != 0 the operator lambda - T is injective if and only if it is surjective (the Fredholm alternative: either (lambda - T) x = y has a unique solution for every y, or the homogeneous equation has a nontrivial solution, and then the inhomogeneous one is solvable exactly for y annihilated by the kernel of the adjoint); (5) a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues tending to 0 (the spectral theorem); (6) integral operators (Kf)(x) = integral k(x, y) f(y) dy with a continuous kernel on a compact domain, or with an L^2 kernel (Hilbert-Schmidt operators), are compact, and so is every diagonal operator on l^2 whose entries tend to 0. Compact perturbations preserve the essential spectrum and the Fredholm index (Atkinson).

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). Given that the long-only gain is the estimation variance the constraint removes at the rows the stack is scored on, the amount of constraint was chosen with the evaluation inputs: a blend w(t) between the simplex and least-squares stacks with t minimising the cross-validated calibration error plus the excess bootstrap variance of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows, and a per-row version t_i = 1/(1 + kappa v_i/median v) that leans to the simplex where least squares is uncertain. P24 (a) HELD: on EMIT the per-cell blend reads +0.08 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 39 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 t* is at or above 0.5 on 30 of 30 cells and the blend reads +0.66 vs least squares; (c) REFUTED: the per-row blend vs the per-cell blend is +0.70 on Y2 and -0.14 on EMIT overall; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P25, split C, SPLIT_SEED 11, the criterion uses no evaluation targets): P25 (a) HELD: on split C the EMIT blend reads +0.63 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 35 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend reads +0.84 vs the simplex (wins 30 of 30) and +0.65 vs least squares; (c) HELD: t* averages 0.34 on EMIT and 0.67 on OCO-2; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Bootstrap-size stability (P28, B = 16 against B = 8 on split B): P28 (a) HELD: t*(16) equals t*(8) on 86 pct of the 70 cells and is within 0.2 on 100 pct; (b) HELD: the blend's mean gain against the simplex moves from +0.08 to +0.06 on EMIT and from +0.83 to +0.83 on OCO-2, and the both-endpoints win count on OCO-2 is 30 of 30 at B = 16; falsifier (agreement below 50 pct or a gain moving by more than 0.5) not triggered. Break test: a fixed midpoint t = 0.5 matches the criterion on OCO-2 (+0.96 / +1.01 against +0.83 / +0.84 on the two splits) but loses 1.6 and 4.4 pct on EMIT where the criterion stays at +0.08 and +0.63 - the criterion's value is knowing, without labels, when not to leave the simplex; the EMIT shortfall against the hindsight-best t is the bias-shift term of the risk identity. Scarce calibration (P30, 240 of the calibration rows per cell, split B): P30 (a) HELD: at n = 240 the simplex beats least squares by +14.10 on EMIT (full calibration +8.83); (b) REFUTED: t* averages 0.22 on EMIT and the blend reads -2.61 vs the simplex; (c) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells and the simplex reads +2.27 vs least squares (full calibration -0.18); falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT) TRIGGERED.
the members' predictions on the rows to be scored are available (transductive setting); their targets are not
the blend w(t) = (1 - t) w_simplex + t w_leastsquares is linear in t, so the cross-validated and bootstrap predictions of every t come from the two base estimators' predictions; the criterion is the 5-fold cross-validated squared relative error on the calibration rows plus the excess pairs-bootstrap variance (B = 8) of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows

[Definition def_regular of arXiv:2608.09105, 'Longest convex chains with i.i.d.\ points'] Given a convex chain $\mathcal{C}$, let $f_\mathcal{C}\colon[0,1]\to[0,1]$ be the maximal convex function starting at $f_\mathcal{C}(0)=0$ and satisfying $f_\mathcal{C}(x)=y$ for every $(x,y)\in\mathcal{C}$.
That is, $f_\mathcal{C}$ is piecewise linear with corners at the elements of $\mathcal{C}$, and $f_\mathcal{C}(1)=1$ unless $(1,y)\in\mathcal{C}$ for some $y\in[0,1)$.

Given $\rho\in(0,\frac12)$, we say $\mathcal{C}$ is \textit{$\rho$-regular} if $f_\mathcal{C}(1-\rho)\geqslant\rho$ and $f_\mathcal{C}(1)=1$.
Otherwise we say $\mathcal{C}$ is \textit{$\rho$-irregular}. 
Note that if $\mathcal{C}$ is $\rho$-regular, then it is $\rho'$-regular for every $\rho'\in(0,\rho]$.
\hfill\ensuremath{\square}
title: Definition def_regular of arXiv:2608.09105

[Definition def:elem_diff1 of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] First, we associate to each labelled tree $\underline{\tau} \in \boldsymbol{\mathfrak{T}}$ the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}^{\underline{\tau}} \eqdef \bigotimes_{n \in N(\underline{\tau})} \R^{{\mcb{m}}}$. 
We introduce this notation since it is natural to write $j$-multi-linear functionals of the noise using duality pairings in $(\R^{{\mcb{m}}})^{\otimes j}$, and since in our trees each node will represent an occurrence of the noise.
We also write 
\[
\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}] \eqdef C^{\infty}\Big( (\R^{{\mcb{n}}})^{N(\underline{\tau})}, \R^{{\mcb{n}}} \otimes \mathcal{H}^{\underline{\tau}}\Big)\;.\]

The elementary differential corresponding to a labelled tree $\underline{\tau}$ will be a map $\underline{\Upsilon}^{\underline{\tau}} \in {\mcb{B}}[\underline{\tau}]$ inductively defined by setting, for $\underline{\tau}$ as in (equation eq:product_of_trees of the paper), and $x_{N(\underline{\tau})} = (x_{n})_{n \in N(\underline{\tau})} \in (\R^{{\mcb{n}}})^{N(\underline{\tau})}$, 
\begin{equ}
\underline{\Upsilon}^{\underline{\tau}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau})}) 
=
\big( \mathrm{d}^{k}V(x_{r(\underline{\tau})}) \big) \big[ \underline{\Upsilon}^{\underline{\tau}_{1}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_1)}),\cdots, \underline{\Upsilon}^{\underline{\tau}_{k}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_k)}) \big]\,,
\end{equ}
where $\mathrm{d}$ here represents taking a differential on $\R^{{\mcb{n}}}$.
The the base case for this induction given by the above formula when $k=0$, that is when $\underline{\tau} = \circ_{r}$, so
\begin{equ}
\underline{\Upsilon}^{\circ_{r}}(x_{r})
=
V(x_{r})\;.
\end{equ}
and we use the canonical isomorphism $\mathcal{L}(\R^{{\mcb{n}}},\R^{{\mcb{m}}}) \simeq \R^{{\mcb{n}}} \otimes \R^{{\mcb{m}}}$.

Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: Let h be harmonic on a finite domain containing the evolution, and stop the process before exit and after at most K jumps. The sum of h over all particle locations is a martingale: sleeping and waking do not change locations, and each jump has zero conditional h-increment. For superharmonic h the corresponding sum is a supermartingale. Consequently, any tight scaling limit for which these stopped quantities are uniformly integrable must preserve harmonic moments and satisfy the superharmonic quadrature inequality. Testing h=1 and h=-1 forces |A|=zeta_a*|Astar|; linear harmonic tests force equality of centroids. Check: The generator calculation is a sum of active-particle discrete Laplacians of h. The jump truncation and spatial stopping make optional stopping legitimate. Removing those stops is a separate step, not implicit in the displayed identity. Obstruction: No proof of tightness, uniform integrability, constant terminal density, or identification of the limiting support is obtained. Necessary moment constraints do not establish the conjectured limit.

[Defn def:rounding of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] For $z\in \mathbb{R}$, we denote by $\widehat{z}$ the unique point in $\varepsilon^{50}\mathbb{Z}$ satisfying $|\widehat{z}| \leqslant |z|$ and $|z-\widehat{z}|<\varepsilon^{50}$.
    This convention ensures that if $z\in J^{\delta}$, then $\widehat{z}\in J^{\delta}$.

    For any $0\leqslant k_1 < k_2 \leqslant n+1$ and any continuous path $\pi : [t_{k_1}, t_{k_2}]\to \mathbb{R}$, we define a path $\widehat{\pi} : [t_{k_1}, t_{k_2}] \to \mathbb{R}$ by setting
    \begin{align*}
        \widehat{\pi}\big|_{[t_{k}, t_{k+1}]} \coloneqq  \Pi_{(t_k, \widehat{\pi(t_k)}), (t_{k+1}, \widehat{\pi(t_{k+1})})}
        \qquad\text{for } k\in \llbracket k_1,k_2-1\rrbracket.
    \end{align*}
    In words, we round $\pi(t_{k_1}), \pi(t_{k_1+1}),\dots,\pi(t_{k_2})$ to $\varepsilon^{50}\mathbb{Z}$, then interpolate between these points with $\mathcal{L}$-geodesics (see also Figure (fig:noise-rounding-eps-times of the paper)).
    Note that if $\pi$ has geodesic-like local transversal fluctuations, then $\widehat{\pi}$ is a mesh path ((def:mesh-path of the paper)).
    Also, if $\pi$ is itself a mesh path, then $\pi=\widehat{\pi}$.

    In our applications,  $\pi$ will itself be piecewise geodesic, so we think of $\widehat{\pi}$ as obtained by \emph{rounding} $\pi$ to $\varepsilon^{50}\mathbb{Z}$.

body:
On the integer spine with unit conductances and a conductance-a dangling leaf at each site, a>0, project both vertices in a cell to its integer coordinate. The rate-one constant-speed walk has variance growth D_CS=1/(1+a), whereas the edge-rate variable-speed walk has D_VS=1. Electrical conductivity per cell is one for every a. The speed masses are respectively 2+2a and 2, so increasing leaf conductance slows the constant-speed walk despite nondecreasing conductivity. This is a periodic-network normalization example, not a counterexample to iid high-dimensional percolation monotonicity or its proposed critical exponent.

Positive dangling conductance a
Diffusion means coordinate variance growth per unit time

[Proposition 3 of arXiv:2608.19396, '\bf Penalisation of Two-Dimensional Brownian Motion'] For any $a > 0$, we have 
$$\mathbf{W}^{(2)} = \frac{1}{a^2} \int_0^{\infty} d \ell (W^{(2, \tau_{\ell}^{(C_a)})} \circ \tilde{P}_a^{(2, \log)} ).$$
 Moreover, for all $t \geq 0$ and all bounded, $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable random variables 
 $G_t$, we have 
$$\mathbf{W}^{(2)} (G_t \mathbf{1}_{g_{C_a} \leq t}) 
= \frac{1}{ \pi} W^{(2)} (G_t \log^+(|X_t|/a))$$
where $g_{C_a}$ is the last hitting time of $C_a$ and $\log^+$ denotes the positive part of the logarithm.

body: [Lemma 7 of arXiv:2609.02732, 'Conservation of mass for solutions of Leibenson's equation on Riemannian Manifolds'] Let $u$ be a non-negative bounded subsolution of (\ref{dtv}) in $M\times [0, \infty)$ with non-negative initial function $u(\cdot, 0)=u_0\in L^{1}(M)\cap L^{\infty}(M)$ and $A\subset M$ be measurable. Suppose that again $\sigma\geq pq$ and set $\lambda=\sigma-\delta$. Then, for all $r, t>0$, \begin{equation} \int_{A_{r}^{c}}u^{\lambda}(\cdot, t)\leq \int_{A^{c}}u_{0}^{\lambda}+\exp\left(-\zeta\left(\frac{r}{(||u_0||_{L^{\infty}}^{\delta}t)^{1/p}}\right)^{\frac{p}{p-1}}\right)\int_{A}u_{0}^{\lambda},\end{equation} where $u_{0}=u(\cdot, 0)$ and $\zeta>0$ depends on $p, q, \sigma$.

[Proposition prop:controller of arXiv:2411.06935, 'Correction to: Multivariate CARMA processes, continuous-time state space models and comple'] For the output process $\mathbf{Y}$ of a L\'evy-driven state space model of the form (P3.5) there exist a $p\in\mathbb{N}$ and matrices $\mathfrak{A,B,C}$ of the form 
	\begin{align}
	 \mathfrak{A} =& \left(\begin{array}{ccccc}
			0 & \mathbb{I}_m & 0 & \ldots & 0 \\
			0 & 0 & \mathbb{I}_m & \ddots & \vdots \\
			\vdots && \ddots & \ddots & 0\\
			0 & \ldots & \ldots & 0 & \mathbb{I}_m\\
			-\widetilde A_p & -\widetilde A_{p-1} & \ldots & \ldots & -\widetilde A_1
		\end{array}\right)\in M_{pm}(\mathbb{R}),\\
	\mathfrak{B}=&\left(0_m,\ldots,0_m,\mathbb{I}_m\right)^T\in M_{pm,m}(\mathbb{R})\text{ and}\\
	\mathfrak{C}=&\left(\begin{array}{ccc}\widetilde B_0, & \ldots, & \widetilde B_{p-1}\end{array}\right)\in M_{d,pm}(\mathbb{R})
	\end{align}
such that $\mathbf{Y}$  is the output process of  a linear state space model in controller canonical form 
	\begin{equation}
		\mathrm{d}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{G}}(t)=\mathfrak{A}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{G}}(t)\mathrm{d}t+\mathfrak{B}\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{L}(t),\quad \boldsymbol{Y}(t)=\mathfrak{C}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{G}}(t),\quad t\in\mathbb{R}.
	\end{equation}
	.

[Proposition 92 (Cutoff factors in the finite-cutoff construction) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] For every finite-cutoff component used in the solution map, the stochastic
cutoff factors occur only at the frequency legs listed below.  The difference
from the uncut component is a finite sum in which at least one listed factor
is replaced by $m_\Lambda-1$.  Hence every such difference is supported where
one listed frequency is at least $c_0\Lambda$.

\begin{center}
\normalfont\small
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}P{0.18\textwidth}P{0.29\textwidth}Y@{}}
\toprule
component & active stochastic cutoff legs & estimate used for the tail\\
\midrule
$\Psi_{a,\Lambda}$
& output/noise frequency $\xi$
& \Cref{lem:baseline-cutoff-tails}\\
$\Theta_\Lambda$
& $\eta$ and $\xi-\eta$
& \Cref{lem:baseline-cutoff-tails}\\
$V_{a,\Lambda}$, $\partial_tV_{a,\Lambda}$
& the two input legs $\eta$, $\xi-\eta$; an auxiliary comparison may also
  carry the output leg $\xi$
& \Cref{lem:first-picard-tail-integral,thm:first-picard-fullspace}\\
$\Gamma_{a,\Lambda}^{\chi,\rho}$
& third chaos: $\eta,\zeta,r$ and optional $\eta+\zeta,\xi$;
  first chaos: $r,-r,\xi$ and optional $\xi-r,\xi$
& \Cref{prop:cubic-third-spectral,lem:cubic-first-cutoff-tail,cor:localized-cubic-terms}\\
$\mathcal D_\Lambda^{a;b}$
& the contracted pair $\ell,-\ell$
& \Cref{prop:localized-diagonal}\\
$\mathcal B_\Lambda^{a;b,c}$
& the two Gaussian legs $\ell,r$ in the covariance synthesis maps
& \Cref{prop:principal-centered-block,lem:far-output,thm:resonant-operators}\\
$\zeta_{a,\Lambda}^{\chi,\rho}$
& only the legs inherited from $\xi_{a,\Lambda}$,
  $\Psi_{a,\Lambda}$, $\Theta_\Lambda$, and $V_{a,\Lambda}$
& the identity \eqref{eq:auxiliary-forcing-expanded} and the preceding rows\\
$\mathscr F_{X,\Lambda}^{\chi,\rho}$,
$\mathscr F_{Y,\Lambda}^{\chi,\rho}$
& only the legs of their displayed stochastic coordinates and operators;
  there is no projection of the full nonlinear source
& \Cref{prop:source-map-continuity,prop:finite-cutoff-reconstruction}\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

For a fixed-profile dyadic family, the distributional components converge
almost surely along the full sequence and the operator components converge in
the pathwise operator topologies of
\Cref{thm:resonant-operators}.  For an arbitrary admissible cofinal sequence,
the distributional components converge in every finite probability moment,
the centered operator components converge in the stated $L^p(\Omega)$
operator norms, and the resulting solution data converge in probability.  Two
non-nested cutoff families have the same limits.

Let (X, mu), (Y, nu) be measure spaces and T a map from a vector space D of measurable functions on X to measurable functions on Y. T is linear in the usual sense; T is sublinear if |T(f+g)| <= |Tf| + |Tg| and |T(lambda f)| = |lambda| |Tf| pointwise a.e. for f, g in D and scalars lambda. For 0 < p, q <= infinity: T is of strong type (p,q) with constant A if ||Tf||_{L^q(nu)} <= A ||f||_{L^p(mu)} for all f in D intersected with L^p; for q < infinity, T is of weak type (p,q) with constant A if sup_{t>0} t * nu({|Tf| > t})^{1/q} <= A ||f||_{L^p(mu)}, i.e. ||Tf||_{L^{q,infinity}} <= A ||f||_p; weak type (p,infinity) means strong type (p,infinity). By Chebyshev's inequality strong type (p,q) implies weak type (p,q) with the same constant; the converse fails (the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator is weak type (1,1) but not strong type (1,1)).
(X, mu) and (Y, nu) are measure spaces
T acts on a vector space of measurable functions containing the functions to which it is applied
0 < p, q <= infinity

\end{displaymath}
\item If $n\geq 2$ is even, 
with $n = 2 \operatorname{mod} 4$, then
$((1-f_{q}):\Phi^{n}:\, ,1)$
converges to $+\infty$ in probability.
\item If $n\geq 2$ is even, 
with $n = 0 \operatorname{mod} 4$, then
$((1-f_{q}):\Phi^{n}:\, ,1)$
converges to $-\infty$ in probability.
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] \textup{(i)} If $\mathfrak G(\mu)>0$ and $\limsup_{|x|\to\infty}(a(x)+\mu)<0$, then $\cA_\R+\mu$ satisfies the bounded maximum principle. The condition $\mathfrak G(\mu)>0$ is, in particular, implied by $\sup_\R(a+\mu)<H_d(q_0)$; the tail condition is still required.

\textup{(ii)} For every bounded $\Omega_0$, one has $B_{\Omega_0,\kappa}>0$ for all sufficiently large $\kappa$. Moreover $\mathfrak U_*\in\R$ and $\Lp(\cA_\R)\le\mathfrak U_*$. Put $\Lambda_*:=\max\{\|a\|_\infty,|\mathfrak U_*|\}$ and let $\gamma_*$ be a Harnack growth exponent depending only on $d,J,q_0,q_1,\|a\|_\infty,\Lambda_*$. If there exist $\beta_+,\beta_->\gamma_*$ such that
\[
\mathfrak U_*+\limsup_{x\to+\infty}\{a(x)+d(M(\beta_+)-1)+q(x)\beta_+\}<0
\]
and
\[
\mathfrak U_*+\limsup_{x\to-\infty}\{a(x)+d(M(\beta_-)-1)-q(x)\beta_-\}<0,
\]
then $\Lp(\cA_\R)$ is simple in the positive cone. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 6 (Silent intervals create atoms) of arXiv:2608.24294, 'Existence of densities and atoms for the running maximum of time-inhomogeneous jump diffus'] Assume that $\kappa:[0,T]\to\R$ is a deterministic measurable function, and that there exists $\delta\in(0,T)$ such that $\sigma(t,x)=0$ for a.e.\ $t\in[0,\delta]$ and all $x$,
and $\kappa(t)=0$ for a.e.\ $t\in[0,\delta]$.
Assume moreover that the drift coefficient is globally Lipschitz in the state variable (for instance, this holds under Assumption~\ref{ass:elliptic}\,\textup{(E1)} or Assumption~\ref{ass:jump}\,\textup{(J1)}).
Then $X$ is deterministic on $[0,\delta]$ and $\Xstar_\delta$ is a deterministic constant $m_0$.
Moreover,
\[
\Xstar_T=\max\Big(m_0,\ \sup_{\delta\le s\le T}X_s\Big),
\]
and hence $\law(\Xstar_T)$ may contain an atom at $m_0$:
\[
\Pbb(\Xstar_T=m_0)=\Pbb\Big(\sup_{\delta\le s\le T}X_s\le m_0\Big).
\]
If, in addition, the shifted post-$\delta$ dynamics satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:elliptic} (or Theorem~\ref{thm:jump}),
then the restriction of $\law(\Xstar_T)$ to $(m_0,\infty)$ admits a density (an explicit atom--density decomposition). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Silent intervals create atoms

[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2608.19151, 'Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning for Controlled Hawkes Jump-Diffusions'] Suppose Assumption~\ref{ass:standing}(S3) and
Assumption~\ref{ass:kernel_approx_strong} hold.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)]
    Let
    \[
        \bar\phi_K(\tau)
        :=
        \sup_{a\in A}
        \norm{\Phi_K(\tau,a)}_{1\to1}.
    \]
    Then
    \[
        \sup_{K\ge1}
        \int_0^T \bar\phi_K(\tau)\,\dd\tau
        <\infty.
    \]

    \item[(ii)]
    For every $K\ge1$, the scalar Volterra equation
    \begin{equation}
        R_K(t)
        =
        \bar\phi_K(t)
        +
        \int_0^t
        \bar\phi_K(t-s)R_K(s)\,\dd s
    \end{equation}
    admits a unique solution $R_K\in L^1(0,T)$. This solution is
    nonnegative and satisfies
    \[
        \sup_{K\ge1}
        \int_0^T R_K(t)\,\dd t
        <\infty.
    \]
\end{itemize}
title: Lemma 1 of arXiv:2608.19151

body:
[Lem 233 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Suppose $\cA_N$ is a $L$-Lipschitz algorithm.
	Then there exists $C(\alpha) > 0$ depending on only $\alpha$ and $c = c(\alpha,L) > 0$ such that
	\beq
		\P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}}
			 \le C(\alpha)
			\,\,\text{and}\,\,
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \le 2
		\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
	Furthermore, for any $k\ge 1$, there exists $C(\alpha,k)$ such that for all sufficiently large $N$,
	\beq
		\max\bigg\{
			\frac{\E[(\|\bG\|_{\op})^k]}
				{N^{k/2}}, 
			\frac{\E[\|\bx\|^k]}{N^{k/2}}
		\bigg\} \le C(\alpha,k)\,.
	\eeq
\begin{proof}
	By Lemma~\ref{l:wishart}, there exists $C(\alpha)$ such that 
	\beq
		
		\P\bigg(
		\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}}
		 \le C(\alpha)
		\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
Since the mapping $(\bG,\bg^\aux) \mapsto \|\bx\|$ is $L$-Lipschitz, the random variable $\|\bx\|$ is $L$-subgaussian.
	Combined with the equality $\E[\|\bx\|^2] = N$ from Definition~\ref{d:Lip}, this readily implies
	\[
		\P\bigg(
		\frac{\|\bx\|}
			{N^{1/2}}
		 \le 2\bigg) 
		 \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,,
	\]
which gives \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail}.
	By Jensen's inequality,
	\[
		\frac{\E\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}}
		\le 
		\frac{\E[\|\bx\|^2]^{1/2}}
			{N^{1/2}}
		 = 1
		 \,.
	\]
Since $\|\bx\|$ is $L$-subgaussian, for any $u\ge1$ we have
	\[\P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg)
		\le \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\| - \E\|\bx\|]}{N^{1/2}} \ge u - 1
		\bigg) 
		\le \exp\bigg(
			-\frac{(u-1)^2 N}{2L^2}
		\bigg)\,.\]
Integrating this bound gives
	\begin{align*}
		\E\bigg[\frac{\|\bx\|^k}{N^{k/2}}\bigg]
		&\le 2^k + \int_{2^k}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|^k}{N^{k/2}} \ge t
		\bigg) \,dt
		= 2^k + \int_2^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du \\
		&\le 2^k + \int_2^\infty \exp\bigg(-\frac{(u-1)^2 N}{2L^2}\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du 
		\le 2^k + 1\,,
	\end{align*}
	where the last inequality holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	Since the mapping $\bG \mapsto \|\bG\|_{\op}$ is $1$-Lipschitz, the random variable $\|\bG\|_{\op}$ is $1$-subgaussian.
	Then \eqref{e:confinement.wishart.restated} implies that $\E[\|\bG\|_{\op}] \le C(\alpha) N^{1/2}$. Then, by a similar calculation as above, we obtain
	\begin{align*}
		\E\bigg[\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}^k}{N^{k/2}}\bigg]
		&\le (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)^k}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}^k}{N^{k/2}} \ge t
		\bigg) \,dt \\
		&= (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg) ku^{k-1} \,du \\
		&\le (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)}^\infty
		\exp\bigg(
			-\frac{(u-C(\alpha))^2 N}{2}
		\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du
		\le (2C(\alpha))^k + 1\,,
	\end{align*}
	where the last inequality holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	This proves \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.moment}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 233 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Lem 14 of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Suppose that $m,k\geq 2$ and $\mathbf j=(\vec j_1,...,\vec j_m) \in \big( \{1,...,k\}\times \{1,...,d\}\big)^m$ such that all $\vec j_i$ are not the same index in the first coordinate, i.e., $(\vec j_1,...,\vec j_m)$ is not of the form $((i,v_1),(i,v_2),...,(i,v_m))$ for some $i=1,...,k$. Let $p\in \mathbb N$ be as in Assumption \ref{a1} Item \eqref{a23}. 
    \begin{enumerate}\item  If $m< 2p$ then $\kappa^{(m;k)}(\mathbf j;\mathbf x)=0$.
    \item  If $m= 2p$ then write $\vec j_r=(i_r,v_r)$ for each coordinate of $\mathbf j$. Then $\kappa^{(m;k)}(\mathbf j;\mathbf x)=0$, unless the set of indices $\{i_1,...,i_m\}$ is of the form $\{a,b\}$, where exactly $p$ of the indices $i_r$ are equal to $a$, and thus the other $p$ indices are equal to $b$.
    \item  If $m\ge 2p$, then there exists $C(m)>0$ such that $$|\kappa^{(m;k)}(\mathbf j;\mathbf x)| \leq C(m)\cdot \Fd\big( \min_{1\leq i <j \leq k} |   x_i-   x_j|\big). $$
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 14 of arXiv:2510.22155

[Defn def:discrete-LPP of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] For $z,w\in\mathbb{R}$, we define 
    \begin{align*}
        \widehat{\mathcal{L}}^\varepsilon(0,z;\delta^{3/2},w) \coloneqq  
        \max_{\pi:\widehat{z}\to\widehat{w}} \int_0^{\delta^{3/2}} d\mathcal{L}\circ \pi,
    \end{align*}
    where the maximum is over all mesh paths $\pi$ with $\pi(0)=\widehat{z}$ and $\pi(\delta^{3/2})=\widehat{w}$. 
    Note that the maximum is indeed attained, as there are only finitely many mesh paths connecting $\widehat{z}$ to $\widehat{w}$.
    Writing $u=(0,z;\delta^{3/2},w)$, we define the \emph{mesh geodesic} $\Gamma_u$ to be the mesh path attaining the above maximum (with ties broken in any deterministic measurable way).
title: Discrete LPP model

[Proposition equ:poisson-limit of arXiv:2507.19554, 'Full extremal process in four-dimensional membrane model'] Suppose that $N_k \rightarrow \infty$ and one has the following limit
	\bequ
		\eta_{N_k, r_k}\rightarrow \PPP\lp Z\lp dx \rp \otimes e^{-\pi t} dt\rp.
	\eequ
	Then, for each $t \in \mbR$, one has
	\bequn	
		\mbP\lp \max_{x \in V_N} h_x^{i} < m_{N_k}+ t \rp \rightarrow \mbE\lb e^{-\frac{e^{-\pi t} }{\pi}Z\lp V_N \rp}\rb.
	\eequn
	And if $M_N- m_N=  \max_{x \in V_N} h_x^{i} - m_N$ converges in law, the random measure $Z\lp dx \rp$ is unique. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2609.02193, 'State-law dynamics of McKean-Vlasov stochastic reaction-diffusion equations on $\mathbb R^'] Assume \textnormal{(A1)-(A4)}. There exist constants
	$\gamma\in(0,\lambda_0/2)$ and $C_H>0$, independent of
	$\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$, such that, for every $t\geq0$,
	$\omega\in\Omega_0$, $x\in H$ and $\mu\in P$,
	\begin{align}
		\left\|
		\varphi_H^\epsilon
		(t,\theta_{-t}\omega,x,\mu)
		\right\|^2
		\leq
		4e^{-\gamma t}\|x\|^2
		+4\epsilon_0^2e^{-\gamma t}
		\|z(\theta_{-t}\omega)\|^2
		+\frac{2L_G}{\lambda_0/2-\gamma}
		e^{-\gamma t}M_2(\mu)
		+R_H^2(\omega)-1,
	\end{align}
	where
	\begin{align*}
		R_H^2(\omega)
		=1+\frac{2L_GR_P^2}{\gamma}
		+2C_H\int_{-\infty}^{0}
		e^{\gamma s}\mathfrak z(\theta_s\omega)\,ds
		+2\epsilon_0^2\|z(\omega)\|^2.
	\end{align*}
	The mapping $\omega\mapsto R_H(\omega)$ is measurable and tempered.
	Hence
	\begin{align*}
		K_H(\omega)
		=
		\big\{u\in H:\|u\|^2\leq R_H^2(\omega)\big\},
		\qquad \omega\in\Omega_0,
	\end{align*}
	is a closed measurable random set belonging to $\mathfrak D_H$.

	Let $B_H\in\mathfrak D_H$, $B_P\in\mathfrak D_P$ and
	$\omega\in\Omega_0$. Then there exists $T=T(B_H,B_P,\omega)>0$
	such that, for all $t\geq T$ and $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$,
	\begin{align*}
		\left\{
		\varphi_H^\epsilon
		(t,\theta_{-t}\omega,x,\mu):
		x\in B_H(\theta_{-t}\omega),\ \mu\in B_P
		\right\}
		\subset K_H(\omega).
	\end{align*}
	Thus $K_H$ is a pullback absorbing random set for the state component in
	$H$, uniformly in $\epsilon\in[0,\epsilon_0]$ and in the
	initial laws in $M_2$-bounded subsets of $P$.

[Thm dig of arXiv:2609.03033, 'An Overview of Einstein $4$-Manifolds'] Let $(M,g_0)$ be as in Theorem (ntp of the paper), and let $N$ be a compact oriented 
manifold of the same dimension. If there is a
smooth map $f: N\to M$ of degree $\ell >0$, then 
any metric $g$ on $N$ satisfies
$$\hat{\zap h} (N,g) \geq \ell \hat{\zap h} (M,g_0).$$
Moreover, if $\dim M > 2$,   equality can only be 
achieved if $f$ is homotopic to a covering map which 
is a local isometry. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2604.06516, 'From stochastic individual-based models to free-boundary Hamilton-Jacobi equations'] For all $t>0$ and $x\in \R$, the family of laws $(\mu^K_{x,t})_{K\geq 1}$ satisfies a large deviation principle on $\mathbb{D}[0,t]$ with rate $1/\log K$ and good rate function $I_{t,x}$: for any subset $A\subset \mathbb{D}[0,t]$,
\begin{multline}
    -\inf_{f\in \mathrm{int}(A)} I_{t,x}(f)\leq \liminf_{K\rightarrow +\infty} \frac{1}{\log K} \mathbb{P}_x\big((X^K_{s\log K})_{s\leq t} \in A\big)\\
    \leq \limsup_{K\rightarrow +\infty} \frac{1}{\log K} \mathbb{P}_x\big((X^K_{s\log K})_{s\leq t} \in A\big) \leq -\inf_{f\in \mathrm{cl}(A)} I_{t,x}(f),
\end{multline}where $\mathrm{int}(A)$ and $\mathrm{cl}(A)$ are the interior and closure of $A$ for the Skorohod topology. \\
    In addition, the family of measures $(\mu^K_{x,t})_{K\geq 1}$ satisfies the Laplace principle with rate $1/\log K$ and rate function $I_{t,x}$ uniformly on compact sets with respect to $x\in\R$, as recalled below. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 9 of arXiv:2604.06516

    \end{itemize}

Let X_1, ..., X_N be random variables on one probability space with laws mu_1, ..., mu_N, and 1 <= k <= N. The family is k-wise independent exactly when, for every index set I with |I| <= k, the joint law of (X_i)_{i in I} is the product measure of the mu_i, i in I. It suffices to check the sets with |I| = k.
